text:
A new video showing Baltimore Ravens quarterback Lamar Jackson back at practice has provided an encouraging update on his NFL injury status ahead of the team’s Week 8 matchup against the Buffalo Bills.

Jackson has missed Baltimore’s last three games while recovering from an ankle injury suffered on October 4 against the Tennessee Titans. His return to practice on Wednesday offers hope that the star quarterback could be available for Sunday’s crucial contest, although the Ravens have yet to confirm whether he will play.

Head coach Jesse Minter previously offered an encouraging assessment of Jackson’s recovery, suggesting the quarterback could be approaching a return.

“I think he’ll be in a pretty good spot, but we’ll know a lot more on Wednesday,” Minter said on Monday.

Wednesday’s practice should provide the coaching staff with a better understanding of Jackson’s fitness and whether he can return to the starting lineup.

MORE: Colts player asks for a trade amid fire sale

Ravens hope Jackson can return against Bills

Jackson’s absence has been costly for Baltimore, which has lost its last two games after winning its first contest without him in overtime against Atlanta.

Backup quarterback Tyler Huntley showed some promise in Week 7, throwing for a personal-best 298 yards against the Cincinnati Bengals. However, he also endured a difficult afternoon, taking four sacks and throwing an interception in a 35-13 defeat.

The Ravens have struggled to maintain consistency without their starting quarterback, making Jackson’s potential return particularly important as the season progresses.

The 29-year-old has already missed three games this season and also sat out three contests last year because of a hamstring injury. Baltimore will be eager to avoid another extended absence for one of its most important players.

MORE: Jerry Jones reveals Cowboys trade deadline plans

Jackson’s return could boost Baltimore

Through four games this season, Jackson has completed 70.8 percent of his passes for 967 yards and six touchdowns, demonstrating his importance to Baltimore’s offense.

His ability to make plays with both his arm and legs provides the Ravens with an added dimension that has been difficult to replace during his absence.

Baltimore enters Week 8 with a 4-3 record after the first seven weeks of the NFL season and now faces a challenging road matchup against Buffalo on Sunday.

Although Wednesday’s practice is an encouraging development, Jackson’s availability remains uncertain until the team provides further confirmation. The Ravens will be hoping their franchise quarterback can return in time to help them get their season back on track.

title: Ravens list Lamar Jackson as full participant in practice - ESPN
authors: Jamison Hensley, Ben Solak, John Keim, Sarah Barshop, Marc Raimondi, Nick Suss, Liz Loza, ESPN Fantasy, Brianna Williams, David Dennis Jr
description:
-- Quarterback Lamar Jackson was a full participant in Wednesday's practice, an encouraging sign for the Baltimore Ravens heading into Sunday's road game against the Buffalo Bills.
It marked the first time Jackson had a full practice since spraining his left ankle 24 days ago.
Jackson, who has missed the past three games, briskly jogged onto the practice field Wednesday but did not run during the media viewing portion of the session.
Ravens offensive tackle Ronnie Stanley acknowledged it will be "a big boost" if Jackson returns against the Bills (5-1).
In 14 quarters with Jackson this season, the Ravens have scored 14 touchdowns.
text:
OWINGS MILLS, Md. -- Quarterback Lamar Jackson was a full participant in Wednesday's practice, an encouraging sign for the Baltimore Ravens heading into Sunday's road game against the Buffalo Bills.

It marked the first time Jackson had a full practice since spraining his left ankle 24 days ago.

"The more you're able to do and respond from and feel from certainly raises your optimism," Ravens coach Jesse Minter said Wednesday.

Jackson, who has missed the past three games, briskly jogged onto the practice field Wednesday but did not run during the media viewing portion of the session. With the ankle taped, Jackson moved around well when throwing passes to wide receiver Zay Flowers and handing the ball off to running back Derrick Henry.

Ravens offensive tackle Ronnie Stanley acknowledged it will be "a big boost" if Jackson returns against the Bills (5-1). Baltimore (4-3) is in last place in the AFC North.

"Lamar is the best player in the NFL, and we all know how good of a player he is," Stanley said. "But we also don't want to rely on him having to carry us as a team."

Baltimore has gone 1-2 with Tyler Huntley filling in for Jackson. The Ravens have failed to score in the second half in losses the past two weeks.

In 14 quarters with Jackson this season, the Ravens have scored 14 touchdowns. In 14 quarters without him, Baltimore has managed just five TDs.

"He's the heart and soul of this team [and] of the offense," Henry said. "So anytime he's out there, it's always great. I know he wants to be out there with us and to put us in the best position to win. He wants the guys to play great as well. So I'll be excited whenever he's back out there, and I look forward to it."

title: Feel the Pain!: Here's Where Packers Are in NFL Injury Rankings - Sports Illustrated
description:
The Packers have a lot of star power on their injury lists, and that’s reflected in Rotowire’s Impact Index.
Along with the possibility of standout receiver Matthew Golden missing the game with a shoulder injury, the Packers have three of the 13 most-impactful injuries this week.
Starters and Key Backups on Injured Reserve: Offense Here is the list of key injuries on offense.
Complicating matters, Skyy Moore, who had been Reed’s replacement, is on injured reserve, as well.
He might be headed to injured reserve, where he’d join his backup, Jacob Monk.
text:
GREEN BAY, Wis. – The injury rate in the NFL is 100 percent, as players like to say. Some injuries are more painful than others, though, and the Green Bay Packers have felt the sting of torn ligaments and sprained muscles more than anyone this season.

According to Rotowire, the Packers are the second-most injured team headed into their Week 8 home game against the Carolina Panthers. That’s just the number of injuries, though. The Packers have a lot of star power on their injury lists, and that’s reflected in Rotowire’s Impact Index.

From that perspective, no team is more impacted by injuries this week than Green Bay. That list is headed by All-Pro edge rusher Micah Parsons and budding star Edgerrin Cooper. Parsons hasn’t played this season due to last year’s torn ACL. The team’s biggest X-factor in replacing Parsons was Cooper, who suffered a torn Achilles in Week 4.

Along with the possibility of standout receiver Matthew Golden missing the game with a shoulder injury, the Packers have three of the 13 most-impactful injuries this week.

Starters and Key Backups on Injured Reserve: Offense

Here is the list of key injuries on offense.

Receiver Jayden Reed, the premier slot player who received a contract extension this offseason, suffered a season-ending back injury in Week 2. The Packers have missed his playmaking ability in the intermediate zones and his run-after-catch skill.

Complicating matters, Skyy Moore, who had been Reed’s replacement, is on injured reserve, as well. Savion Wiliams missed the first five games due to an ankle injury but has made a few impact plays upon his return.

What would really complicate matters is if Matthew Golden is out. “I sure hope so,” coach Matt LaFleur said on Tuesday about Golden’s status. He would not have practice on Monday or Tuesday; the team will get on the field for some individual drills on Wednesday, which will be important in determining Golden’s status for the game.

Running back Chris Brooks started the Week 4 game at Tampa Bay but went down with an ankle injury and was placed on injured reserve. Thursday’s game will mark his third game on the sideline.

Tight end Luke Musgrave suffered a neck injury during the offseason practices and there is no estimated time for a potential return.

Right tackle Zach Bako-Bewele suffered a season-ending knee injury one play after Reed was injured against the Jets. The Packers signed him to a huge contract extension before last season. By the end of this season, he will have played about 32 percent of the snaps over two years.

Center Sean Rhyan, who was re-signed to a lucrative three-year contract just before the start of free agency, suffered a high-ankle sprain on the fourth snap at Detroit. He might be headed to injured reserve, where he’d join his backup, Jacob Monk.

“We got some time yet before we determine that, I would say,” LaFleur said.

Left guard Aaron Banks never landed on injured reserve but the team’s highly paid left guard has played in 22 snaps this season due to knee and toe injuries.

Starters and Key Backups on Injured Reserve: Defense

Here is the list of key injuries on defense.

Edge Micah Parsons remains on the physically unable to perform list due to last year’s torn ACL. He might make his practice debut next week. Without him, the team’s four edge rushers have 5.5 sacks and 64 pressures in seven games. Detroit’s Aidan Hutchinson has five sacks and a league-high 42 pressures in six games.

Defensive tackle Javon Hargrave suffered a torn Achilles at the end of the Chicago game and will miss the rest of the season. He wasn’t great and perhaps not worth the contract, but he had six pressures in four games, which is one more than Devonte Wyatt in seven games.

Defensive tackle Warren Brinson, who looked primed for a Year 2 jump, missed the start of the regular season with a calf injury and then suffered a groin injury during his first week of practice. He’s on injured reserve and might not be back until late in the season.

Defensive tackle Jonathan Ford won a spot on the roster because of his stoutness against the run. He’s on injured reserve with a calf injury. Fortunately for the Packers, Jordon Riley made his season debut at Detroit after missing the first six games following last year’s torn Achilles.

Linebacker Edgerrin Cooper was having a dominant, breakout season before suffering a torn Achilles in Week 4 at Tampa Bay. The Packers are fortunate to have quality backups but Cooper really is that cliché one-of-one player. Even while missing the last three-plus games, he leads the team with six tackles for losses.

Linebacker Zaire Franklin will miss a second consecutive game with an injured shin. He’s the team’s defensive captain.

What About Packers-Panthers Game?

From that perspective, Green Bay will be facing its kindred spirit on Thursday. According to Rotowire, the Panthers have a league-high $90.0 million of salary cap tied up in injured players. The Packers are on their heels, ranking second with $86.8 million. They are head and shoulders ahead of the rest of the league from the financial component.

The Packers, who are coming off a bitter loss to Detroit last week, were crushed by the Falcons on Thursday night in Week 3. They must shake off the pain and inflict some pain on the Panthers.

“We’ve got to be better than we were last time we played a Thursday night game here at home, and I know we will be,” quarterback Jordan Love said. “So I think, in terms of preparation, it’s always tough on a short week. Everything kind of just gets jam packed.

“And then especially in terms of trying to get your body back, we’ve got a lot of guys that are injured right now. So, it’s always tough. You’re never going to make excuses, but we’ve definitely got to be a lot better than we were last time we played the Thursday game.”

description:

He is expected to miss the rest of the season, a source told ESPN, confirming a report by the Houston Chronicle.

text:
HOUSTON -- The Texans' wideout group took another hit Wednesday when Jaylin Noel was placed on injured reserve. He is expected to miss the rest of the season, a source told ESPN, confirming a report by the Houston Chronicle.

The second year wideout from Iowa State suffered turf toe after getting tackled in the fourth quarter Sunday against the New York Giants. The injury occurred during one of his kick returns as Noel fall awkwardly while getting tackled.

The 2025 third-round pick leads the Texans in receiving yards (331) on the season and provided the offense with another dynamic playmaker opposite Pro Bowl wideout Nico Collins. Noel was averaging 17.4 yards per reception.

The Texans do have options to replace Noel. Wideout Tank Dell finally returned in Week 7 after missing 22 months with a devastating knee injury from Dec. 2024. The Texans also traded for former No. 4 pick Marvin Harrison Jr. after Week 5. Harrison caught a touchdown pass against the Giants and Dell led all Texan wideouts in receiving yards (43) in the game.

The Texans signed running back Emari Demercado to the 53-man roster in a corresponding move Wednesday.

The Texans are 2-5 as they enter their bye week.

text:
GREEN BAY, Wis. – As is typically the case for a Thursday night game, the Green Bay Packers will be a banged-up bunch for their game against the Carolina Panthers.

The Packers held a walk-through practice on Tuesday. If they would have practiced, they would have been down four starters. One of them was Travis Glover, who has started the past four games at right guard.

More on that and the injury report in a moment. But first, there was a potential big update on the status of Micah Parsons.

First, Micah Parsons

The Packers didn’t designate Micah Parsons for return this week because the team doesn’t actually practice this week, which would mean one-third of his 21-day return-to-play window would have been wasted.

How about next week?

“I sure hope so,” coach Matt LaFleur said on Wednesday evening.

There was a touch of optimism there, though LaFleur was quick to remind that it will be a medical decision before the superstar pass rusher returns to practice.

“I’m itching for it, though, for sure,” LaFleur said.

Will Kevin Zeitler Start at Right Guard?

Glover is dealing with a knee injury and didn’t play particularly well against the Lions. If he’s not ready, will Kevin Zeitler make his long-awaited debut?

“You shall see,” LaFleur said.

Zeitler was inactive against Detroit and has played only on special teams in his two appearances.

“If we need him, absolutely,” LaFleur said when asked if Zeitler is ready to contribute on offense. “I think he's done a nice job. Here's a guy that came in and didn't have an offseason, didn't have training camp, and he's kind of gradually working his way back into it.”

Good News and Bad News for Packers

Linebacker Zaire Franklin would not have practiced due to the shin injury sustained at practice last week and will not be ready for Thursday, LaFleur said. That means a secon consecutie week for Isaiah McDuffie and Ty'Ron Hopper.

Receiver Matthew Golden (shoulder and foot) did not practice. Along with Christian Watson, Golden is the driving force in the passing game. Without him, the Packers would be incredibly shorthanded in terms of passing-game playmakers.

“I sure hope so,” LaFleur said when asked about Golden’s availability, “but we're still kind of working through it. You're not getting any real reps. Everything's pretty much walk-through. We will have a short indy [individual drills period] tomorrow, but to move guys around and see how they look, but certainly hopeful for him.”

The fourth and final player to not practice was center Sean Rhyan, who suffered a high-ankle sprain early in the loss at Detroit and will miss “at least” four games, according to Matt Zenitz of CBS.

LaFleur wouldn’t say if John Williams would get the start after playing well in his first career snaps from scrimmage. The other options are Jager Burton and Donovan Jennings.

“We'll see. We're kind of working through everything right now,” LaFleur said.

There was some good news, though. Defensive tackles Devonte Wyatt (ankle) and Anthony Campbell (ankle) would not have practiced on Monday but would have been limited on Tuesday. Campbell was one of the standouts against Detroit.

Panthers Update

Same as with Green Bay, four Panthers starters would not have practiced on Monday: defensive tackle Bobby Brown III (hand), cornerback Akayleb Evans (triceps/knee), left guard Damien Lewis (knee) and outside linebacker Jaelan Phillips (hamstring). Brown and Coker, though, moved to full participation on Tuesday.

Still a DNP was Phillips, who signed a four-year, $120 million contract in free agency this past offseason. He has 2.5 sacks in five games but was inactive last week against Tampa Bay.

“We’re [going to] try to get him back for this game but, again, the recurring same hamstring,” Panthers coach Dave Canales told reporters on Monday. “It’s still that kind of a tight window, so it'll be close on that one.”

Evans started three of six games and has two pass breakups. Brown is the 332-pounder in the middle of Carolina’s defense.

Not on the injury lists are the starting offensive tackles, left tackle Ikem Ekwonu and right tackle Taylor Moton. They are on injured reserve. Former Packers starter Rasheed Walker has struggled in place of Ekwonu. According to Pro Football Focus, he’s tied for the NFL lead with 26 pressures allowed.

Quarterback Bryce Young was full participation for a second consecutive day as he handles an ankle injury.

This will be Green Bay’s third game against him, late in his rookie season in 2023 and again last year.

“It's been pretty remarkable to watch him,” LaFleur said. “The one thing that jumps off tape is just how he anticipates, and he is not scared. I mean, he'll stand in there, he'll get blasted, he'll get rid of the ball, but he throws into tight windows with a lot of anticipation, and he's got people to throw to.”

Packers Tuesday Injury Report

Did not participate: LB Zaire Franklin (shin), RG Travis Glover (knee), WR Matthew Golden (shoulder/foot), C Sean Rhyan (ankle).

Limited participation: G Aaron Banks (knee/toe), DT Anthony Campbell (ankle), edge Brenton Cox (quad), DT Devonte Wyatt (ankle).

Full participation: CB Benjamin St-Juste (hamstring).

Panthers Tuesday Injury Report

Did not participate: CB Akayleb Evans (triceps/knee), LG Damien Lewis (knee), OLB Jaelan Phillips (hamstring), G Torricelli Simpkins (ankle).

Limited participation: None.

Full participation: DT Bobby Brown III (hand), WR Jalen Coker (shoulder), QB Bryce Young (ankle).

Among four practicing in a limited capacity — along with a Pro Bowl wide receiver sharing the same last name — Ben Brown had been ruled out during what became a 26-19 win over the New York Jets and was listed as a non-participant leading up to what became a 30-24 loss to the Chicago Bears. And with a hamstring injury sending fellow interior starter Alijah Vera-Tucker to injured reserve prior to the 8:15 p.m. ET kickoff, August trade acquisition Walter Rouse and October signing Matt Pryor stayed in next to center Jared Wilson at Soldier Field.

There’s more options to sort through now for an offensive line that has conceded a total of two sacks over the past two games.

RB Jaylen Wright (foot, quad)

Head coach Mike Vrabel’s quarter of the division listed eight full participants. Count the eldest statesman on the cornerback depth chart among them. No. 7 hasn’t dressed for a game since handling all 59 defensive downs during the 29-26 upset of the Buffalo Bills at Highmark Stadium.

“Not trying to rush the process, but really trying to be efficient at recovering and being able to get back out there and be a guy that my team can depend on,” Davis told reporters of his three-game absence on Wednesday. “I think the worst is just sitting on the sideline watching plays being made or being a bystander. Last year I played in every game, so this year I was looking to do the same. A bit disappointing not being able to do that, but I’m back here and I’m ready to go.”

title: Falcons-Buccaneers: Top Storylines & Key Matchups in Week Eight
description:

– In Week Seven, two of the four NFC South teams won in impressive fashion against one of the league's division leaders.

text:
The 2-5 Tampa Bay Buccaneers return home to play another critical game against an NFC South foe, the 3-4 Atlanta Falcons. The Buccaneers won on the road in Charlotte in Week Seven in impressive fashion, handling the division-leading Carolina Panthers, 43-13, with an unstoppable ground game and a five-sack effort from the defensive front. Now they will try to make it 2-0 with the division, which appears to be up for grabs in 2026. Kickoff on Sunday is scheduled for 1:00 p.m. ET at Raymond James Stadium, with FOX handling the local broadcast.

The Buccaneers secured their third-largest margin of victory in a road game against the Panthers, scoring on offense, defense and special teams. Bucky Irving, Kenny Gainwell and Sean Tucker all contributed big numbers to a rushing attack that rang up 258 yards, fourth most in a game in franchise annals. Outside linebacker Yaya Diaby had three of the team's five sacks and defensive lineman Calijah Kancey scored on a fumble return to get the rout started in earnest. Zyon McCollum had his first interception of the season as the Bucs held Bryce Young, the NFL's leading passer, to 163 yards, and even became the first player in franchise history to return a blocked extra point attempt for a two-point conversion. Baker Mayfield only had to throw 11 passes in his return from a thumb injury but one of those was a nifty improvisational touchdown strike to wide receiver Tez Johnson.

Atlanta also notched a big win in Week Seven, knocking San Francisco from the unbeaten ranks with a 29-20 decision that was sealed by linebacker Kendal Daniels' interception and fumble recovery on the 49ers' last two drives. Quarterback Michael Penix had his best outing of the season so far, throwing for 213 yards, three touchdowns and no interceptions. Running backBijan Robinson didn't score in the win but did pile up another 122 yards from scrimmage; he leads the NFL through Week Seven with 907 yards from scrimmage and is averaging 5.4 yards per carry. Heady safety Jessie Bates also had a pick off Purdy and forced a fumble while breaking up two passes. Atlanta's offense has averaged 31.0 points per game over the past five weeks, which includes an impressive 35-14 win at Atlanta as well as the most recent dispatching of the 49ers.

Here are four major storylines as well as four head-to-head player battles to keep an eye on as the Bucs square off against the Panthers on Sunday afternoon:

TOP STORYLINES

Who Is Actually the Class of the South? – In Week Seven, two of the four NFC South teams won in impressive fashion against one of the league's division leaders. The other two were beaten at home and scored a combined 23 points. This week, the two former teams coming off victories will square off at Raymond James Stadium when the Falcons visit the Buccaneers. Will the outcome of that game suggest that one of those two teams is actually the one to beat in the NFC South race? The Panthers, despite a 43-13 loss to the Buccaneers, would surely beg to differ and are, in fact, still in first place in the division, a half-game ahead of Atlanta and 1.5 up on the Bucs and Saints. The reality is that nothing will be decided on Sunday in Week Eight, as there is still quite a bit of intra-divisional play still to come. The Buccaneers, in fact, are just now playing their first two of six games against division foes. Still, giving how sharp both teams looked in Week Seven, Sunday's matchup definitely looks like an opportunity for one team to make a statement in a division race that is suddenly very tight and four teams deep despite none of them owning a winning record.

Which Team Will Be Able to Run the Ball? – The Bucs have run for 240-plus yards in two of their last three games, but it's worth noting that those games came against Dallas and Carolina teams that both ranked in the bottom five in the league in rush defense. Atlanta, meanwhile, has quietly built a very stout defensive front with Gervon Dexter, Brandon Dorlus and Maason Smith and is allowing only 88.9 rushing yards per game. Did that unit show some cracks last week, however, in allowing 123 yards to the 49ers, only 39 of which came from a banged-up Christian McCaffrey? Similarly, Atlanta's offense revolves around running back Bijan Robinson, who as noted above leads the NFL in yards from scrimmage. He runs behind a very strong offensive line anchored by tackle Jake Matthews and guard Chris Lindstrom. That group will have its work cut out for it against the NFL's second-ranked rush defense, which is reaping the benefits of adding A'Shawn Robinson next to Vita Vea to form an interior wall that is very difficult to crack. The Bucs want to form their offensive identity around a consistently productive rushing attack and first- and second-down successes to set up short third downs. The Falcons would surely love to take the pressure off Penix by getting Robinson going early and often.

Home Delivery – The Buccaneers have won two of their last three games, both victories coming in impressive fashion, and both on the road. Tampa Bay had a chance to get a leg up in the division with a three-game homestand in the first month but the losses snowballed against the Browns, Vikings and Panthers, and then two weeks later the team surrendered a 16-3 fourth-quarter lead in a dispiriting overtime defeat at the hands of the Steelers. Because this is a season in which all the NFC teams got home games for their "17th game" against an AFC opponent, the Buccaneers still have five more chances to notch victories in front of the home crowd, starting on Sunday against the Falcons. It is highly unlikely that Tampa Bay will come out on top of the crowded NFC South race if it doesn't start flexing its homefield advantage, which still includes visits from all three division foes.

Ramping Baker Up – The Buccaneers did not go into their Week Seven game against Carolina trying to pound the ball on the ground because they wanted to limit Baker Mayfield's exposure in his first game back from a dislocated thumb. The impetus for planning a run-heavy script was the Bucs' desire to control the game clock and keep Carolina's high-flying offensive off the field, and to hopefully expose what had been ranked as one of the NFL's most porous run defenses. Still, the unintended consequence of Mayfield only have to throw 11 passes, including only five down the field, wasn't exactly a bad thing. The quarterback wore a glove with a little extra protection behind his thumb and reported no ill effects from his first game action in a month, but didn't have to stress it very much. Obviously, that particular script is not going to happen often – the 11 passes were the fewest the Bucs have thrown in a victory since the 1970s – and at some point the Bucs are going to need the Mayfield who threw for 12,237 yards and 95 touchdowns over his first three seasons as the team's starting quarterback. The Bucs want to run the ball, as noted above, but given the Falcons' tough run defense will they potentially dial up the number and length of Mayfield's downfield attempts in his second start back from the injury?

KEY MATCHUPS

1. Falcons TE Kyle Pitts vs. Buccaneers S Tykee Smith

Kyle Pitts has been an issue for the Buccaneers' defense since the Falcons drafted him fourth overall in 2021, the earliest draft pick ever used on a tight end. He has missed a couple games in the head-to-head series over the last five years, but in the eight games he has played against Tampa Bay he has 629 yards (78.6) per game and six touchdowns, by far his best output against any Atlanta opponent. Though he got off to a bit of a slow start this season, with two catches in the first three weeks combined, he has five grabs in each of the Falcons' last three outings and has scored four touchdowns in that span. He was drafted so early because he has an elite combination of size, speed and athleticism for the tight end position and can make plays on all three levels of the defense. Last year in Week 15 he caught 11 passes for 166 yards and three touchdowns against the Buccaneers. The Bucs' defense won't have one specific defender assigned to covering Pitts, and surely linebacker Alex Anzalone will be a big part of that formula. But Atlanta does like to split Pitts out like a receiver and when that happens he could be covered by slot corner Keionte Scott or versatile safety Tykee Smith. Smith is a good matchup for the tight end as he has coverage skills but is also a hard-nosed defender who invites contact with bigger players and is a sure and rugged tackler. Smith is coming off a strong effort in the Bucs' win at Carolina in which he got his first interception of the season by baiting Bryce Young into a throw to what he thought was an uncovered John Metchie.

2. Buccaneers G Cody Mauch vs. Falcons DT Gervon Dexter

The Falcons made two trades to fortify the interior of their defensive front this offseason, getting Gervon Dexter from the Bears and Maason Smith from the Jaguars. Those two have slid in next to Brandon Dorlus, a 2024 fourth-round pick who is having a breakout season, and are making it tough for opponents to run the football. Atlanta's run defense, as noted above, ranks fourth in the NFL after finishing 24th last season. Dexter has also been getting pressure on opposing passers (as has Dorlus) and he ranks fourth among all NFL defensive tackles with 24 QB pressures. His 13.6% pressure rate ranks sixth in the league and they include 1.5 sacks. Cody Mauch is an integral part of a Buccaneers' offensive line that is starting to round into its dominant form from 2024 after a bit of an uneven start to the 2026 season. Mauch has steadily increased his size and strength since being drafted in the second round in 2023 and is capable of moving defenders off their spots in the run game. The Buccaneers' rushing attack has risen to third in the NFL primarily by running its backs between the tackles on gap schemes. In addition, StatsPass credits Mauch with only allowing one sack so far this season, none since Week Three, and he has only been called for one penalty in the last four games combined.

3. Falcons T Jake Matthews vs. Buccaneers OLB Yaya Diaby

Matthews, the sixth-overall back way back in the 2014 draft, is essentially an institution in Atlanta at this point, having started 203 games and counting over 13 seasons. He is a technically proficient blocker who uses his long arms to deliver quick punches to keep pass rushers off balance. Even at the age of 34, he still moves well in space, helping the Falcons spring Bijan Robinson on outside runs with regularity. Atlanta's rushing attack is ranked sixth in the league and the Falcons' line is coming off a very strong game against the 49ers in which Penix was not sacked once and only hit three times on 34 dropbacks. Matthews, however, will have a challenging matchup this Sunday against edge rusher Yaya Diaby, who primarily rushes the passer from his side of the line. Diaby is coming off the first three-sack game by a Buccaneer defender since Devin White in 2020, and he did it against Carolina's line basically with straight bull rushes. Diaby possesses a quick first step but that is best utilized when he converts speed to power and simply drives his man back into the quarterback's lap. Diaby has 16 QB pressures on the season, according to NFL Next Gen Stats, and is tied for the Bucs' lead with eight "quick" pressures, in which he gets to the passer in 2.5 seconds or less.

4. Buccaneers QB Baker Mayfield vs. Falcons S Jessie Bates

We don't often feature quarterbacks in this Key Matchups section because there really isn't one defender on the opposite side who is in a one-on-one battle with him. And, indeed, this is the first time Mayfield or any Bucs quarterback has appeared in this section. However, there are times when the opposing team has a very smart safety who is capable of matching wits with the opposing team's passer and affecting the passing game in a variety of ways. Bates belongs in that category. So far this season, Bates has 40 tackles, one interception, four passes defensed, two forced fumbles and one fumble recovery. Now in his ninth season, Bates has 18 interceptions over the last four-plus seasons and he's been a second-team AP All-Pro in two of those campaigns, including last year. Mayfield will be playing his second game since returning from the right thumb dislocation that cost him three contests, and he will almost certainly be asked to throw more than the 11 passes he had in Carolina last Sunday. Mayfield is just as experienced as Bates and can diagnose how a defense is trying to trick him into the wrong decisions with the football. He will need to be aware of Bates' location at all times on Sunday.

The work builds on research released in August that estimated between 25% and 98% of players had CTE based on a study of brains donated by players and their families.

text:
A new study from a team of researchers in Boston estimates that nearly three-quarters of NFL players who died between 2008 and 2023 had chronic traumatic encephalopathy, or CTE.

The disease is caused by repeated hits to the head, whether they cause a concussion or not. It can only be diagnosed after death.

The work builds on research released in August that estimated between 25% and 98% of players had CTE based on a study of brains donated by players and their families. The researchers at Boston University, Mass General Brigham and the Concussion & CTE Foundation wanted to explore how including data from players who didn’t donate their brains might affect the estimate.

The results were published Wednesday in JAMA Network Open.

The researchers used statistical methods to analyze data from more than 2,300 players, including some who donated their brains, as well as death records for players who died over the 16-year period. They looked for causes of death by neurodegenerative diseases like dementia.

“The importance of this number is knowing that football played at the professional level is a real risk for this disease, and it's time for all of us to work together on ways of prevention, ways to keep our players safe,” said Dr. Ann McKee, a neurologist and neuropathologist who directs the Boston University CTE Center and worked on the study.

Former Patriots linebacker Ted Johnson said he wasn’t surprised by the researchers’ estimate.

“I am certainly alarmed by that figure. That's clearly an epidemic,” he said. “It's a huge issue for all athletes that play sports in which there's potential to have head trauma.”

He suspects he has CTE himself after a decade playing in the NFL, and estimated he experienced 100-plus concussions over his football career.

Johnson said he suffers from symptoms including depression, anxiety, difficulty with impulse control, sleep issues and irritability. He said he’s learned to manage his symptoms through a combination of medications and lifestyle changes.

McKee said she hopes this new study will serve as a wake-up call about the need to take CTE seriously.

“This is a preventable disease,” she said. “We can take actions that lower the risk by raising the age [kids] start playing football or not having full contact in practice.”

Other steps she recommended include reducing the number of games in a season, improved monitoring for athletes of the number of head hits they sustain over a season, and reducing the number of hits to the head overall, regardless of whether they cause a concussion.

McKee said although this finding is grim, she’s optimistic that in the next few years, doctors will gain the ability to diagnose people with CTE while they’re living. They’ll then be able to start finding treatments for the disease, she said.

Johnson said the ability to diagnose CTE in living athletes would be “a game changer.”

“I wonder what the landscape of football would look like if you can go get a test for little Johnny and he's in high school, and the results come back and it's not positive,” he said. “What does that do to the long-term viability of the game?”

When asked for comment, an NFL spokesperson referred to a statement on the group's previous research, saying the league “continuously strives to make the game of football safer, including by implementing strategies to reduce concussions and head impacts.”

The spokesperson added that the NFL community has access to resources for physical and mental wellbeing. The NFL has also implemented rule changes and a new concussion protocol and is pushing for the development of safer helmets.

text:
The Detroit Lions are getting their "energy bug" – and one of the best safeties in the NFL – back on the field.

Lions safety Kerby Joseph returned to practice Wednesday, Oct. 28, for the first time since a chronic knee condition knocked him out of the 2025 season.

A first-team All-Pro selection in 2024 and the NFL leader with 20 interceptions since 2022, Joseph has not played since last Oct. 12 in a Lions loss to the Kansas City Chiefs.

The Lions have 21 days to activate Joseph to the 53-man roster or keep him on the physically unable to perform list the rest of the season.

"He’s with us but he kind of hasn’t been, so to get him back in the fold and be around the guys and really be a part of it is, I think that’s significant, man," Lions coach Dan Campbell said. "I know certainly for him but for us, too, to have the guy around because he’s an energy bug man and obviously he’s a productive player, he’s a good football player. So you get those two to come back, I think that helps."

Joseph has been dealing with a cartilage condition in his knee since last summer and the ailment limited him to six games last season.

At his best, Joseph is one of the top playmaking defensive backs in the NFL, and his potential return – he will not play in this weekend's game against the Minnesota Vikings, but is expected to return before Thanksgiving – comes at a time when the Lions (4-2) are fighting for a playoff spot in the competitive NFC North and just got their other Pro Bowl safety, Brian Branch, back on the field.

Branch had an interception in the Lions' win over the Green Bay Packers on Sunday, Oct. 25, his first game since tearing the Achilles tendon in his right leg last December.

Joseph said this summer he was "super optimistic" about returning to action early this season, but he missed part of training camp for personal reasons, which delayed his rehab.

One of the Lions' most gregarious players, Joseph was noticeably morose while dealing with his injury last season, but has been upbeat in his interactions with reporters and fans this fall. He attended the Detroit Catholic Central-Birmingham Brother Rice football game at Ford Field over the weekend, when he walked through the stands high-fiving spectators, and he was on the sideline celebrating plays with teammates in the Lions-Packers game.

"Everybody loves Kerby, man," Campbell said. "He’s a good teammate and he brings a ton of energy, and so we’ve kind of – look, he’s been here but it’s like I told him, man, I wanted his focus to be on the rehab. Now he would be in meetings some, he’s in team meetings, but really the priority a lot is in the mornings, man, he’d go out there and make sure that he’s getting all that work done."

Campbell said Joseph has "passed every test to this point" in his rehab and has regained the strength in his injured knee and quad "to a point where it’s equal with the other leg."

The next step, Campbell said, is to integrate Joseph into football drills and see how his knee responds.

"He’s kind of passed all those tests from what we’re doing out there [in rehab]," Campbell said. "So now that he’s passed all those tests it’s about getting him out there and literally, ball’s in the air, it’s a handoff, him breaking from the post and doing it over and over and over, and real explosive reps with other bodies around. And we’re not even there yet. This’ll be – he’ll do some individual, all that, but we will be progressing to get into that late week, early next week and then here we go. So yeah, he’s checked all those boxes. And the rest is just, how does he react to football, like movement skills of true football, real bodies and the intensity of it?"

Last week, Joseph posted a video on TikTok of change of direction drills he was doing at the Lions practice facility, and on Wednesday he wrote on X, "Don't ever doubt me again in your mutha (emoji) life."

"It’ll be great to get him back out there with the guys," Campbell said. "I know he’s excited, we are, but we’ve still got a ways to go but this is a step in the right direction."

text:
Week 8 of the 2026 NFL season will bring several injury questions, with some key players hoping to return while others deal with injuries suffered in Week 7. Lamar Jackson is among the big names who could return to the field in the coming days. However, after the recent game against the Bengals, the Ravens’ QB said he was “not even close to” his “full capability.”

With several players dealing with injuries, team practice reports should provide a clearer picture of their availability by Friday. For now, the latest updates offer an early look at who could take the field this weekend.

Official report: only Thursday’s game is set

The NFL’s official Week 8 injury report is still limited. Only Thursday night’s game between the Panthers (3-3) and Packers (4-3), which will stream on Prime Video, has listed practice participation. The reports for Sunday and Monday’s games are not yet available because those teams have not released their practice information.

Green Bay wide receiver Matthew Golden did not practice. Packers guard Travis Glover and center Sean Rhyan also sat out.

For Carolina, cornerback Akayleb Evans, guards Damien Lewis and Torricelli Simpkins III, and linebacker Jaelan Phillips did not practice. Quarterback Bryce Young was a full participant.

Lamar Jackson closes in on a return

Baltimore Ravens quarterback Lamar Jackson is one of the biggest names to watch this week. He has been out since injuring his ankle in Week 4, but NFL Network’s Ian Rapoport reported Tuesday that Jackson is expected to play Sunday against the Bills.

“I expect, based on the people I’ve spoken with, that Lamar Jackson will play this week. He’ll be on the field this week against the Buffalo Bills…He’s believed to be as close to 100% as he has been, and the Ravens do expect him to play,” the senior NFL insider said, as posted by podcaster Kevin Oestreicher.

Yahoo’s analysis identifies Jackson as the league’s only major quarterback injury concern this week. His practice participation will be important, as he could be limited or listed as questionable.

Jackson’s return would be a major boost for Baltimore’s offense. Wide receiver Zay Flowers has been productive this season and could benefit from having his starting quarterback back.

Running Backs: a crowded watch list

Running back is one of the biggest injury concerns heading into Week 8. Several teams are waiting for updates on key players.

Breece Hall (Jets): Hall missed Week 7 with a quadriceps injury, leaving Braelon Allen to handle more of the workload. Yahoo expects Hall to return Sunday against the Raiders. However, Allen could keep a role, especially on passing downs.

Aaron Jones (Vikings): Jones left late in Week 7 with a knee injury. He is considered day-to-day and reportedly avoided a serious injury. Jordan Mason stepped up with 68 rushing yards on 15 carries. Even if Jones plays against the Lions, Mason could remain the better fantasy option.

Saquon Barkley (Eagles): Barkley returned after missing two games but suffered a back injury in Week 7. NBC Sports reported that the injury may be less serious than his earlier hamstring problem, but Philadelphia has not provided an update. The Eagles are also dealing with the loss of Jalen Hurts, who is out for the season with blood clots.

Jeremiyah Love (Cardinals): Love has missed two games with an ankle injury and could return against Dallas. Bam Knight has rushed for 128 yards on 22 carries in his absence, which could lead Arizona to share carries among three running backs.

Christian McCaffrey (49ers): McCaffrey is dealing with a mild hamstring strain. San Francisco’s Week 8 bye should give him extra time to recover.

Receivers and Tight Ends

Several pass catchers are also dealing with injuries.

Jaylen Waddle left Denver’s Week 7 win with a chest injury. His status is uncertain ahead of the Broncos’ divisional matchup with the Chiefs.

Kansas City wide receiver Rashee Rice has missed time with a hamstring injury. If he returns, the Chiefs could have more options in the passing game.

Houston wide receiver Jaylin Noel suffered a turf toe injury, and the team is still assessing its severity.

Colts tight end Tyler Warren has missed two straight games with a groin injury. Yahoo recommends keeping expectations in check if he returns this week.

Season-ending losses reshape rosters

Some teams have already lost key players for the rest of the season. Jalen Hurts, Jaxson Dart, De’Von Achane, Terry McLaurin, and Jayden Higgins are among those listed as out for the year. Several other notable players are on injured reserve.

These absences have created opportunities for backups and other players to take on bigger roles.

What to watch before kickoff

Wednesday through Friday will be important as teams release their official practice reports. Players who miss practice or take part only on a limited basis early in the week could enter the weekend with questionable tags.

Fantasy managers and bettors should pay close attention to Lamar Jackson, Breece Hall, Aaron Jones, Saquon Barkley, and Jeremiyah Love. Their practice participation and final injury designations should provide a better idea of who is likely to play in Week 8.

text:
It's Week 8 of the 2026 NFL season, and we're under two weeks away from the trade deadline. Insiders Jeremy Fowler and Dan Graziano have been calling sources around the league for the latest news and notable buzz.

Which teams are most likely to bring in help before the Nov. 10 deadline? Which players are likeliest to end up in a new city? And will the Colts continue dealing players? Jeremy and Dan have updates on the trade market. Plus, we look into what's happening with the struggling Jets and what's going on in the chaotic AFC North, where the Browns are in first and the Ravens are in last.

It's all here, as Jeremy and Dan answer big questions, hand out useful fantasy football nuggets and empty their reporting notebooks heading into Week 8.

Jump to:

Aggressive teams at the deadline

Players likely to move | Colts dealing

Jets changes | AFC North chaos

Fantasy advice | More intel

Which team is most likely to be aggressive in acquiring help at the deadline?

Fowler: The Chiefs appear poised to do something at wide receiver. Injuries to Rashee Rice and Tyquan Thornton have created holes in the passing game that running back Kenneth Walker III can't mask alone. The Chiefs have managed to win games despite those injuries, but Sunday night in Seattle was a reminder of how ugly things can look without adequate downfield playmakers.

Enough receivers will be available in the coming weeks, so the Chiefs can get good value trading for the high-impact players or lower-cost options. The Colts' Josh Downs would be a fit for the Chiefs. The Browns' Jerry Jeudy would also fit, though Cleveland is not inclined to deal him now barring a significant offer.

Graziano: The Chiefs always seem to do something at wide receiver at the deadline. Usually it's a smaller move such as Kadarius Toney or late-career DeAndre Hopkins, but the team has a history of targeted trade-deadline additions at the position. I expect Kansas City to be active in trying to add a player or two to boost the offense, be that another pass catcher, an offensive lineman or both.

The teams that are most interesting to me are the surprises. Would the first-place Giants believe they're in position to trade a draft pick or two for a win-now player? Would the AFC North-leading Browns feel compelled to reward their current roster for its surprising first-half success by adding a player who can help take them to the next level? We saw the Colts do this last year with the big swing for Sauce Gardner.

Of course, last year's Colts are proof that this approach doesn't always work, but what do you think? Would the Browns veer from their long-term building plans to try to make a 2026 run with Deshaun Watson at QB?

Fowler: Cleveland is a low-key team to watch at the deadline. The Browns are 5-2 and like to make deals. Defensive line help will be available if they tap into it. And adding a versatile blocker, either at tight end or H-back, would be timely, perhaps providing a player similar to what Todd Monken had in Baltimore with Patrick Ricard.

Seattle has already made a move with the deal for Pro Bowl guard Quenton Nelson. Edge rusher and running back are positions Seahawks GM John Schneider could monitor, as well.

Graziano: Yeah, Tuesday was a big day in the NFC West arms race. It makes me wonder what the Rams are thinking. They obviously made their big moves in the offseason, but things haven't worked, and everyone's favorite superteam has fallen behind the 49ers and Seahawks in the division. I wonder whether there's another move for the Rams to make -- they could use a speedy wide receiver if one is available -- and whether they still have the draft picks and/or desire to add more to a roster that was already supposed to be loaded.

I'm also very curious to see what the Jaguars do. They see themselves as a top AFC contender. I agree with them, but they could use one more piece up front on defense. Remember, the Jags were kind of a surprise at last year's deadline with their move for Jakobi Meyers, who helped fuel their second-half run.

Which player are you most confident will get traded somewhere before the deadline?

Fowler: Let's go with Jaguars receiver Brian Thomas Jr. Several execs I've spoken to believe Thomas' days in Jacksonville are numbered due to his diminished role in Year 3. He has trade value, and the Jaguars would be smart to explore that option. One potential deterrent: Jacksonville is in a winning window and needs all hands on deck for the stretch run. Thomas, at worst, still commands defensive coverage, but he hasn't caught a pass in the past two games and was essentially benched in London in Week 6.

None of the top trade options around the league is a slam dunk to happen, but place Thomas in the Marvin Harrison Jr. category of a receiver badly needing a fresh start. The safer bet might end up being Vikings wide receiver Jauan Jennings, who isn't a primary option in that offense and is also a trade candidate.

Graziano: Thomas is my answer, too. He clearly hasn't been a big part of Jacksonville's offense since coach Liam Coen arrived last season. Thomas would surely prefer to either be a bigger part of the Jaguars' offense or go to a team where he can have a sizable role. And there are plenty of teams around the league that still view him as a high-end talent at a premium position and would give up something of value to get him.

Like you said, this closely mirrors the Harrison situation. Thomas is two months younger than Harrison, was also drafted in the first round in 2024 and showed enough promise as a rookie that there's reason to believe a change of scenery could bring out the best in him. Thomas hasn't made any public noise about wanting out, but neither did Harrison. Still, Harrison and his agents were able to work with the Cardinals behind the scenes to find a solution that made everyone happy. I expect the same thing to happen for Thomas.

Going back to your Jennings mention, I agree that the most likely guys to be traded are the slightly lower-profile names if simply because they won't cost as much to add. But I also imagine Cardinals edge rusher Josh Sweat will be of interest to teams needing defensive help over the next couple of weeks.

Fowler: Yeah, Dan, Sweat certainly fits the profile of a prime trade candidate, and some around the league have linked the Cowboys to his services.

What about the Colts? Are more moves coming after they dealt Quenton Nelson and DeForest Buckner?

Graziano: With the Colts tearing things down, veteran wideouts such as Keenan Allen and Laquon Treadwell might have appeal as depth players on contenders that need help at receiver. Defensive tackle Grover Stewart and wide receiver Josh Downs are also on expiring contracts and didn't get extensions this offseason.

The guy who did get an extension, running back Jonathan Taylor, might be the most interesting of the bunch. Even after his recent extension, Taylor has a tradeable contract. The Colts would have to absorb $10 million in dead money next year, and the acquiring team would have to take on whatever prorated portion of Taylor's $8 million salary plus bonus compensation is left for this season. He's scheduled to make $16.02 million next year, and right now that's not guaranteed, though it converts to a full guarantee five days after the Super Bowl.

So technically, you could acquire Taylor without any commitment beyond this season, but you'd also retain the ability to keep him past 2026 if you are comfortable with that price. I believe Tennessee's Tony Pollard is the more likely running back to be dealt, ahead of Taylor or Saquon Barkley, but if the Colts are in full rebuilding mode, you can't rule anything out.

Fowler: Talks are heating up quickly. Nelson had interest from several suitors before going to the Seahawks, including the Packers, thus expediting his market. Assistant GM Ed Dodds' phone will be lighting up this week. Buckner was also a player people were watching before he was dealt to the 49ers on Tuesday.

Downs has emerged as a hot name this week because multiple teams looking for receiver help have shown interest. But the Colts are thin at receiver already, so trading Downs would severely limit the offense, though my sense is he would not be against a change of scenery. (Update: Downs requested a trade on Wednesday morning.) And as multiple people around the league pointed out Tuesday, trading Taylor isn't a slam dunk because unlike Buckner and Nelson, he is not an impending free agent. He will also be a boon for whoever is coaching the Colts in 2027, be it current head man Shane Steichen or an outside hire.

How long until we see changes for the Jets?

Graziano: Most people I talk to think Aaron Glenn will get to coach through the end of this season before the team evaluates the two-year sample and decides whether to bring him back for a third. The caveats are that owners are unpredictable and that this particular owner fired his last head coach relatively early in the 2024 season. Glenn has some things going for him that Robert Saleh didn't, mainly his connection with the franchise from his time as a Jets player. Ownership likes Glenn and wants to be proved right about him being a good head coach.

That said, he has struggled with a few tasks specific to head coaches, most prominently end-of-half clock management. And his choice of Frank Reich as offensive coordinator after one year of Tanner Engstrand is coming under criticism as the offense struggles to score points. A defensive head coach is often done in by his inability to find the right offensive coordinator, so unless the Jets get things turned around on offense by the end of this season, that could be a detrimental data point for Glenn's chances to stick around.

Fowler: My sense after asking around to those in the industry who closely follow such things is that Glenn likely will get some time to attempt to right the ship, but the hot seat conversation is real, and this job is on the radar for potential change at some point. It's important to note that the Jets were not viewed as a playoff-caliber team in the offseason or preseason. They're a young team in transition, and they're right to expect modest progress. On that front, they look more competitive and more capable, but they're still 2-5, which sort of offsets those first two points.

Glenn can lift his standing in two areas: better game management/situational football and maximizing the playmakers on offense with improved overall play. This stat from ESPN Jets reporter Rich Cimini is shocking: The Jets have been outscored 107-6 in the final two minutes of the second quarter under Glenn. Glenn must prove that he can manage the clock better at the end of halves. And this offense should rank better than 27th in the NFL given its talent level. Garrett Wilson is already frustrated -- again.

Graziano: And that's not good. One reason the Jets moved on from Aaron Rodgers after the 2024 season was concern over his relationship with Wilson and their belief that they had to make sure the wideout was happy and wanted to be there long term.

So here's the way I see it with the Jets. Glenn doesn't have to make the playoffs this season to keep his job and never did. But this is a team with three first-round picks in April and a plan to somehow, some way, finally find its long-term franchise quarterback. What the Jets want to have established by the end of this season is at least a foundation of a winning culture and an environment in which a young quarterback would be in position to quickly thrive and be happy. It's hard to look at the Jets right now and think they're on either one of those tracks. There is time to turn it around, but if it keeps going the way it has so far, this is absolutely a situation we'll be watching for a potential change.

Fowler: I also suspect that any major changes would be limited to the coaching staff. General manager Darren Mougey is ascending and has acquitted himself well through the past two years. His trades have New York positioned for three top-12 picks in April's draft as it currently stands. The roster is improved. Whoever the head coach is in 2027 will be in a good situation ... on paper. Ownership is viewed as a hurdle in some league circles, though it sounds like Woody Johnson wants to change that narrative and could be patient with Glenn as a result.

Browns in first? Ravens in last? What are you hearing on the upside-down AFC North?

Fowler: That the Browns are no fluke. I'm not ready to crown them the division winners, but they are well-stocked with young talent. Deshaun Watson has rediscovered (at least some of) his old form, and the schedule is soft. Cleveland has faced three teams with losing records, and three of its next four opponents are also below .500. It's at least a good enough schedule to keep things interesting.

The Steelers aren't lighting it up offensively but are creating an identity with star running back Jaylen Warren and heavy personnel (two tight ends or six offensive linemen). Pittsburgh seems to be in a similar spot to where it was in recent seasons -- good enough to win nine or 10 games and sneak into the playoffs but lacking juice beyond that. But what it's doing with heavier packages, including two-tight-end sets, has me intrigued. And don't discount the Steelers improving their roster at the deadline. Either way, this is shaping up to be the most balanced division in football.

Graziano: I don't believe the Browns or Steelers are as good as their records indicate. I mean, Watson is 27th in the league in QBR, and Cleveland has allowed 13 more points than it has scored. This is a mirage, along with some really good coaching by Todd Monken. And the Steelers just keep eking out these grueling wins against mediocre competition and looking a lot like they did for the past half-decade of the Mike Tomlin era.

But in Cincinnati, the Bengals have the one clearly elite unit in the AFC North, and it's the offense that hung 35 points on the Ravens in the second half Sunday. Cincinnati's defense is also playing at a higher level than we're used to watching. Based on what we've seen (and yes, I watched the Bengals lose in Pittsburgh with my own eyes thanks to two horrible mistakes on punt plays), I have Cincinnati as the class of this division, and I believe that's how it will play out in the end. Sunday was a statement game for the Bengals, and the statement is, "We are better than you are."

Fowler: The Bengals might be the most dangerous. We knew going into the season that they needed just passable defense; Joe Burrow and his side of the ball could handle the rest. That lopsided win in Baltimore on Sunday was a statement on both accounts. Cincinnati is convincing as a whole, but its ground game remains concerning. Last season's rushing attack ranked 29th in the league, and after hoping for improvement, this season's group ranks ... 30th. Teams that rank near the bottom in rushing typically don't make the playoffs. Burrow can overcome this issue at times, but that's hard to do over 17 games.

So while I mostly agree with you on Cincinnati's interdivision potential, I'm taking Baltimore for the division if Lamar Jackson is back this week and for the duration of the season. Here's to expecting Baltimore to tighten up and prove the Cincinnati game was an aberration.

Where are you at with the Ravens, Dan? History tells us that a hobbled Jackson equates to eight- or nine-win seasons for Baltimore. But the team's ceiling remains high.

Graziano: That seems to be the consensus opinion and has been since the offseason -- that Baltimore has a strong roster and should be a top AFC contender when everyone's healthy. But I have concerns.

The Ravens definitely need Jackson back as soon and as healthy as possible. This isn't graduate-level NFL analysis. He is as big a difference-maker as there is in the league. The Ravens can get by without him, but they cannot excel in that state -- and excel is what they're going to have to do to win this division (even if I'm not with you yet on the level of good play being displayed by the two teams atop the AFC North right now). The big problem the Ravens have is that the two games they've lost without Jackson are to the Browns and Bengals, both of whom are ahead of them in the division and now have a tiebreaker edge as well.

Jackson's health isn't the only issue. Derrick Henry looks a step slow for the first time and is getting stuffed at a high rate in short-yardage situations. The defense's disappearance in the second half Sunday must sound some alarm bells, doesn't it? Wasn't this supposed to be the Trey Hendrickson revenge game? The new coaching staff is unproven and hasn't had to manage a team through the inevitable ups and downs of a season. I believe Jesse Minter is a good coach who can do it, but we have not seen whether he can or will. We don't really know what the current, post-Harbaugh version of the Ravens is or how it will hold up as the season goes along.

What is your best piece of fantasy football advice for this week?

Graziano: After the week I just had in fantasy, my best advice is to not ask me for advice. But since you're insisting ... try to trade for Seahawks RB Jadarian Price. He's back at practice this week after missing the past four games while on injured reserve with a chest injury. I have no idea whether he'll play this week or how much, but he'll be back at some point soon. He was their first-round pick this year, and they just traded for Nelson, a move that will help their run game immensely.

Yes, Zach Charbonnet is close to returning, but he's also Zach Charbonnet, not Bijan Robinson. At best, the Seahawks will use Charbonnet the way they always have, which leaves room for someone else to produce at a high level. Price has had fumble issues and rookie growing pains, but the Seahawks drafted him because they saw him as a ready-made prospect who could help this season. Given how much Nelson can improve the run game, that Seattle's remaining schedule is friendly for fantasy running backs and that Price is probably sitting in someone's IR spot in your league, you might be able to get a steal.

Fowler: Grab insurance plays at RB such as the Colts' Seth McGowan. This is the time of year when RB depth thins due to injury. The Colts' trade plans could result in a deal for Jonathan Taylor, which would open up the backfield for McGowan. Even if they don't trade Taylor, McGowan is probably worth the roster spot if you have one to spare. The Titans' Tyjae Spears is also tempting if Tennessee gets a great offer for Tony Pollard.

What else are you hearing this week?

Graziano: On the day the Giants told Jameis Winston that he was being benched for J.J. McCarthy, offensive coordinator Matt Nagy was leaving the team facility when he walked past a room where two Giants players sat talking. The two players were Winston and McCarthy, and they were reviewing the work the team had done that day, which was focused on third downs. Winston, who has been working in this offense since the spring, was trying to reinforce some key concepts for McCarthy, who has been there for a month and was just about to have his first week of practice with the starters. Neither player noticed Nagy, and he didn't interrupt their conversation, but he couldn't help but smile as he walked to his car.

The vibes are really good around the Giants right now. They were strong even before Sunday's upset victory over the Texans in Houston. Giants coaches were ecstatic about the way running back Cam Skattebo had handled the situation that saw his role in the offense greatly reduced for Week 6 after a costly fumble in Week 5. I spoke to Skattebo after Sunday's game, in which he rushed for 124 yards including the 42-yard overtime scamper that set up Devin Singletary's game-winning touchdown. He told me he felt the coaches had handled the situation "respectfully" and hadn't put him in a position where he felt embarrassed, and that he'd received and agreed with the message.

For his part, McCarthy did what the Giants' coaches were hoping he'd do on Sunday. He managed the operation of the offense cleanly, led the group with confidence and stayed within the game plan. Head coach John Harbaugh pointed out after the game that there were no procedural penalties with the offense, remarkable considering how new to it the starting quarterback was. Harbaugh also used the word "joy" multiple times to describe the feeling around the Giants right now, and he practically bounced out of his postgame news conference when it was done.

Look, it's only one game (and one quarter the week before against the Saints), and it's far too soon to fully trust what this team can be with McCarthy leading it. But they've clearly come together as a group in Harbaugh's first year. They're identifying their leaders -- Abdul Carter gave the fiery halftime speech that asked his teammates to leave everything out on the field in the second half -- and drawing top-level performances out of players at every level of the roster. Defensive coordinator Dennard Wilson put cornerback Deonte Banks on star Texans receiver Nico Collins for large parts of the game Sunday, and Banks shut Collins down.

The Giants head into their bye week in first place, and knowing they'll still be there when they come out of the bye with two division games in five days. But they go on bye encouraged by the idea of what they can be with McCarthy running the offense, and they believe the break gives banged-up players like left tackle Andrew Thomas time to heal up and come back healthier for the second half of the season. It's hard to know if they can capitalize on this feel-good start, but it sure is easy to see where all the good feelings are coming from.

Fowler: Trading a franchise staple is not easy. But three-time All-Pro guard Quenton Nelson garnered real value on the trade market, and the Colts decided to open the floodgates. Here's how it went down: The Colts were transparent with Nelson during the process, reaching out Monday to stress that the team wanted to send him to a good situation. Through those talks, the Colts knew that Seattle was an appealing option for the player. Green Bay was also on the radar as an attractive option. So Nelson didn't have control of the trade, but his input was accounted for. Several teams had shown interest, including the Packers, Bears and Eagles.

The Seahawks put together a compelling package including third- and fifth-round picks. On Tuesday, interim GM Ed Dodds called Nelson into his office to deliver the news about the Seattle trade, about which Nelson was fired up. He slides immediately into the left guard spot and improves an offense that ranks 17th in rushing and would like to improve there. The addition of Nelson -- plus the impending return of running backs Jadarian Price and Zach Charbonnet -- should fuel the running game.

Nelson is slated to be a 2027 free agent but both sides plan to work through that once he gets to Seattle as early as today. The Seahawks typically are comfortable trading for future free agents and letting them play it out. That was the case last year with wide receiver Rashid Shaheed, who was moved at the deadline but didn't re-sign with the team until around free agency. The Colts got an early jump, but more deals are coming. The Chargers have resisted thus far, but teams believe that could change over the next week. The Cardinals remain a team to watch. The team is still in transition and needs roster improvements. Is it finally time for Budda Baker to find a new home after 10 seasons in the desert? We explored that in our top 25 trade candidates list.

Graziano: The Raiders did nothave any serious discussions this week about sitting veteran starting QB Kirk Cousins for rookie Fernando Mendoza, whom they think is coming along very well but still isn't as ready as they'd like him to be when they make him their starter. The plan all along has been to sit Mendoza as long as possible, and I personally would be surprised to see him start any of the Raiders' next five games at least. They have a bye in Week 13, and I think after that is the earliest they'd start to seriously consider it. Remember, this isn't just a Klint Kubiak decision. The entire organization, including their very active part-owner Tom Brady, is invested in making sure Mendoza is a success, and Brady has been vocal about his belief that rookie quarterbacks need to develop from the sideline.

Cousins has deficiencies at this point in his career, and the Raiders believe that ultimately -- when he's ready -- Mendoza's mobility and arm strength will benefit their offense. But Cousins is also leading the league in touchdown passes and is third in passing yards through seven weeks, and the Raiders don't see him as their biggest problem at the moment. They'd like to get their anemic running game going, as only the Packers are averaging fewer rushing yards per game. And they need to be better up front in the middle of their defense to keep other teams from putting games away in second halves.

At 3-4, the Raiders are a game and a half out of an AFC playoff spot at this point ahead of this week's cross-country trip to play the struggling Jets. They aren't ready to give up on their season. And while swapping Mendoza in for Cousins may not constitute a give-up per se, the point here is for the situation to be as good around Mendoza as possible once they make that move. They don't believe they're there yet.

Fowler: Mystery surrounds the Eagles' plans. It's unclear at this point whether GM Howie Roseman conducts a fire sale. But some rival teams are expecting at least mild unloading. Perhaps the most interesting team is the Tampa Bay Bucs, who typically are not subtractors by nature. Normally, this would be a natural time for a roster mini-reset. But despite the 2-5 record, the Bucs are alive in the NFC South, which they've won four of the past five years. Win enough divisional games and the overall record doesn't matter as much. I do believe, had the Bucs lost last week to fall to 1-6, they would be actively discussing dealing players.

Graziano: We didn't really address the Eagles in our trade-deadline portion of this column, but my sense is that things could go either way -- or a little bit of both -- for them ahead of the trade deadline. They have veterans on expiring contracts (cornerback Riq Woolen, receiver Hollywood Brown and tight end Dallas Goedert) who could be of interest to contending teams and help Philly out with draft-pick compensation. But the Eagles are loaded with picks already thanks to previous trades. They dealt their 2027 third-rounder for Jonathan Greenard but are projected to get a third-round compensatory pick due to the free agent loss of Jaelan Phillips. And they have extra first- and second-round picks in the 2028 draft due to the trades of A.J. Brown and Cam Jurgens. The Eagles aren't desperate to refill their coffers.

But they'll always listen, in both directions. If they get a good enough offer for a player who isn't part of their future plans, as was the case with Jurgens a couple of weeks ago, they'll be open to it. And if they see a chance to add a player who might be more than a two-month rental, as the Texans did with Marvin Harrison Jr., they'll be open to that as well.

The big name that everyone will want to know about is Saquon Barkley, but (A) he's clearly injured right now, even though he tried playing through it Monday night and (B) he's a running back who turns 30 in February and is due to make $16 million in 2027 and $19.2 million in 2028. As of now, the only guarantee of that future money is $2.5 million in 2027. If Barkley shows he's healthy in the next couple of weeks, it's possible a team would take a shot on him as the potential answer to its run game issues. But it's never a guarantee with running backs that the team trading them gets enough in return to justify the deal. In this year's NFC East, the Eagles can surely convince themselves they still have a shot to compete in spite of their current five-game losing streak and injury problems. So they're not trying to give Barkley away.

Fowler: The Lions' plan for Jahmyr Gibbs is simple: Give him the ball a ton. For good reason: Gibbs has waited years to be the primary back and is built for it. Opposing coaches have noted he's stronger than he was when entering the league in 2023. He can handle the carries. But it's worth noting that Gibbs has 166 touches through seven games, which equates to 470 touches over 17 games. That would be the most since James Wilder's 492 in 1984, and it doesn't feel sustainable; Gibbs' previous career high is 320 last season. Backup Sione Vaki has 16 carries on the season, several of which came in garbage time against Arizona.

Eventually, Detroit could add an RB2. The Lions have been in contact with former rushing champion Kareem Hunt, a free agent who visited the team in the preseason. The Lions' thinking is simple: Giving Gibbs the ball is better than just about any alternative, and the Lions are trying to win games. But his durability over the course of a long 17-game season is something to watch.

Fowler: Packers head coach Matt LaFleur addressed last week's officiating issues in the loss to the Detroit Lions with his team, hoping to turn the page with a quick-turnaround Thursday night game vs. Carolina looming. LaFleur told his team at the beginning of this week that the Lions game is "over," and Green Bay can't dictate how games are officiated, per safety Javon Bullard.

The Packers were flagged for two roughing the passer penalties late, along with an unnecessary roughness call on a play that did not appear blown dead. The Packers are toeing the line between physicality and discipline (they have eight roughing the passer penalties this season) but know they will need both to overcome the Panthers on Thursday night. The last time Green Bay lined up on a weekday game, Atlanta embarrassed the Packers 35-14. The Packers plan to avoid a repeat at all costs.

Graziano: Aaron Rodgers' odd claim that the idea of an "international week" of games was discussed during the 2019-20 CBA discussions created a lot of confusion around the league Monday, in particular among people who were there and remember nothing of the sort ever coming up. Rodgers' concept of a week in which every team in the league plays an international game in exchange for an extra bye week during the regular season makes no logistical or common sense, and multiple people who were involved in the CBA talks said it was never a point of discussion among players and owners. One person said they vaguely remembered Rodgers himself bringing up the idea in a meeting of just player leaders (not in a negotiating session with the league) and it being ignored or dismissed by the rest of the people in the conversation.

This was at a point in time, remember, when union representatives were gathering in Carmel, Indiana, during the scouting combine to hammer out the final details of a deal that would be voted on a week or so later, and when Rodgers was trying to scuttle that deal because he thought players shouldn't agree to it unless owners offered to make all offseason workouts voluntary in exchange for a 17th regular-season game. So if you're wondering whether this "international week" was ever treated as a viable idea, you can move on to other things in your life and remember that a large portion of what Aaron Rodgers has said publicly over the past six or seven years is utter nonsense.

Fowler: Injury updates ... The Lions are optimistic about wide receiver Amon-Ra St. Brown playing despite an ankle tweak from last week. Detroit knows St. Brown is one of the toughest players in the league and is able to play through various issues. Last year, he played on a high-ankle sprain on three days' rest to dominate on a Thursday night.

Bears running back Kyle Monangai (turf toe) has missed the past three weeks, but his chances are better of playing this week.

David Bailey’s promising rookie season could face a setback.

He is dealing with a groin injury and did not practice on Wednesday.

Bailey finished the Jets’ 28-25 loss to the Dolphins on Sunday but felt “lingering” discomfort on Monday.

“I see [him] as seeing how the week goes,” head coach Aaron Glenn said about Bailey’s status for the Jets’ Week 8 game against the Raiders on Sunday at MetLife Stadium.

Bailey, whom the Jets drafted with the No. 2-overall pick, has been a rare bright spot in another otherwise dreary season.

He’s recorded 5 ½ sacks, nine quarterback hits, three forced fumbles and seven tackles for loss across his first seven games in the NFL. He broke out with three sacks during the team’s Week 5 win over the Browns, earning him a Rookie of the Week honor.

It’s part of larger injury uncertainty on the defensive line.

T’Vondre Sweat (knee) also did not practice on Wednesday. Neither did Joseph Ossai, who missed the last two weeks with an ankle injury. Both Sweat and Ossai are considered week-to-week, Glenn said.
