text:
Denver Broncos wide receiver Jaylen Waddle (chest) "suffered an aggravation of his previous chest injury" on Sunday, according to NFL Network's Ian Rapoport. His status for this weekend's game against the Kansas City Chiefs "will be determined at a later time," according to Rapoport. That seems to be a roundabout way of saying Waddle has an uncertain status going into Week 8.

"There is hope" the receiver will be able to play against the Chiefs, according to KUSA-TV's Mike Klis. Waddle is expected to be listed as questionable on the team's injury report later this week, Klis reported Wednesday.

Waddle went down in the fourth quarter of Sunday's game after a botched end-around. After landing on his own fumble, Waddle initially stayed on the ground before later walking to the sideline and then walking into the locker room with staff members. After an eventual 30-16 win, Broncos coach Sean Payton apologized for calling the "dumb" play that led to Waddle's injury.

Denver announced Waddle as questionable to return against the Arizona Cardinals, but the 27-year-old receiver did not finish the game. He was previously limited in two days of practice last week with a chest injury.

Waddle caused a bit of a panic when he was spotted wearing a walking boot after a game earlier this season, but that foot injury did not cause him to miss any games. Waddle also had an injury scare against the Seattle Seahawks in Week 6, but later returned to the game.

The dinged-up receiver has totaled 26 receptions for 276 yards and one touchdown through the first seven games of the season. That's surely not the kind of production the Broncos were hoping for when they traded a first-round draft pick (and more) to the Miami Dolphins in exchange for Waddle earlier this year.

text:
Zac Taylor and his team are running back onto the practice field this afternoon after the Week 7 win over the Baltimore Ravens. Cincinnati unfortunately had to put Erick All (knee) on season-ending injured reserve with his third career torn right ACL, and Kyle Dugger (quad) isn't playing this week against Tennessee.

Other than that, Cincinnati doesn't have many injury issues to worry about. Names like WR Andrei Iosivas (finger) and CB Jalen Davis (hamstring) have both been out the minimum four weeks on short-term IR.

They should be back to normal practices soon. It's just been a horrible few days for All, while Dugger is "week to week" with his injury.

"It's awful for him," Taylor said about All. "He's been through this a couple of times before. We'll be there to support him in his recovery and rehab. But it just sucks for him. This means so much to him. He's worked so hard to get himself back."

The Bengals are currently the seventh seed in the AFC as they keep trying to push for an AFC North title.

They are 3-2 in the AFC and cannot afford a loss to the one-win Titans. Bottling the second-half output from Sunday and sprinkling it into every game moving forward won't hurt the Bengals' chances of contending this season.

"I just am really proud of our guys, to be flat out honest with you," Taylor said about beating Baltimore. "I am just proud of the way they responded. When you coach, and you're in that position, and you think you know how they're going to respond, but to just see everybody step up at every position, every coach, and respond that way on the road in the second half – it just makes you really proud, and that's what makes you fired up. It's nothing more than that. It's your team responding the right way and putting together a significant win, and it fires you up."

Cincinnati's defense has been so much better in 2026 compared to last season.

The Bengals rank 11th in the NFL in EPA/play allowed (26th last season).

"If we're going to continue to be great in the red zone and really good at short yardage, it's going to be really difficult for people to put points up on the board, and we got to take a lot of pride in that," Taylor said. "And sometimes it's after long drives where you've been on the field for eight minutes, and it's defeating because they've converted third downs and gotten big plays, and you got to overcome adversity, and then you got to just buckle up and hold them to a field goal."

Cincinnati takes on the Titans at 1 p.m. ET on Sunday.

title: Study estimates that 75% of former NFL players who died between 2008-2023 had CTE
description:
A new study estimates that nearly 75% of all NFL players who died between 2008 and 2023 had chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE) neuropathology.
Researchers caution that the new study’s estimate of prevalence only applies to former NFL players after death.
It does not predict how many living former players have CTE or how many active players are impacted.
This estimate was made possible by understanding the differences between NFL players whose brains were donated and NFL players whose brains were not donated.
Among the 387 deceased NFL players that were studied, 362 (94%) had some degree of CTE neuropathology.
text:
A new study estimates that nearly 75% of all NFL players who died between 2008 and 2023 had chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE) neuropathology. CTE is a neurodegenerative disease that has been diagnosed in individuals with substantial exposure to repetitive head impacts. It can only be definitively diagnosed after death.

This study, a collaboration among researchers at Mass General Brigham, Boston University and the Concussion & CTE Foundation, was published in JAMA Network Open Open external link in a new window . Researchers caution that the new study’s estimate of prevalence only applies to former NFL players after death. It does not predict how many living former players have CTE or how many active players are impacted.

The new findings build on an August 2026 study Open external link in a new window from the same research group that estimated that between 25% and 98% of former NFL players who died between 2016 and 2021 had CTE. The wide range reflected uncertainty about how representative brain donors were of the overall NFL population. Brain donors are more likely to have symptoms believed to be related to CTE, a concept known as selection bias.

“These findings are concerning, but they do not mean former NFL players are destined to develop dementia,” said co-author Daniel Daneshvar, MD, PhD Open external link in a new window , Chair of Physical Medicine and Rehabilitation at Mass General Brigham and Earl P. and Ida S. Charlton Associate Professor at Harvard Medical School. “In our clinic with former players, particularly those in midlife, we have had success improving cognitive symptoms, mental health and quality of life through both targeted treatments and proactive brain health strategies. While we cannot yet treat the underlying CTE pathology, our goal is to bend the curve of brain aging, extend brain healthspan and help players feel and function better throughout their lives.”

For the new study, researchers analyzed selection bias to estimate the prevalence of CTE in players they didn’t directly study. This estimate was made possible by understanding the differences between NFL players whose brains were donated and NFL players whose brains were not donated. Among the 387 deceased NFL players that were studied, 362 (94%) had some degree of CTE neuropathology. Researchers then studied available records of death certificates from the National Death Index for all 2,362 NFL players from this era, which included data on how many died of neurodegenerative disease and had dementia.

Researchers also analyzed other factors associated with brain donation, including cognitive symptoms, age at death, position and years played in the NFL. From this analysis, they estimated that former players with cognitive symptoms were about five times more likely to have their brains donated by their family than those without such symptoms. They used this estimated selection ratio to adjust the 94% prevalence of CTE observed among brain donors to an overall estimate of 74.5%.

This is the first estimate of CTE neuropathology prevalence among all 2,362 deceased former NFL players, including those who did not have their brains donated and were not measured directly. In comparison, CTE is rare in the general population and has been seen in less than 1% of thousands of brain donors to community brain banks in the United States, Australia, Austria and Brazil.

Not every player with CTE pathology will go on to develop symptoms, particularly in cases of early-stage disease. Among players who do develop symptoms of CTE, common manifestations include cognitive impairment, behavioral changes and dementia. Dementia is a general term for a severe decline in memory, reasoning and language function that interferes with everyday functioning and independence. Previous studies have shown NFL players develop dementia at four times the rate of the population. No other environmental or occupational exposure ever studied is known to have increased dementia risk at death by that much.

“We would like to thank the former NFL player community for their support of this research that is answering an important public health question on the relationship of tackle football and CTE,” said Yorghos Tripodis, PhD, senior author of this study and professor of biostatistics at Boston University School of Public Health. “We recognize these findings may cause concern for the community of living players and their families. We want them to know that we and others are standing by to provide support, and that we have hope for those living with CTE. Discoveries from the brain bank have already brought us significantly closer to a diagnosis during life, at which point our most important goal will be to develop effective treatments for CTE.”

Former NFL players concerned about their brain health should consider being evaluated by a clinician who specializes in neurodegenerative conditions. While it's not always possible to eliminate long-term risk, identifying and addressing modifiable risk factors can support brain health and improve quality of life.

text:
The Buffalo Bills’ players and coaches may have been on a bye week over the last several days, but that wasn’t the case for the majority of teams in the league in Week 7 as the NFL was jam packed with plenty of exciting action last weekend.

For Buffalo’s upcoming opponent—the Baltimore Ravens—things weren’t so exciting on Sunday, though, as the AFC North squad fell short at home to the Cincinnati Bengals, 35-13, after originally leading 13-0 at halftime. The loss marked the team’s second straight in its division to fall to 4-3 on the season under first-year head coach Jesse Minter.

Furthermore, Baltimore appears to have lost an important member of its offensive line during the last matchup with Cincinnati, as well, as NFL insiders Ian Rapoport and Mike Garafolo reported on Tuesday morning that Ravens’ starting offensive guard Olaivavega “Vega” Ioane, who was selected at pick No. 14 overall in the first round of the 2026 NFL Draft out Penn State this past spring, suffered a MCL sprain against the Bengals.

A 22-year-old native of Graham, Washington, Ioane was the fourth offensive lineman selected in the first round of April’s draft, but he was also the first guard to go off the board.

Seen by many talent evaluators as a sure-fire NFL starter, Ioane seamlessly transitioned into the starting lineup for Baltimore this offseason.

Making starts at right guard and center out of necessity due to various other injured players going down earlier this season up front for the Ravens, the former Nittany Lions’ lineman has been a solid presence along the offensive line during his first season as a professional.

In fact, according to the NFL’s Next Gen Stats, the 6-foot-4, 326-pound thumper allowed only a 4.6% pressure rate entering Week 6, and he surrendered zero sacks in 163 pass-blocking snaps (84 at RG, 79 at C), as well, making him the highest-rated rookie guard in the NFL in that critical department.

Baltimore’s list of ailments keep compounding entering Week 8

For that reason, the news of Ioane being sidelined for at least “a little bit” is certainly brutal information to receive at this juncture of the season, especially considering that Baltimore’s franchise veteran quarterback Lamar Jackson is likely set to return to the lineup after missing the past three games with an apparent ankle injury.

If the rookie stalwart is unable to suit up against the Bills this weekend at Highmark Stadium in Orchard Park, then it will mean that the Ravens will be trotting out their sixth different offensive line combination through the first eight weeks of 2026 campaign.

And, while that’s a sight that Buffalo’s AFC counterpart likely doesn’t want to see this weekend, it’s certainly a situation that the Bills and defensive coordinator Jim Leonhard will have to capitalize on.

Bills’ interior DL needs to dominate with Ioane likely out

Whether it be up-and-coming defensive star Deone Walker or former top-10 pick Ed Oliver on the interior of Buffalo’s defensive front, someone on the defensive line needs to dominate their battle with Baltimore’s backup at right guard on Sunday.

The matchup between the Bills and Ravens has future playoff implications written all over it, so it’ll be imperative that Buffalo takes full advantage of any areas of weakness that their upcoming opponent might have.

The objective for first-year head coach Joe Brady has seemingly always been to reach the No. 1 seed in the AFC during his inaugural season as the head man in charge in Western New York, and that goal appears to be more in reach than ever before entering November 2026, especially after the Kansas City Chiefs just dropped their first game of the season on Sunday Night Football against the Seattle Seahawks.

Out of the bye week, Brady and Leonhard must create a plan of attack to push forward with vengeance over the final 11 games of the season.

Exploiting Baltimore’s shortcomings up front would be a great place to start on Sunday.

concussionandcte

Verified

40m

A new study estimates 75% of former NFL players who died between 2008-2023 had CTE.

It’s a difficult number to confront, especially for former players and families already concerned about their brain health. But it’s also an important step forward in understanding CTE.

For years, researchers have found CTE in a high percentage of former NFL players whose brains were donated to science. But what about the players whose brains weren’t donated? This new study helps answer that question by accounting for potential bias in brain donations, providing a more representative estimate of CTE among deceased former NFL players.

As former NFL quarterback @hasselbeck puts it, knowing what we’re up against gives us a better chance of winning. And there’s reason for hope.

Every new discovery brings us closer to understanding CTE, developing ways to diagnose it during life, and ultimately finding effective treatments. This research can also help inform efforts to make the game safer for future generations.

Importantly, these findings don’t tell us how many living NFL players have CTE, and not everyone with CTE pathology develops symptoms.

For former players and families concerned about their brain health, you are not alone, and help is available.

Visit ConcussionAndCTE.org/HelpLine for guidance and support. Former NFL players can also access resources through The Trust Powered by the @NFLPA, the NFLPA’s Professional Athletes Foundation, and the NFL Life Line (800-453-0078), which provides independent, confidential support 24/7.

The study was published today in JAMA Network Open and led by @bu_cte in collaboration with @massgeneralbrigham and the Concussion & CTE Foundation.

text:
While on a short week, an injury to starting right guard Travis Glover could force the Green Bay Packers to finally give veteran Kevin Zeitler a chance to start along the offensive line on Thursday night against the Carolina Panthers.

Glover, who has started the last four games at right guard, is dealing with a knee injury and was estimated as a non-participant on Monday and a non-participant during Tuesday's walkthrough. After playing every snap against the Detroit Lions on Sunday, Glover reported the knee injury after coming into the facility on Monday.

Coach Matt LaFleur wasn't willing to give away his plans if Glover can't play, but Zeitler, who signed with the Packers nearly a month ago, has to be an option.

Is he ready to go?

“If we need him, absolutely. I feel confident with him,” LaFleur said.

Zeitler had surgery in the offseason and didn't get a training camp, so he required a ramp up period physically on top of learning a new offensive system. Since arriving in Green Bay, Zeitler has not played a single snap on offense, and he was inactive on Sunday in Detroit.

“I think he's done a nice job," LaFleur said. "Here's a guy that came in and didn't have an offseason, didn't have training camp, and he's kind of gradually working his way back into it.”

The Packers will release a final injury report with status designations on Wednesday. Expect to see Glover with one of the three designations: questionable, doubtful or out.

There are other options if Glover can't go. Veteran Mekhi Becton was signed from the practice squad on Monday. Aaron Banks is finally getting healthy. Donovan Jennings has started games at guard in 2026.

But it might be Zeiter's time.

"We knew it was going to be fluid. Any time you have a guy that's new to it, you have to let it happen naturally. When he's ready to roll, he'll be out there," LaFleur said.

It's possible that moment is finally arriving for Zeitler.

title: Jalen Hurts, player safety and the NFL's ethical tipping point - Andscape
description:
PHILADELPHIA — On Monday, Philadelphia Eagles quarterback Jalen Hurts was missing in action in a 38-21 loss to the Dallas Cowboys.
For Philadelphia, the curious high point of Monday evening’s NFL game was the induction of team owner Jeffrey Lurie into the Eagles Hall of Fame.
Lurie, who purchased the franchise in 1994, is generally regarded as one of the more enlightened NFL team owners.
The NFL and the National Football League Players Association have agreed to collaborate on an investigation of the Hurts saga.
What I am suggesting is that the NFL once again is creeping toward an ethical tipping point.
text:
PHILADELPHIA — On Monday, Philadelphia Eagles quarterback Jalen Hurts was missing in action in a 38-21 loss to the Dallas Cowboys. This was the fifth consecutive defeat for Philadelphia, but the team and the league may have lost something far more significant during this stretch:

Credibility and trust.

For Philadelphia, the curious high point of Monday evening’s NFL game was the induction of team owner Jeffrey Lurie into the Eagles Hall of Fame. Lurie, who purchased the franchise in 1994, is generally regarded as one of the more enlightened NFL team owners.

But his induction seemed ill-timed considering the mystery that continues to swirl around the blood clots that have Hurts out for the season.

As of Monday night’s game, there had not been a statement from Eagles ownership or medical staff about the series of medical decisions earlier this month that appeared to put Hurts’s health at risk. And now the Eagles are engulfed in a nightmare of a season highlighted by Hurts’s absence.

Hurts traveled to London for the team’s game on Oct. 11 against Jacksonville and was cleared to play a day after being diagnosed with a superficial blood clot. The game ended disastrously for the Eagles, who blew a late lead by allowing a long kickoff return that set up the Jaguars’ walk-off field goal to win.

That loss began a spiral that deepened Monday, when Philadelphia lost its fifth consecutive game to the Cowboys.

Hurts was ruled out for the season on Oct. 19 after tests revealed that the clot in his left calf had spread to his lungs. Eagles fans are getting a glimpse of what life could be without the 28-year-old quarterback who has led the franchise to two Super Bowls, winning one.

But all of this goes beyond wins and losses. Hurts may be a casualty of the NFL’s unchecked ambition to make money.

The NFL and the National Football League Players Association have agreed to collaborate on an investigation of the Hurts saga. This in and of itself is a potential conflict of interest and a test of whether the NFLPA is truly independent and operating in the best interest of players.

The expanded international menu of games puts the NFL at odds with its stated concerns for player welfare. This season, the NFL is sponsoring a record nine regular-season games outside the United States — spanning seven cities across four continents.

For the league, these international trips mean new markets, new audiences and new revenue. For players, the trips represent another set of demands on bodies already compromised by the rigors of a violent sport. The long flights and the altered routines mean less time to recover.

But everyone is making money hand over fist: team owners, players, and partners. Even those of us who write about and broadcast league activities have unending source material. Yet, sometimes the hypocrisy slaps you in a way you can’t ignore.

New York Giants running back Cam Skattebo called out the NFL on Sunday after he was penalized for unnecessary roughness because he lowered his helmet during a run. This is a penalty rarely called on offensive players.

Skattebo addressed the controversial call after Sunday’s overtime victory over Houston, expressing frustration with what he viewed as inconsistent treatment from the league.

“The NFL loves to post me when I do stuff like that, but then also wants to take stuff from me,” Skattebo said. “I’m going to run the ball like I want to run the ball.”

Skattebo was humorously defiant as he delivered a message about the possibility of future penalties and fines.

“If I’m going to continue to get flags for it or fined for it, guess I’m going to play for free,” he said.

Skattebo will no doubt receive a message from the league to tone it down. The NFL loves his recklessness, but likely not his insight.

Meanwhile, through all of this, the NFL insists it has everything under control: It cares about player safety, international schedules are carefully planned, and gambling partnerships are responsibly regulated.

But at a time when guardrails that get in the way of making money are being removed, it’s reasonable to ask the NFL if its guardrails are strong enough to contain its ever-expanding commercial interests.

Since being exposed two decades ago for mishandling concussions, the NFL has framed itself as a paragon of player safety — all while deepening ties with a gambling industry that profits off on-field performance.

The league pats itself on the back for establishing safety guardrails even as it sends players around the world to play regular-season games.

I’m not naïve. The NFL is built on violence. Violence is the NFL’s most unique and attractive selling point. Players and coaches routinely — and proudly — talk about football having a 100% injury rate. We’ve all become anesthetized to the violence and the reality that, on every other play, someone is slow getting up or carted off the field.

The league dodged a bullet three seasons ago when Damar Hamlin survived a cardiac arrest suffered during a Monday Night Football game. We accept the violence, write about it, and write around it.

But there’s something troubling about the Hurts situation, even as we move on to Week 8. You have a star quarterback, the face of the franchise, one of the faces of the league, who’s out for the season not because of a torn ligament or sprained ankle or dislocated shoulder, but because his organization may have misjudged a life-threatening illness. And its reaction to the potential misjudgment comes off as a coverup.

I am not suggesting that the trip to London and back caused or aggravated Hurts’s blood clots. We don’t know. What I am suggesting is that the NFL once again is creeping toward an ethical tipping point.

The league is a unique industry that runs on the blood, sweat, broken bones and torn ligaments of young men who willingly lease their bodies in pursuit of fame, fortune and a hefty payday. In pursuit of new markets and money streams, the NFL seems to be willing to cross every line.

It’s up to owners like Lurie to prove their Hall-of-Fame mettle by reining in this monster before somebody gets hurt. We may have already passed that point.

The Kansas City Chiefs had an uphill battle against the Seattle Seahawks on Sunday Night Football.

The Chiefs entered Sunday's matchup without starting right tackle Jaylon Moore, who was sidelined by a concussion, and left tackle Josh Simmons, who remained out with a back injury. They were also missing injured receivers Rashee Rice and Tyquan Thornton.

That showed up in the final score, as they were dominated 20-3. However, in the fourth quarter, when the game was still conceivably within reach, a critical error from Xavier Worthy left Patrick Mahomes uncharacteristically frustrated.

Fans, though, weren't fully sure if his reaction was justified.

Fans Take Notice of Patrick Mahomes' Frustration With Xavier Worthy

Coming into the game, the Chiefs had a top-10 unit in PFN's Offense Impact Metric. But a lot of that had to do with the explosion from Kenneth Walker III, who leads the league in rushing yards by a sizeable margin.

The passing game left a lot to be desired, and that was before their two best receivers went down with injuries. Against the Seahawks, as Walker struggled and finished with just 36 rushing yards, the depleted receiving corps wasn't enough to sustain the Chiefs.

Things came to a head in the fourth quarter. In what was shaping up to be their best drive of the game, the Chiefs came up to the 45-yard line. On 1st-and-10, Mahomes threw a perfect ball for Worthy to catch and run.

However, Worthy failed to secure the pass, prompting a visibly frustrated reaction from Mahomes. Although Kansas City continued moving the ball afterward, the possession ultimately ended without points when Harrison Butker missed a 45-yard field goal.

Worthy finished with only three catches for 11 yards on six targets, underscoring Kansas City's inability to generate meaningful production from its available wide receivers.

"You don't often see Patrick Mahomes show frustration like this," Henry McKenna of Fox Sports was quick to notice. "But after Xavier Worthy's drop… the QB was upset."

"Cause he's seen this for 3 years," one fan argued for Mahomes. "He's sick of this [expletive]… And I don't blame him."

One fan jokingly claimed, "He was seeing ghosts of Toney and Moore there," while another fan explained, "Inconsistency is the running theme for Chiefs WRs in recent years. Yes, Mahomes' reaction is warranted. Worthy making catches last week, then dropping crucial ones is absurd."

For one fan, though, it was becoming a more common sight to see Mahomes upset. With the offensive unit not working as seamlessly as it has over the years, he believes they have lost the punch they once had.

"You see frustration from Mahomes plenty of the time, especially over the last few years as the offense has performed worse and worse,"the fan claimed. "Should've known that things would never stay the way they were with Kelce & Hill."

For one fan, though, one drop from Worthy couldn't take away from an all-around underwhelming night for Mahomes. Coming into the game at number 10 in PFN's Quarterback Impact Metric, he finished with just 165 yards and an interception.

"Mahomes was awful," one fan announced. "So, let's not blame Worthy for Mahomes not being able to handle the Hawks' defense."

It remains to be seen if this was a blip for the Chiefs, given the particularly strenuous circumstances in this game, or a canary in the coal mine for the problems plaguing this roster. Still at 5-1, they are at the top of the AFC West, but the margin for error is slim.

With the Denver Broncos hot on their heels, Week 8's game could have major implications. And with the wide receiving room looking like it needs a clear upgrade, this game may have been the most obvious indicator of their need for a difference-maker.

title: How NFL Injury Protection Works After a Player Is Released - Football Nation
description:
The ordinary Injury Protection Benefit applies to the season after the injury season.
Injury Protection focuses on a severe football injury and future physical inability.
NFL Football Operations explains that injury guarantees are negotiated contract protection, while Article 45 creates a separate collectively bargained benefit.
Related Football Nation guide: How NFL Termination Pay Protects Vested Veterans The Article 45 qualification test Article 45, Section 2 requires the player’s contract to have been terminated by his club.
Guaranteed Paragraph 5 Salary for the next two seasons offsets Injury Protection and Extended Injury Protection dollar for dollar.
text:
A player can be released while still unable to play and still have a path to compensation in a later season. That path is NFL Injury Protection. It is a collectively bargained benefit, not a promise that every injured player receives the rest of his contract.

Information cutoff: October 28, 2026 at 3:57 AM Central. The governing source is the 2020 NFL and NFLPA Collective Bargaining Agreement, which runs through the 2030 season. This guide explains Article 45 as written and is educational, not legal advice.

What Article 45 protects

Article 45 covers a severe football injury from an NFL game or practice when a club terminates the player’s contract and the player remains unable to play through the required examination process. The ordinary Injury Protection Benefit applies to the season after the injury season. Extended Injury Protection can apply to the second season after the injury.

This is different from Termination Pay. Termination Pay protects certain vested veterans after a release for performance or roster reasons. Injury Protection focuses on a severe football injury and future physical inability. It also differs from an injury guarantee written into an individual contract. NFL Football Operations explains that injury guarantees are negotiated contract protection, while Article 45 creates a separate collectively bargained benefit.

Related Football Nation guide: How NFL Termination Pay Protects Vested Veterans

The Article 45 qualification test

Article 45, Section 2 requires the player’s contract to have been terminated by his club. The player must then satisfy each required condition.

1. The season ending condition

Section 2(a) says the player must have been physically unable to participate in all or part of the club’s final game because of a severe football injury, as certified after an examination by the club physician. Club authorized surgery in the following offseason can also satisfy this part.

2. Required rehabilitation

Section 2(b) requires the player to complete the reasonable and customary rehabilitation required by the club. The club pays those rehabilitation costs even if it no longer employs him.

3. The benefit physical

Section 2(c) requires the player to fail the club examination for Injury Protection on or before August 1 in the next season. The exam must be identified in writing as the Injury Protection examination. The club cannot avoid liability by refusing a timely exam when the player cooperates.

4. The contract link

Section 2(d) addresses an expired contract. If the player signs with the prior club for the next season, eligibility can continue when every other condition is met. A contract with a new club does not create the benefit under that new contract.

The examination is injury specific. It is not a general judgment that the player can never play again. A player may be unable to perform his position at the required NFL level on the exam date and still recover later.

What the benefit pays in 2026

Article 45, Section 3 starts with 100 percent of the player’s Paragraph 5 Salary for the season after the injury. Paragraph 5 Salary is the contract’s base salary. For the 2026 League Year, the benefit is capped at $2.1 million.

Guaranteed Paragraph 5 Salary for the next two seasons offsets Injury Protection and Extended Injury Protection dollar for dollar. Payments arrive in equal weekly installments no later than the first regular season game, and they stop if the player signs with another club for that season. A player may receive the ordinary Injury Protection Benefit only once during his NFL career.

The salary cap treatment is split. Article 45, Section 4 assigns up to $1.26 million of a 2026 payment to the prior club’s Team Salary. The balance, up to the $2.1 million maximum, is a Player Benefit Cost.

Related Football Nation guide: How Void Years Work in NFL Contracts and the Salary Cap

Extended Injury Protection

Sections 7 and 8 create a second layer for the second season after the injury. The player generally must have qualified for the first benefit, must have a contract covering the second season, must remain unable to play because of the same severe football injury, must continue the required rehabilitation, and must fail the former club’s designated examination before June 1.

For 2026, Extended Injury Protection equals 100 percent of Paragraph 5 Salary for that second season, capped at $1.05 million unless the player negotiated greater protection. Guaranteed salary offsets it. The benefit is also limited to once in a career and stops if the player signs with another club for that season.

Article 45, Section 12 sets separate deadlines. An ordinary Injury Protection grievance must be initiated by October 15 of the League Year in which the benefit is claimed. A player seeking the extended benefit must notify the former club and the NFL in writing by January 31 that he believes he remains physically unable to play.

Two realistic examples

Example 1: base salary below the cap

A defensive tackle suffers a serious knee injury in December, misses the club’s final game, follows the club rehabilitation plan and fails the Injury Protection physical before August 1. The club terminates his contract. His next season Paragraph 5 Salary is $1.4 million and none is guaranteed. If the other Article 45 conditions are met, the benefit begins at $1.4 million because that salary is below the 2026 maximum.

Example 2: salary above the cap with an offset

A receiver has a $3 million Paragraph 5 Salary scheduled for the next season and $800,000 of that salary is guaranteed. He satisfies Section 2. The 2026 benefit is first limited to $2.1 million, then the $800,000 guaranteed salary offsets the benefit. The remaining Article 45 amount is $1.3 million. If the facts or contract language differ, the result can change.

Injury grievance, injury settlement and Injury Protection are not the same

The NFLPA describes an injury grievance as a claim that a player was released while unable to play. It generally seeks salary from the season of release and must usually be filed within 25 days. Article 45 protection concerns later seasons and uses its own deadlines. The NFLPA also warns that an injury settlement can end treatment obligations, current year salary claims and future Injury Protection rights. Released and settled should never be treated as interchangeable.

A roster transaction such as injured reserve answers a different question. Remaining under contract on injured reserve is not the same as being released and pursuing Article 45 benefits. Activation from the physically unable to perform list signals roster availability, not an Article 45 award.

Related Football Nation guide: What Does IR Mean in Fantasy Football?

Related Football Nation report: Lions Place Tom Kennedy, Ben Bartch and Devin White on Injured Reserve

Related Football Nation report: Steelers Activate Jalen Ramsey From PUP

Football and roster consequence

The rule gives clubs a financial reason to track severe injuries beyond the season in which they happen. A release does not automatically erase the prior club’s obligation. Medical certification, rehabilitation records, exam dates and the old contract all matter. For a front office, the question is not simply whether the player occupies a roster spot. It is whether Article 45 creates a future payment and cap charge.

Fantasy consequence

An Injury Protection claim is evidence of a serious recovery problem at a defined exam date, but it is not a return timetable and it does not predict a depth chart role. Fantasy managers should treat it as context that the player was not ready for football activity when examined. The next actionable checkpoints are a new contract, a passed physical, roster placement and practice participation. The benefit itself does not make the player more likely to produce fantasy points.

The strongest counterargument

The strongest criticism is that Injury Protection sounds broader than it is. That criticism is fair. The benefit is conditional, capped, offset by guaranteed salary, tied to strict medical and filing steps, and generally available only once in a career. It is not full contract insurance. Its value is narrower: it prevents a qualifying severe football injury from becoming a total financial cliff merely because the club terminated the contract.

Common misconceptions

Misconception: every player released while hurt gets the next year’s salary. Reality: Article 45 requires the severe football injury, rehabilitation, examination and contract conditions in Section 2.

Misconception: the benefit means the entire contract is guaranteed. Reality: the calculation uses Paragraph 5 Salary, applies a 2026 maximum and includes offsets.

Misconception: filing an injury grievance automatically secures Article 45 money. Reality: the grievance for the release season and the later season benefit are distinct claims with different rules and deadlines.

Misconception: a player receiving the benefit cannot return. Reality: payments stop if he signs with another club for that season. The rule protects recovery, not retirement.

Frequently asked questions

Does the club pay rehabilitation costs after release?

Yes, when the rehabilitation is the reasonable and customary treatment required under Article 45, Section 2(b). Section 13 also assigns reasonable rehabilitation and club requested examination travel costs to the club.

Can a player collect the benefit twice after two different injuries?

The ordinary benefit is limited to once during an NFL playing career. The extended benefit also has a once per career limit.

Does workers’ compensation disappear?

No. Article 45, Section 11 coordinates the benefits. It treats 50 percent of Injury Protection payments as equivalent to workers’ compensation indemnity and permits a corresponding offset against qualifying state indemnity awards, but not medical coverage awards.

What should readers watch next?

The next checkpoints are the August 1 ordinary benefit physical, the October 15 ordinary claim deadline, the January 31 extended notice deadline and the June 1 extended benefit physical. Individual players should rely on the NFLPA and qualified counsel for case specific advice.

title: 2028 NFL Draft Picture Uncertain as Projected No. 1 QB Suffers Season-Ending Injury
description:
Four games into the season, Kamario Taylor had 14 touchdown passes, an unbeaten Mississippi State team, and a place in the Heisman conversation.
His breakout also carried implications beyond the Bulldogs’ season, putting him among the quarterbacks to watch for the 2028 NFL Draft.
“Sources: Mississippi State star QB Kamario Taylor will miss the rest of the season, as he faces surgery on his injured toe.
His injury interrupted that early momentum just as Mississippi State entered the tougher stretch of its SEC schedule.
The Macon, Mississippi, native has expressed his commitment to staying at Mississippi State.
text:
Four games into the season, Kamario Taylor had 14 touchdown passes, an unbeaten Mississippi State team, and a place in the Heisman conversation. His breakout also carried implications beyond the Bulldogs’ season, putting him among the quarterbacks to watch for the 2028 NFL Draft. But sustaining that rise would prove more complicated than his fast start suggested.

“Sources: Mississippi State star QB Kamario Taylor will miss the rest of the season, as he faces surgery on his injured toe. Taylor has an appointment today to get his toe checked out by a specialist and could have surgery as early as tomorrow. He’s expected to make a full recovery,” ESPN’s Pete Thamel reported on X.

Taylor first injured his toe during Mississippi State’s win over Missouri on September 26. The school announced the decision on Tuesday. The goal is to help him recover in time for the 2027 season. Thamel shared more details in another post.

“Sources said that Taylor pushed hard to play after the injury. It became clear that time and rest weren’t going to get to him to a point where he could be effective.”

Taylor tried to play against Alabama on October 3 and Oklahoma on Saturday, but the injury clearly affected him. He left both games early and missed the Bulldogs’ October 17 game against LSU.

Against Oklahoma, Taylor appeared to hurt his toe further when he was tackled during a scramble. Mississippi State lost the game 23-15. However, head coach Jeff Lebby said Taylor had aggravated his existing injury and had not suffered a new one.

The injury comes at a difficult time for Taylor. Before it happened, he was one of college football’s breakout stars. He helped Mississippi State start the season 4-0, with wins over Minnesota, South Carolina, and Missouri. The Bulldogs also climbed into the national top 25.

That start also put Taylor in the Heisman Trophy conversation. Through four games, he was tied for the national lead with 14 touchdown passes and had climbed to third in BetMGM’s Heisman odds. His injury interrupted that early momentum just as Mississippi State entered the tougher stretch of its SEC schedule.

His performance against then-No. 19 Missouri was a highlight. Taylor completed 27 of 38 passes for 360 yards, three touchdowns, and one interception.

Taylor finished his season with 1,460 passing yards and 17 touchdown passes. He completed more than 65% of his passes before the injury cut his season short.

He also contributed on the ground, finishing with 147 rushing yards and one touchdown on 46 carries. That brought his combined passing and rushing production to 1,607 yards and 18 touchdowns.

At 6-foot-4 and 230 pounds, Taylor is already attracting attention as a future NFL prospect. He currently ranks No. 1 on the consensus big board for the 2028 NFL Draft.

Taylor belongs to the 2025 recruiting class, meaning the 2027 season would be his third year in college. The 2028 NFL Draft would follow that season.

For now, the focus is on his recovery. Surgery is expected to help him get ready for the 2027 season, and Thamel reported that Taylor is expected to make a full recovery. However, it remains to be seen how missing the rest of this season will affect his future draft evaluation.

Mississippi State, meanwhile, has struggled since its strong start. The Bulldogs are 4-3 overall and 2-3 in SEC play after losing three straight games to Alabama, LSU, and Oklahoma. No. 11 Texas is next on their schedule.

With Taylor out for the season, Lebby must choose a starting quarterback. He has not named a replacement, but the decision rests between Billy Puckett, who has already filled in for Taylor this season, and Appalachian State transfer AJ Swann.

As the Bulldogs prepare to move forward without him, Taylor will focus on surgery and recovery ahead of the 2027 season. His procedure could take place as early as Wednesday. The Macon, Mississippi, native has expressed his commitment to staying at Mississippi State.

text:
Green Bay Packers superstar Micah Parsons is getting closer to his long-awaited return from last season's torn ACL.

Head coach Matt LaFleur told reporters on Monday he's hoping the dynamic edge-rusher returns to practice next week:

Parsons, 27, was traded by the Dallas Cowboys to the Packers ahead of the 2025 season and was having a fantastic debut season, registering 41 tackles (12 for loss), 12.5 sacks, 27 quarterback hits, two forced fumbles and a pass defensed in 14 games.

But he tore his ACL during a December matchup against the Denver Broncos, ending his season and calling into question when he would be able to return for the 2026 campaign.

The Packers could use him back. The team is tied for 15th in the NFL with 16 sacks on the season, though the pass defense has been solid in general (208 YPG, ninth in the NFL). Still, the team finds itself last in the loaded NFC North despite being 4-3 overall and has gone just 1-2 against its divisional rivals thus far.

Next week would make for a logical potential return point, at least to practice. Because the Packers play on Thursday night this week against the Carolina Panthers, they'll have a longer runway before a Week 9 contest against the New England Patriots. But the team also has a Week 11 bye, which means Parsons' return to game action might be delayed until Week 12.

"At the end of the day, that's the medical," LaFleur told reporters about how it will be decided to clear Parsons for practice. "I'm itching at it though, for sure."

Bo Nix opened up the Broncos offense with a 62-yard touchdown run. More importantly, the third-year quarterback began to push the ball downfield more against the Arizona Cardinals than he did during Denver’s previous six games.

text:
What started as a slip has turned into a spiral for the 2-5 Eagles, who have now dropped five straight games with a roster that is battered and bruised.

And that’s reflected in the national power rankings, where the Eagles sit among the bottom 10 teams in the NFL following a 38-21 loss to their division rival Dallas Cowboys on Monday.

The Eagles have another NFC East matchup against the Commanders on Sunday Night Football (8:20 p.m., NBC). Here’s how they rank across several outlets heading into Week 8.

ESPN: 23rd

Moving down two spots, the Eagles fell to 23rd on the ESPN Power Rankings.

And even though there has been a lot that has gone wrong for the Eagles, ESPN’s Tim McManus sees a bright spot in the Eagles offense: Wide receiver Dontayvion Wicks, who they acquired in April through a trade with the Packers.

» READ MORE: Jalen Carter, Jordan Davis and an Eagles D-line that was torn apart by the Cowboys

“He quickly established himself as the No. 2 wideout behind DeVonta Smith, ranked second on the team in receiving yards (284), first in catches that resulted in a first down (16) and tied for first in receptions of 20-plus yards (three),” McManus wrote. “An ankle injury sidelined him for Monday night’s game against the Cowboys.”

Monday night was the first game Wicks has missed this season and he is listed as questionable for Week 8.

The Athletic: 23rd

With Halloween on Saturday, The Athletic was celebrating early by finding something spooky with each team in its power rankings. The Eagles, who fell from 20th last week to 23rd, gave Josh Kendall and Chad Graff a lot to choose from.

The Birds may have even presented Graff and Kendall with too many options, leaving them with no choice but to name “this whole season” as the scariest thing about the Eagles right now.

“Make it five straight defeats in a season that’s quickly unraveling following the loss of Jalen Hurts,” Graff and Kendall wrote. “The offense is a shell of its former self. Even the Vic Fangio-led defense struggled on Monday night, forcing just two punts from the Cowboys, while allowing more than 400 yards of offense.”

Bleacher Report: 24th

Bleacher Report moved the Eagles down one spot to 24th heading into Sunday’s matchup against the Commanders.

Moe Moton was quick to point out how the Eagles remained competitive with backup quarterback Tanner McKee, who appeared more comfortable against the Cowboys.

“Philadelphia is in a lost season, though,” Moton wrote. “McKee won’t salvage it, and Saquon Barkley couldn’t finish the game because of a back injury. The Eagles are free-falling in the power rankings following a fifth consecutive loss, and they should be sellers at the trade deadline.”

» READ MORE: Murphy: Vic Fangio had no answers for the Cowboys’ run game, which raises questions for an Eagles team on the brink

Yahoo! Sports: 26th

Yahoo! Sports is the only outlet on this list that has the Birds moving up in the rankings, with a small bump from the 27th spot last week.

But that didn’t mean Frank Schwab was holding back in his assessment of a team “that started the season with legitimate hope of being a Super Bowl contender” and now ”could end up with a top-five draft pick in April."

“There is still enough talent on the roster to be competitive in games, but the effort in the second half against Dallas wasn’t inspiring,” Schwab wrote. “Young teams can sometimes play well in the second half of the season as they keep fighting, like the Saints did last season. That usually doesn’t happen for teams that have recently won a championship, were expected to compete for another this season and are already out of the race before the end of October.”

NFL.com: 28th

The lowest ranking from the Eagles this week came from NFL.com’s Nick Shook, who has Philly as a bottom five team at 28th, for the second week in a row.

text:
GREEN BAY, Wis. (AP) — Green Bay Packers running back Josh Jacobs’ season debut showed that he couldn’t instantly solve all of the problems with the NFL’s lowest-ranked rushing attack.

Now that he has a game under his belt, Jacobs is confident that he has shaken off the rust that came from missing the first six games of the season while on the commissioner’s exempt list. The three-time Pro Bowl selection says it’s imperative for the running backs to play more physically as Green Bay adjusts to injuries on its offensive line.

“Sometimes you’re going to have to break them tackles and you’re going to have to keep your feet running,” Jacobs said Tuesday. “You’ve got to give guys the energy and the juice to feel like you’re carrying it. It could be a bad play. You got a pile and you push the pile or whatever. That’s stuff that gets guys energized and ready to go play.”

Jacobs rushed for 36 yards on 11 carries and caught five passes for 55 yards in a 20-17 loss at Detroit that marked his first game since pleading no contest last month to misdemeanor charges of battery and criminal damage to property stemming from a May altercation with his then-girlfriend.

With the Packers driving for a potential go-ahead score on Sunday, Jacobs couldn’t hang on to a pass in the end zone with the score tied and about 3 1/2 minutes left.

“I felt like I beat him so early (that) when I saw the ball, I kind of tried to slow down for the ball, but that’s a play that literally hit both hands,” Jacobs said. “Whenever it hit any hand, for my standard, I feel like you’ve got to catch it.”

The Packers (4-3) are counting on Jacobs to boost a running game that has struggled heading into Thursday night’s game against the Carolina Panthers (3-3).

Green Bay’s 59.9 yards rushing per game are nearly 15 fewer than anyone else.

The only other team in the past 35 seasons to average fewer than 60 yards per rushing through its first seven games was the 2019 Cincinnati Bengals with 53.1.

Considering those numbers, it’s remarkable that Green Bay is above .500. Since 1933, the other 13 teams that averaged below 60 yards rushing through their seven games went a combined 11-79-1 during that stretch.

“If we want to be the team we want to be, we’ve definitely got to improve the run game,” quarterback Jordan Love said.

Carolina could be just what the Packers need.

The Panthers are coming a 43-13 home loss to Tampa Bay in which they allowed the Buccaneers to rush for 258 yards. Green Bay’s season rushing total didn’t reach 258 yards until its fifth game of the season.

But an offensive line decimated by injuries could have trouble creating running room.

Starting center Sean Rhyan (ankle) and backup Jacob Monk (quadriceps) got hurt against Detroit, with Monk landing on injured reserve. Packers coach Matt LaFleur said it’s uncertain whether Rhyan might end up on injured reserve as well.

Green Bay’s center for most of the Lions game was John Williams, who had never played a single snap on offense in his two-year career before Sunday.

Right guard Travis Glover has a knee issue that leaves his status uncertain for Thursday. The Packers already lost right tackle Zach Bako-Bewele to a season-ending knee injury last month.

All those offensive line injuries could make Jacobs’ job tougher. He’s ready to pick up the slack by gaining yards after contact.

“We’ve still got to make plays, and that’s a part of it,” Jacobs said. “Breaking tackles, grinding out those hard yards … turning a 2-yard run into a 4-yard run. That’s things that motivate the guys and also motivate the play-caller. So that’s something that we’ve definitely got to do.”

NOTES: LaFleur said LB Zaire Franklin (shin) will miss a second straight game Thursday. … WR Matthew Golden is on Green Bay’s injury report with shoulder and foot issues. Although the Packers had a walk-through Tuesday and didn’t practice Monday, the Packers estimated that Golden would have been held out each of those days. … LaFleur was asked about the possibility All-Pro edge rusher Micah Parsons could return to practice next week as he continues his recovery from a torn anterior cruciate ligament. “I sure hope so,” LaFleur said.

AP Pro Football Writer Josh Dubow contributed to this report.
