text:
EVANSTON, Ill. — New research from Northwestern’s Kellogg School of Management finds that injury matters less in the NFL than is often assumed. With the exception of highly paid quarterbacks, losing players — even the high-dollar ones — to injury is not as fatal to a team’s success as one might think.

“Ultimately, the NFL is a ‘next man up’ league, where non-stars fill the role of stars reasonably well. My research shows that the team of the injured player would not see a substantial change in their on-field success, the only exception being the highly paid quarterback,” said Joel Shapiro, clinical associate professor of managerial economics and decisions sciences and lead author of the study.

The study, which was published in Sports Economics Review earlier this month, suggests that passing on a talented player because he’s injury-prone, or paying heavily to replace an injured starter midseason, may cost more than the injury and recovery itself. The findings indicate spending money on depth may go further than spending money on durability.

“Executives who want to build a winning team need to ask hard questions about their star players,” Shapiro said. “If a backup can fill in for a few games without a lot of negative impact on winning, how much does the star really add? Our research suggests the answer is ‘less than their pay suggests.’”

Method

NFL teams spend exorbitant amounts of money on players when building out rosters. The injury risk of the potential players often factors into the contract decisions in the front office. Shapiro measured how much success a team gives up when a percentage of payroll is unavailable due to injury.

The study analyzed two primary data sources covering NFL regular seasons spanning from 2012 through 2022. The player-level dataset contained 22,584 player-season observations across 6,235 unique players — linked to a specific team and season. The team-level dataset contained seasonal win totals, games played, win percentage and playoff qualifications for all 32 franchises across the study period.

Shapiro introduced a new measuring tool to weigh the impact of injury on a team: Percent Cash Wasted (PCW), which is the share of payroll paid to players while they’re injured.

Using the data, Shapiro examined the relationship between PCW, team winning percentage and playoff qualification. He matched the players to their teams in each year to create a measure of PCW for each team for each year and then assessed how its PCW affected team success.

Shapiro explained the difference between his study and others in the field is quantifying the relationship between winning and the economic cost of injury. Measuring it for the first time is an important step for this domain, he said.

Findings

Researchers found that NFL teams are more resilient to injury than is commonly assumed: After controlling for expected team quality, a seven-percentage-point reduction in PCW created only one additional win over a 17-game season.

“Teams lose less payroll to injury than I assumed, about 10% in an average season,” Shapiro said. “And that lost payroll costs fewer wins than I expected. Most assume a team could win noticeably more just by staying healthier. Our research shows it can’t.”

The study found that with most roster positions, the cost of injury is modest enough that teams may be overweighting it in personnel decisions.

“The exception is franchise quarterbacks, where evidence suggests there are far more apparent performance consequences for a team when the QB is taken out,” Shapiro said.

He continued: “The difference in winning between a $10 million player and his backup is smaller than most people would think,” Shapiro said. “An injury of the $10 million player puts far more payroll on the sidelines. At most positions, backups fill in reasonably well, so teams may be paying too much for durability.”

A team needs to keep about 7% more of its payroll on the field instead of sidelined due to injury. On average, that means about $11 million in salary needs to be kept on the field to win one more game across the entire season.

“A healthy star still contributes, and at most positions his injury costs relatively little in wins,” Shapiro said. “Quarterback is where the concentrated risk is real and where protecting the investment matters the most.”

The data doesn’t give explanation on why quarterbacks are the exception, but Shapiro theorizes it’s simply because the quarterback is the most important position on the field. “He touches the ball on every offensive play, and most of the offense’s decisions run through him,” Shapiro said. “That makes the starter’s health investment worthy.”

Shapiro hopes his research helps executives make better decisions on how to allocate their payroll. “The next step is to assess what each dollar buys when the player is not injured,” he said. “Measuring the contribution of stars relative to their replacements, position by position, would show where premium contracts earn their cost and where the money would win more games elsewhere on the roster.”

title: The Ball Knower's Notebook: Just How Real Are the Vikings? - The Ringer
description:
The Ball Knower’s Notebook is back after another week of NFL action!
What Went Well: Minnesota Blitzing Daniel Jones Into Oblivion The Vikings are somehow 6-0 despite having a totally unwatchable offense.
Kansas City attempts an inside zone run out of 13 personnel (one back, three tight ends).
When he saw cornerback Keisean Nixon waiting to cover him, he stopped his route—exactly as he should against zone coverage.

text:
The Ball Knower’s Notebook is back after another week of NFL action! In each edition, we take a look at the best and worst from the most recent slate of games, digging into the film and using our takeaways to gain a better understanding of the story this season is telling us.

We’re seven weeks in now, so we know that preseason predictions have already fallen to pieces, and whatever overcorrections we’ve made since have probably been proved wrong, too. But instead of throwing my hands up and resigning myself to existential “anything can happen” axioms, I’m going to lean on what I know best—good (and bad) defense. Minnesota’s continued blitzing dominance, Tampa Bay’s incredible performance against Carolina, and Seattle’s near-perfect execution against Kansas City are all featured in today’s Notebook. We also took some time to appreciate quarterback J.J. McCarthy, receiver Drake London, and why it’s so damn hard to play linebacker in this league. Let’s talk some ’ball.

What Went Well: Minnesota Blitzing Daniel Jones Into Oblivion

The Vikings are somehow 6-0 despite having a totally unwatchable offense. They rank 23rd in points per game even though they’ve played defenses like Miami’s, New Orleans’s, and most recently Indianapolis’s in Sunday’s ugly 16-10 win. Minnesota is winning almost exclusively because of its defense, which is top three in points allowed, yards allowed, and turnovers forced per game. And that unit is absolutely dragging the Vikings toward the playoffs no matter how poorly the rest of the team plays.

Defensive coordinator Brian Flores should go ahead and clear space on a shelf for the Assistant Coach of the Year award, because there’s no other assistant in the same galaxy when it comes to giving their team a winning edge. Flores has Minnesota first in the league in blitz rate so far this year at 68 percent, and there’s a 25.9-point gap between its defense and second place—a greater distance than what’s between second and last place.

Purple jerseys are crowding the line of scrimmage on every snap, then flying into the backfield from all angles, making this defense one of the most fascinating units I’ve ever watched. One of my favorite subplots of Flores’s blitzes is seeing when the percentages spike and letting that indicate how much—or how little—respect he has for a quarterback’s ability to solve his defensive puzzle. Flores reached new heights on Sunday, blitzing the Colts’ Daniel Jones at the highest single-game mark this season—and the highest rate a Flores defense has hit since 2023, his first year with Minnesota. Jones was flummoxed all day, finishing the game with four sacks, an interception, and barely over 100 yards passing. And as much as I wanted to watch the film and just laugh at the absurdity of any offense getting blitzed this often, the tape made me kind of sad for Jones. I don’t know how anyone is supposed to consistently sort out where the unblocked defenders might be coming from when they’re going up against Flores. But I’ll do my best.

After I watched Minnesota’s blitzes this week, it seemed to me that they were based around where the tight end lined up. In the first clip, Minnesota is in its “8-up” defensive front, with just three defenders off the ball and the rest threatening to rush the passer. After the snap, the unblocked rusher (safety Harrison Smith) comes from the top of the screen, blitzing between the tackle and tight end, where no offensive player can account for him, and the Vikings drop two defenders from the line of scrimmage to play a three-deep, two-under zone blitz.

This is called an “eyes” concept, meaning that the two underneath defenders’ zones aren’t fixed to a specific spot; rather, they’re dictated by where the quarterback is looking. Dropping defenders based on the quarterback’s eyes makes it more likely that the underneath guys will get into the passing window of the quarterback’s “hot” read, and the pass rush will get home before the quarterback has time to find another option. No one is open when Jones starts feeling the pressure, and he concedes a sack to Smith as a result.

Flores has also done a great job of attacking offenses when they’re under center trying to set up play-action passes. He’s blitzing offenses a mind-numbing 78 percent of the time when they’re under center, the third-highest rate since 2020—trailing only himself in 2023 and the 2020 Steelers. Blitzing under-center offenses is a great tactic because quarterbacks have to turn their backs to execute a play-action pass and won’t have any idea where the rushers are coming from or what coverage lurks behind them. In the clip below, Minnesota is blitzing the “open” side—away from the tight end—to get rushers in Jones’s face once he completes the run fake. None of the Vikings get through unblocked, but the blitz forces the Colts’ offensive line into one-on-one matchups. And because the Colts were trying to set up a passing concept involving just two receivers, Minnesota’s “eyes” blitz once again leaves nobody open and forces Jones to concede another sack to the Vikings pass rush.

When a defense gets into an offense’s backfield as often as Minnesota’s does, it’s no surprise that they have a chance to win every week. And if people are at home watching and feel like this defense is getting by with a gimmick—they’re not totally wrong. But remember: Buddy Ryan’s 46 defense was a gimmick, too, as were the “Blitzburgh” Steelers under Dick LeBeau and Dom Capers. The “gimmick” in question just happens to be blitzing so relentlessly that opposing quarterbacks and offensive coordinators fall to their knees. This approach has proved itself effective in every era of football, and it’s why I’m going to keep betting on the Vikings to compete this season regardless of how awful their offense has been.

What Went Well: Seattle Shutting Down Kenneth Walker III

Chiefs running back and Super Bowl LX MVP Kenneth Walker III was the NFL’s leading rusher through the first six weeks of the season, and he came into Sunday night’s game against the Seahawks hoping to show why his former team still needed him. Instead, Seattle won 20-3 and proved that the most important pieces of their championship group were still on the roster. Walker finished with just 36 yards on 14 carries, the lowest output he’s had in a game with 10 or more carries since Week 14 last season. And without his ability to create big gains on the ground, Kansas City didn’t have any hope of moving the ball against the league’s best defense.

Everyone knows that Seattle’s front seven is as good as it gets, but the Seahawks don’t just cut their defensive linemen loose to wreak havoc on run plays. There’s an added layer of technical brilliance on top of all their talent that keeps them a step ahead of opposing offenses. I want to take a look at why that is so that everyone has a clear understanding of why the combination of their talent and the execution of head coach Mike Macdonald’s scheme is so dominant.

First, there’s the way Seattle’s raw talent impacts the game, starting with the clip below. Kansas City attempts an inside zone run out of 13 personnel (one back, three tight ends). Because the Seahawks are in “nickel” (five defensive backs on the field), the Chiefs have a theoretical size advantage that should open up space for Walker in the run game. But this run ultimately loses a yard on a tackle by linebacker Tyrice Knight because the Seahawks still deploy the right defensive scheme to stop the run. By walking safety Nick Emmanwori down to the line of scrimmage, Seattle presents a traditional 3-4 defensive front and allows its defensive linemen to occupy blockers long enough for Knight to run through an open gap. Pay close attention to linemen Leonard Williams and Demarcus Lawrence, who both destroy Kansas City’s tackles and take away any space for Walker to cut back or bounce outside.

In the next clip, Kansas City knows that Seattle is going to stay in nickel personnel, so it decides to leave three receivers on the field and attempts to force the Seahawks to give it a 4-3 type of front—which makes it a little easier to double-team defensive tackles and get interior linemen up to the linebackers. If brute strength can’t move the Seahawks off the ball, surely cunning schematics will open up a crease, right? Wrong. This attempt to run inside zone is just as useless as the last one, because Williams is still unblockable one-on-one and defensive end Derick Hall sets the edge so well that Walker (again) is unable to escape. Seattle has true ass-kickers up front.

Pure offensive mass couldn’t get it done, and neither could smaller bodies in condensed formations. So eventually, Chiefs head coach Andy Reid said “screw it” and decided to see whether the offense could create enough literal space across the field to find Walker a running lane. In the next clip, Kansas City is in the shotgun and using a 3x0 formation, meaning that there’s a tight end opposite the three-receiver set. From a coaching perspective, this is one of the best ways to put stress on a defense: Putting a tight end on one side often forces a corner into the box, and the three-receiver side often puts the nearest linebacker in space. Doing this makes a defense pick its poison: either playing with one high safety to load the box and keep the corner from fitting the run, or playing with two high safeties to protect a linebacker from being matched up against a slot receiver.

Knowing that Seattle loves to play with two-deep safeties, Reid and Kansas City’s offense has to assume that running the ball here will gain at least a few yards. Wrong again, and this is where the sophistication of Seattle’s defense kicks in. Up front, Williams is executing a “primary-to-secondary” technique against a double-team, knifing past Kansas City’s left tackle to cut Walker off, then disengaging after Walker cuts back. In doing so, Williams makes life easier for three defenders: Knight, middle linebacker Ernest Jones IV, and safety Julian Love. Cutting Walker off means that Jones doesn’t have to hurry to his gap responsibility and that Knight can be patient and fit whatever gap Williams doesn’t. And because Knight can be patient defending the run, Love isn’t in a hurry to clean up any missed tackles or open gaps left between the tackles. This is beautiful execution by Seattle’s front, and it’s the reason they can stop the run so effectively without having to commit extra bodies.

I said in Winners and Losers this week that Kansas City probably won’t ever have to deal with a defense like this again, and that bodes well for its run game. But for the rest of the teams on Seattle’s schedule: good luck.

What Went Well: J.J. McCarthy’s Unforeseeable Game

I don’t care how much of an optimist his biggest fans are, there’s no way anyone would’ve reasonably expected quarterback J.J. McCarthy to lead this Giants offense to a 27-21 overtime win over the Texans, especially not by averaging 9 yards per pass attempt and completing 71 percent of his throws.

McCarthy was as close to reaching a flow state on Sunday as he’s ever been in the league, and offensive coordinator Matt Nagy set him up for success by relentlessly attacking every weak point in Houston’s underperforming defense. In the clip below, New York lines up in a 3x0 formation similar to what we discussed in the Seahawks-Chiefs game. In Seattle’s example, I mentioned how these formations force defenses to make hard decisions between defending the run or the pass—but it’s also an extremely effective way to uncover whether a defense is playing in man or zone coverage.

When McCarthy gets to the line of scrimmage and sees safeties lined up over tight ends Thomas Fidone and Isaiah Likely, he knows Houston’s playing man-to-man. A clean pocket gives him enough time to confirm the coverage and find his mismatch: receiver Malik Nabers, who’s running a fade route against cornerback Kamari Lassiter. Lassiter’s had a beleaguered year in coverage already, and he probably can’t cover someone as explosive as Nabers on his best day. Nabers gets a step on him and tracks McCarthy’s back-shoulder throw for a gain of more than 40 yards.

Nagy must have anticipated that Houston’s defense would be more aggressive against McCarthy given how poorly he played as a starter last season, so he used that aggression to his advantage. In the next clip, McCarthy finds rookie receiver Malachi Fields for an easy chain-moving completion on a corner route, throwing into a wide-open void in Houston’s coverage. The Texans are playing what looks like a form of “2-read”—a variation of Cover 4 that can morph into Cover 2 depending on what routes the receivers run. If the slot (or inside receiving threat) runs a route to the flats, the cornerback converts from a deep zone player to a flats defender (instead of asking a linebacker to chase that route down) and forces the quarterback to hold the ball longer looking for downfield options.

The one hole in this coverage is between the corner and safety—which the corner is supposed to mitigate by sinking into that hole and then rallying up to any checkdowns. But because Fields is lined up inside the numbers (and thus closer to the ball), he has more space to run into the hole in the zone before the corner recognizes what’s happening, and McCarthy slings it to him as the throw is available.

McCarthy wasn’t carried by Nagy on Sunday, though—he was in an excellent rhythm and made some plays out of structure as well. In the clip below, Houston tries to turn up the pressure with a zone blitz, rushing linebacker Henry To’oTo’o and cornerback Derek Stingley Jr. McCarthy does an excellent job of evading Stingley’s unblocked pressure, stepping up in the pocket, and keeping his eyes downfield long enough to find an open Nabers crossing the field. These were the kinds of plays that eluded McCarthy when he was in Minnesota. Frankly, he was one of the worst quarterbacks I can remember watching whenever he was pressured. The fact that he’s making plays like these in his first start as a Giant has to be a relief for him, and a potentially season-saving development for New York’s offense.

The Texans have been a rough watch on defense this year, so I’m holding space for the possibility that McCarthy’s impressive performance on Sunday might not suggest a career revival. But I did see enough to at least convince me to approach his next start with more intrigue than doubt—and a bit more belief in Nagy’s ability to put his players in position to succeed.

What Went Well: Tampa Bay’s Dominant Defensive Showing

The Buccaneers don’t always rank among the league’s elite defenses, but every once in a while, head coach Todd Bowles can dial up a great game plan. I’ve watched him make the Eagles offense look like a high school operation in the playoffs, I’ve seen him flummox great quarterbacks like Dak Prescott, and I’ve seen him stay a step ahead of top-tier play callers like Kyle Shanahan and Sean McVay.

Bowles has been in his bag so far this season, despite Tampa Bay’s 2-5 start, and Sunday’s 43-13 win over what was a hot Panthers team is the latest showing in his strong campaign. The Bucs blew Carolina out despite recording just 64 passing yards. Tampa Bay’s defense set the offense up with several scoring opportunities thanks to four forced turnovers and five sacks.

We talked earlier about how effective Minnesota’s defense is at crowding the line with blitzers—and how Seattle wins by taking the opposite approach, sitting back with two-deep safeties and forcing offenses to earn their yards the hard way. Tampa Bay exists between those two worlds, using several different coverage concepts to keep quarterbacks guessing but still being willing to send enough pressure to force mistakes. In the clip below, Panthers quarterback Bryce Young is goaded into an interception by Tampa Bay’s zone blitz. Once again, we see an offense in a 3x0 formation, but Bowles declines to participate in the run vs. pass dilemma. Instead, he decides to blitz two defenders from Carolina’s three-receiver side. This is an intentional choice to force Young to throw the ball to a “hot” read, and Young doesn’t see that safety Tykee Smith is waiting for the quick throw the entire way. You can see Young’s reaction after the interception, recognizing that he allowed Bowles to fool him into a poor choice.

Bowles doesn’t always have to play the all-or-nothing game that comes with blitzing, either. In the next clip (a strip sack turned touchdown), Carolina is trying to run a “dagger” concept to pick up a big chunk through the air. But Tampa Bay is playing a Cover 4 concept that creates brackets on the deepest receivers in each safeties’ area—meaning multiple receivers are double-teamed as they run deep downfield. The only option for Young is a deep in route, which needs time to develop, therefore leaving him vulnerable in the pocket. Edge rusher Al-Quadin Muhammad closes in and knocks the ball out of Young’s hand.

You know a defense has the upper hand when blitzes are creating interceptions and good coverage is leading to sacks. Young hasn’t looked as bad as he did Sunday all year long, a credit to Bowles’s play calling. If Bowles keeps dialing up game plans like what we’ve seen so far this year, Tampa Bay can reclaim this division and get back in the playoffs.

All-22 Spotlight: Drake London’s Red Zone Touchdown

All season I’ve been saying that Cover 4 is a necessary coverage in the red zone and hoping that a team would get beaten in a way that justifies my rationale. Finally we have the perfect example after Atlanta’s 29-20 upset win over San Francisco: receiver Drake London’s 21-yard touchdown catch.

In the clip below, Atlanta motions running back Bijan Robinson out to receiver to create an empty set, and San Francisco rotates into a Cover 3 zone in hopes of taking away quick underneath throws. Atlanta’s not looking for a quick dump-off, though; it’s running a “four verts” concept to push the ball into the end zone. London has to fight through an underneath defender’s attempt to reroute him in the slot, but there’s no one left to cover him once he gets up the field. Quarterback Michael Penix Jr. drills the throw to London before San Francisco cornerback Renardo Green can break up the pass.

Penix does a good job of moving the safety out of the middle of the field, but therein lies the problem for the 49ers defense. Cover 4 would give them another defender in this exact area and would have been a more effective way to force a pass underneath. Without the extra deep defender, there’s just too much space to cover downfield, and Penix doesn’t have to be perfect—he just has to get the ball into the end zone.

Defensive coordinator Raheem Morris has been doing an otherwise good job this season, but this was too easy a touchdown for the Falcons. I’d bet we see the 49ers in Cover 4 anytime they’re in the red zone next week.

All-22 Spotlight: Robert Spillane and Christian Elliss Take Ben Johnson’s Bait

As a former linebacker and current coach, I can’t emphasize enough how little you see with your own two eyes during a play. There’s a saying in football: See a little to see a lot, which essentially means putting the puzzle together without seeing the entirety of its shape. A motion in one direction might mean that the ball is going the opposite way, or the route of one receiver might tell you what the entire passing concept may be. Guess right often enough, and you’ll be hailed as one of the game’s best.

We don’t often talk about when those guesses go terribly wrong, though. Robert Spillane and Christian Elliss are one of the better linebacker duos in the league, but even they can be caught gambling at times—and Bears head coach Ben Johnson sought them out on a few occasions in Thursday’s 30-24 win over the Patriots. In the clip below, Chicago uses a play-action pass to set up a variation of a “dagger” concept—where the slot receiver runs a deep crossing route instead of the usual vertical. Spillane clearly assumes it’s the traditional version of this passing concept and tries to jump underneath the deep in route, never even noticing receiver Luther Burden III screaming across the field behind him. Elliss bit on the play-fake way too hard and ran himself out of his coverage area, leaving nobody close to tackle Burden once he catches the ball.

Johnson and quarterback Caleb Williams found loads of success attacking the voids left by New England’s linebackers on Sunday, completing 11 of 14 passes between the numbers for 163 yards and a touchdown. I’d bet New England spends a little more time in passing drills this week, making sure Elliss and Spillane have a better feel for what’s happening behind them.

All-22 Spotlight: Penei Sewell … Slot Receiver?

Shout out to my Ringer colleague Lindsay Jones, who made sure I didn’t miss this in the midst of Sunday’s action.

When I first heard that Lions tackle Penei Sewell ran a route in the red zone, I figured Dan Campbell was getting too cute with a reverse pass or some formation that made it impossible for Green Bay’s defense to track Sewell as he released on a screen.

What I didn’t expect was Sewell lining up in a bunched-receiver set and then running a drag route to set up a “mesh” concept with receiver Jameson Williams. Not only did Sewell run the route how he was supposed to, he even executed some of its finer details. When he saw cornerback Keisean Nixon waiting to cover him, he stopped his route—exactly as he should against zone coverage. When outside linebacker Barryn Sorrell dropped in coverage underneath Sewell’s drag, he shuffled back into an open area to make himself available again. And because he executed this so well, he drew enough attention from linebacker Ty’Ron Hopper that it opened up a passing lane for quarterback Jared Goff to find Williams—and for Williams to run into the end zone. Sewell has real gravity as a receiver, enough to be a decoy for one of the fastest players in football.

text:
SANTA CLARA – Coach Kyle Shanahan’s 49ers have another injury to worry about entering the bye week with their first-place, 6-1 record. It’s apparently not a major injury, however, even if it involves a marquee player.

Running back Christian McCaffrey’s leg injury, sustained on the opening drive of Sunday’s 29-20 loss at Atlanta, has been reframed as a mild hamstring strain, after initially being dubbed as a quadriceps issue.

“We’re pretty optimistic about it,” Shanahan said Monday in a conference call with reporters.

So optimistic that McCaffrey is expected to benefit from this week’s bye and be available for the 49ers’ next game, Nov. 8 against the Raiders.

“My leg just died on me and I tried to get it going for the whole rest of the game,” McCaffrey said postgame, after totaling 69 yards on the first drive but just 31 yards afterward as he tried to loosen up his leg.

As short-handed as the 49ers were in Atlanta with just four wide receivers in uniform, Shanahan is expecting post-bye returns from Mike Evans (Achilles), Deebo Samuel (hamstring) and Demarcus Robinson (ankle).

Defensive end Nick Bosa (calf) also figures to be available for that Raiders matchup after missing the past five games, and the 49ers’ defense also could welcome back safety Marques Sigel (ankle), defensive tackle C.J. West (knee) and linebackers Luke Gifford (hamstring) and Garrett Wallow (groin).

“All those guys have a chance after the bye but none are guaranteed,” Shanahan said. “It’s a big week of rehab for all of them.”

As for rookie wide receiver De’Zhaun Stribling, the 49ers are hoping for a December comeback after he required ankle surgery following the season-opening win over the Rams in Australia.

KICKER SITUATION

Kicker Eddy Piñeiro, after missing a point-after or field-goal attempt in five straight games, is not facing immediate competition.

“As far as I’ve heard, we don’t have any plans on that right now,” Shanahan said of potential tryouts.

Piñeiro missed a point-after attempt following a fourth-quarter touchdown Sunday, his fourth miss in 25 point-after tries this season; he is 6-of-9 on field-goal attempts after making 31-of-32 last season through the playoffs as Jake Moody’s Week 2 successor.

Shanahan said Piñeiro’s off-target trend did not influence a fourth-quarter decision to bypass a 41-yard field-goal attempt and instead go for it on fourth-and-10, resulting in a sack and no points. “I didn’t think a field goal was going to change much. I also thought we could get that first down,” Shanahan said. “So no, the kicking situation didn’t have anything to do with it.”

TRADE TALK

While general manager John Lynch and the personnel staff are discussing trade scenarios “seven days a week,” Shanahan said he will “watch stuff” over the bye week, too. The trade deadline is Nov. 10.

“If there’s stuff that makes sense to improve our team in any spot, we’d love for that to happen,” Shanahan said. “The obvious injury spots to us have been at receiver and D-line. We are getting a number of guys back at both positions, but that doesn’t exclude us from looking for help.”

KIRK’S DEBUT

Christian Kirk played 20 of the 66 offensive snaps in his 49ers’ debut, and although he wasn’t targeted, he did impress Shanahan, who said; “He did a good job in separating and running his routes right. He played really well in the run game too. I thought he blocked well and it was a good game to keep working to get his feet back under him, but I thought it was a good step in the right direction.”

Eagles vs. Cowboys predictions for Week 7 of the 2026 NFL season

The Eagles (2-4) are hosting the Dallas Cowboys (2-4) on Monday Night Football in Week 7. Let’s get to our predictions:

Reuben Frank (4-2)

They began the season with great expectations, they’re 2-4 although they beat the Commanders early in the season, they’re on a losing streak, they can’t run the ball, their hotshot 34-year-old coordinator is under fire and as bad as things have gone, they’re still in the NFC East race. This is all true for the Eagles but also for the Cowboys. Two struggling teams that are mirror images in a lot of ways meet at the Linc Monday night and whoever wins will find themselves back in the NFC East race. Whoever loses is in big trouble. As bad as the Cowboys have been, they still have a dangerous offense led by Dak Prescott, who has thrown a record-223 passes at the Linc without an interception and is 10-5 in his career against the Eagles. The Cowboys’ offense is the best unit in this game and I’m not sure the Eagles have the defense to keep them under 27 points, and I don’t see how the Eagles’ offense we’ve seen this year can match that.

Cowboys 27, Eagles 19

Dave Zangaro (5-1)

Could the Eagles win on Monday night? Sure. Am I picking them? Nope. We’ve reached a stretch of three division games that could really determine the outcome of this season and they’re all winnable. But even going against an awful Cowboys defense, I just don’t have enough faith in the Eagles’ offense to pick them in this game. The Eagles finally get back Saquon Barkley and now DeVonta Smith and Dontayvion Wicks are out. This offense is like a sinking boat; every time you plug one hole, another opens up. And without Jalen Hurts, the Eagles are left with Tanner McKee trying to right the ship. It’s a tough sell to think that side of the ball is suddenly going to figure it out.

I expect a good effort from the Eagles’ defense but they’re probably going to have to take some chances against an explosive offense and that means they could get beat a few times with explosives. But the defense has to try to generate some offense going forward. It’s unavoidable but it’s also not ideal, especially against a Cowboys offense that has a dangerous passing attack. The Eagles should be able to keep it close but I have this as the fifth straight loss.

Cowboys 24, Eagles 17

title: Saquon Barkley injury update as Eagles RB leaves 'Monday Night Football' vs Cowboys
description:
The Philadelphia Eagles got Saquon Barkley back from a two-game absence due to a hamstring injury in Week 7 against the Dallas Cowboys.
Saquon Barkley injury update Barkley addressed his injury during a postgame media availability.
"Saquon Barkley had been in and out of the medical tent since the Eagles offense was last on the field."
Did Saquon Barkley get hurt?
Eagles RB depth chart The Eagles have three running backs available for Monday's game against the Cowboys.
text:
The Philadelphia Eagles got Saquon Barkley back from a two-game absence due to a hamstring injury in Week 7 against the Dallas Cowboys.

While Barkley was able to return to the field, it was clear he was being hampered by an injury throughout the contest.

Barkley's struggles began on his first carry. The 29-year-old broke off a 29-yard run but appeared to pull up at the end of it before going out of bounds.

Barkley left the field for a couple of plays but later returned to the field. He played sporadically in the first half, alternating playing time with Dameon Pierce while attempting to stay loose on the sideline and also spending time in the blue medical tent.

Barkley went to the locker room early, presumably for further medical evaluation, but returned to the field for the second half. He ripped off a 12-yard run on the first play of the half before walking gingerly to the sideline.

Barkley remained on the sideline for the remainder of the Eagles' drive, which chewed up the first 9:16 of the third quarter. He was spotted grimacing while standing on the sideline and did not have his helmet on while watching the Eagles' drive take place.

Barkley returned to the field for the first snap of the Eagles' next drive but went back to the sideline after one run, which was negated by a penalty.

Here's what to know about Barkley's status as the Eagles look to earn a needed win over the Cowboys.

Saquon Barkley injury update

Barkley addressed his injury during a postgame media availability. He explained he had tweaked his hamstring on his opening carry of the game and later hurt his back while trying to compensate for the ailment.

"That's how the body works. Sometimes, something is a little banged up and you overcompensate a little bit," Barkley explained. "Just gotta get to rehab and just continue to work."

Barkley didn't express too much concern about the maladies and acknowledged he really wanted to be able to push through them to try to help the Eagles against the Cowboys. He just couldn't do it but will now turn his attention toward getting healthy for the remainder of the season.

"I just gotta find a way to get healthy," Barkley told reporters. "It's annoying, but that's what I'm dealing with so far in the season."

The Eagles did not provide an update about Barkley's status until the fourth quarter of the contest. Barkley was originally deemed "questionable" to return with a back injury but did not play again after his status was revealed.

And ESPN's Lisa Salters provided an update from the sideline earlier in the contest. "Saquon Barkley had been in and out of the medical tent since the Eagles offense was last on the field." Salters reported during the broadcast. "No injury designation on him of course. You see him back out there. The Eagles say they're just trying to manage this hamstring issue."

Barkley racked up 71 total yards and a touchdown on nine touches against the Cowboys.

Did Saquon Barkley get hurt?

Yes, Barkley appeared to get hurt on his first carry of the game. He pulled up while running through Dallas' defense and chose to run out of bounds as a result.

Barkley later got medical treatment on the sideline but tried to play through the injury. He played sparingly in the first half and took the opening offensive snap of the third quarter before exiting again. He played one more snap after that before exiting the game for good.

Who is Saquon Barkley's backup?

Dameon Pierce is Barkley's backup for their Week 7 game against the Cowboys. The 26-year-old veteran has been with the Eagles since signing in March 2026. He began the season on the team's practice squad before being elevated to the 53-man roster amid injuries to Barkley and Tank Bigsby.

Pierce entered Monday's game having totaled 49 yards and a touchdown on 23 carries. He scored his second rushing touchdown of the season in the second quarter against the Cowboys.

Eagles RB depth chart

The Eagles have three running backs available for Monday's game against the Cowboys. They are as follows:

Saquon Barkley

Dameon Pierce

Elijah Mitchell

Mitchell spent part of the 2026 NFL offseason with the Eagles before the team released him on Aug. 11. He rejoined the practice squad on Oct. 16 and was elevated to third-string back for Philadelphia against Dallas.

The Eagles also have Bigsby and Will Shipley in their organization, but both are on injured reserve (IR).

Seahawks Planning to Open Jadarian Price Practice Window

Jadarian Price Nearing Return Amid Up-and-Down Start

text:
It's been six weeks since the Los Angeles Rams placed Myles Garrett on injured reserve, and they still don't know when he'll return to the field.

Or, if they do, they're not sharing it.

Head coach Sean McVay was asked on Monday about whether the Rams would open the 21-day practice window for Garrett's return from injured reserve. Per the Rams website, McVay said he hadn't yet spoken with senior vice president of sports medicine Reggie Scott and didn't know if Garrett would return to practice this week.

Thus, the wait continues.

Garrett's missed 6 games since struggling in Rams debut

Garrett has been on injured reserve since Week 2 after undergoing arthroscopic knee surgery and was required to miss a minimum of four weeks. Initial reports stated there was hope that he could return after those four weeks. Subsequent reporting shifted the timeline to six weeks. He's missed six games since going on IR, and further updates about his condition and return have been sparse.

McVay was asked about Garrett's status Monday after telling reporters last week that there's "a possibility" he could return to practice this week. That statement coincided with a report from NFL Network's Ian Rapoport that it's "likely that he returns to practice next week." As of Monday, uncertainty remains.

Even when Garrett returns to practice, that doesn't mean he'll be ready to play the following game. Once his practice window is opened, Garrett will have 21 days to be activated to the 53-man roster or be placed on season-ending injured reserve.

The Rams, meanwhile, are in a fight to make the playoffs after starting the season as favorites to win the Super Bowl. They beat the Raiders on Sunday to improve to 3-4 and have winnable upcoming games against the Chargers, Commanders and Cardinals.

Even if they win all three, they'll be 6-4 in a competitive NFC playoff race with one of the league's toughest schedules down the stretch. After a Week 11 bye, the Rams will close their season with games against the Packers, Chiefs, 49ers, Cowboys, Seahawks, Bucs and then the Seahawks again in their season finale.

In short, the Rams don't have much margin for error, and the return of the reigning, two-time Defensive Player of the Year would provide a much-needed boost.

Rookie Reggie Virgil is expected to get more snaps at the X along with Kendrick Bourne and Simi Fehoko.

text:
PHILADELPHIA, P.A. — It’s not exactly the cavalry riding to the Eagles’ offensive rescue for Monday night’s home game against the Cowboys, but it’s better than nothing.

Just hours before kickoff, Philly filled its three spots on the 53-man roster, adding:

Left guard Landon Dickerson

Tight end Grant Calcaterra

Tight end Eli Stowers

Calcaterra and Stowers have yet to play this season after being placed on injured reserve before the season opener. What’s interesting about these three names is that Zach Ertz is not among them. The thinking had been that the Eagles made a deal with the veteran tight end to return to Philly in exchange for adding him to the roster at some point.

This feels like the point, yet it didn’t happen.

Ertz is out of practice squad elevations, so the only way he can play again for the Eagles is to be added to the roster. Clearly, the team is higher on Calcaterra and the rookie Stowers right now.

Speaking of the practice squad, the Eagles elevated outside linebacker Keyshawn James-Newby for a second straight game and running back Elijah Mitchell.

Meanwhile, Saquon Barkley is expected to return to the lineup after missing two games with a hamstring injury. Adding Mitchell gives the Eagles three running backs for Monday’s game, as he and Barkley join Dameon Pierce.

Eagles hope offensive additions can spark run game

The return of Barkley and Dickerson should help the Eagles find some traction in the running game, and that would help Tanner McKee, who will make his second straight start in place of injured Jalen Hurts.

In last week’s loss to the Panthers, McKee attempted 45 passes while running the ball just 12 times against a Panthers defense that was one of the worst at stopping the run in the league. The Bay Buccaneers showed the Eagles how bad that run defense was on Sunday when the Bucs torched Carolina on the ground, with 49 runs for 258 yards. Baker Mayfield threw just 11 passes.

Yet, the Eagles insisted on letting McKee throw the ball and never took advantage of the Panthers’ inability to stop the run.

A more balanced attack against the Cowboys might help the Eagles snap a four-game losing streak. Having McKee throw the ball another 40-plus times doesn’t feel like a recipe for success, especially with the Eagles missing their top two playmakers—DeVonta Smith (hamstring) and Tay Wicks (ankle).

That leaves the Eagles with a decimated receiver corps that includes rookie Makai Lemon, Darius Cooper, Hollywood Brown and Elijah Moore.

text:
Hinshaw partner Scott Seaman was recently quoted in Law360 Insurance Authority, examining the significance of a New York appellate court’s ruling regarding how many “occurrences” are involved for purposes of insurance coverage for the National Football League’s (NFL) concussion litigation settlement.

What the Court Ruled

Earlier this month, New York’s Appellate Division, First Judicial Department, held that each former player’s alleged injury was at least one separate occurrence.

Because of that ruling, the excess insurer does not have to indemnify the NFL for the uncapped multidistrict litigation settlement with former players.

Its fifth-layer policy covered a portion of any loss exceeding $51 million. The court said coverage would instead fall under a primary policy issued for the same 2001–2002 policy period.

The Ruling’s Implications on Insurance Coverage Litigation

Scott explained that a party’s position on the number of occurrences often depends on where its policy sits in the coverage program. “As this case illustrates, where a party stands on the number of occurrences issue may depend upon where it sits on the coverage chart.”

He also said the court’s decision shows that the number of occurrences is still a major issue in insurance litigation. Coverage turns on the size of the loss, where each policy attaches, and whether aggregate limits apply.

Additionally, Scott noted that the First Judicial Department applied New York’s “unfortunate event” test in a straightforward way. “Although the claims shared some commonalities, the claims of over 20,000 former players who participated in approximately 10,000 games over multiple decades in approximately 90 different stadiums did not share the same ‘temporal and spatial’ characteristics to unify them as one occurrence,” he explained.

text:
Detroit Lions coach Dan Campbell gave a couple of injury updates in his Monday afternoon press conference, and it's mostly good news.

Let's start with Amon-Ra St. Brown. I'm guessing many weren't aware St. Brown was even dealing with an injury, as he never exited the game and wasn't given a specific injury designation on Sunday. However, Detroit Football Network's Justin Rogers noted that the Lions did not make him available in the locker room because he was getting treatment for a swollen ankle.

Campbell said they expect to sit St. Brown for Wednesday's practice, but they're optimistic he'll be okay and are hoping he'll be ready to go for Thursday.

"He and Ennis (Rakestraw), I think those guys will probably sit Wednesday, but the plan is to get them going Thursday, and I think that they'll be fine. They should be good," Campbell said, before adding. "Now, we'll see when we get there, but—yep."

St. Brown is coming off his best game of the season, hauling in nine catches for a season-high 153 yards. That's the fifth-most yards he's had in a single game for his career. Obviously, missing him would be a big deal, but Campbell doesn't sound too concerned at the moment.

The Lions are expecting the same trajectory for cornerback Ennis Rakestraw, who did leave the game early with an ankle injury.

"It's not major, he's got a little ankle here," Campbell said. "We feel like, as of right now, he'll be at practice on Thursday. That's kinda what we're looking at. But we don't feel like it's major as of today."

Rakestraw was part of a pretty massive cornerback rotation against the Packers. Rakestraw (21 snaps) shared playing time with D.J. Reed (61), Roger McCreary (67), Rock Ya-Sin (14), and Khalil Dorsey (14). It was a game plan inspired by the Dallas Cowboys' attack against the Packers to keep the players fresh. Campbell said it's an approach they will continue to consider moving forward.

"I think there was also merit for a number of those guys plays," Campbell said. "Letting them all kinda play, getting some reps and using them in different situations, different packages."

Seattle Seahawks left tackle Charles Cross is expected to miss time after an MRI revealed that he suffered a high ankle sprain in the team's win over the Kansas City Chiefs on Sunday night, a source told NFL Network's Ian Rapoport.

A source told Rapoport that the hope is Cross can return in one or two weeks.

Cross limped off the field in the fourth quarter and did not return. Josh Jones finished the game and is now in line to start the Seahawks' Week 8 game against the Chicago Bears on "Monday Night Football."

The Seahawks also lost wide receiver Rashid Shaheed to a knee injury Sunday that kept him out of the second half. On his Seattle Sports 710-AM radio show Monday, coach Mike Macdonald said, "the early returns are positive."

Macdonald also said on his radio show that the Seahawks will open up the 21-day practice window this week on rookie running back Jadarian Price, who has spent the past four games on injured reserve due to a chest injury.

Price, the team's first-round pick, is one half of their desired backfield duo along with Zach Charbonnet, who has yet to make his season debut following February ACL surgery. Charbonnet was inactive Sunday after a full week of participation in practice.

"We're sticking to our plan where he's still going to practice in a full capacity and then we'll evaluate as the week goes on and go from there," Macdonald said.

text:
The Houston Texans got hit with a reality check in their Week 7 loss vs. the New York Giants, as they would end up falling short in an overtime defeat, 21-27 that now sinks them to a 2-5 record on the year heading into the bye.

However, it seems the Texans were also hit with a key injury in their wide receiver room in the midst of their Week 7 loss, according to head coach DeMeco Ryans.

And that injury was to none other than second-year wide receiver Jaylin Noel, who ended up leaving in the middle of Sunday's contest against the Giants before inevitably being unable to return.

What DeMeco Ryans Said About Jaylin Noel's Injury

Per DeMeco Ryans' post-game press conference following Houston's loss vs. the Giants, the Texans' head coach revealed that Noel had suffered a turf toe injury against New York.

"Jaylin Noel had a turf toe injury. He's still being evaluated," Ryans said on Sunday.

Obviously, there's not a ton of information that we can gather from Ryans' post-game comments when it comes to Noel's status moving forward. However, a turf toe injury––depending on the exact severity––is one that can lead to some missed time for any player in the league.

Noel finished the game against the Giants with just two receptions for a loss of three yards. According to KPRC2's Aaron Wilson, Noel was also reportedly in a walking boot following the Texans' loss.

The good news for the Texans is that they'll be heading right into their bye week following the events of their Week 7 loss. Which means, for Noel, he'll have an extra week of rest to bank on before he'll be tasked with suiting up for Houston's next game.

However, even with that extra time off, there's a chance that Noel could be due to miss some time for the Texans moving forward–– which would undoubtably be a big loss to Houston's offense knowing how strong of a start to the season the second-year wideout has had through seven weeks.

Through the start of the Texans' season, Noel has put together a total of 19 receptions for 331 yards and two receptions, really becoming one of the team's most noteworthy playmakers in the passing game, even with the immense depth that's come to surround him in the wide receiver room.

His ability as a downfield playmaker, someone who can excel after the catch, and even as a kick returner has shown up big in his second year pro. Yet, depending on just how bad his new turf toe injury might be, there's a chance the Texans will be forced to push ahead without him for a few games moving forward.

If Noel is due to miss any time for the Texans' offense, C.J. Stroud will be forced to lean on some other playmakers in this wide receiver room that does have the depth to support a solid offense, even without the second-year talent.

Keep an eye on the obvious candidates of Nico Collins and Marvin Harrison Jr. to likely see more responsibilities in the Texans' offense in the weeks ahead.

Yet, you can also expect guys like Kayshon Boutte, Xavier Hutchinson, and Tank Dell to step up and provide the playmaking this offense could desperately utilize without one of their more potent names at the position group altogether.

We'll likely know more on Noel's long-term status a bit better once we get to next week's practice leading up to the Texans' Week 9 battle vs. the Los Angeles Chargers. However, certainly brace for the possibility that this offense could be without Noel for some stretch of time, depending on how bad the toe injury is truly deemed to be.

title: Gamechanger for Excess Insurer: Court Concludes NFL Player Concussion Claims ... - Tressler LLP
description:
AIGLIC issued the fifth layer excess liability policy to the NFL that followed form to the TIG primary Policy.
The AIGLIC Policy provided the same coverage for damages covered by the TIG Policy.
The court also overturned the Supreme Court’s finding that NFL football was a “product” under the PCOH coverage.
The lower court had concluded the term “product” could, as a matter of “common speech” include intangible items like NFL football.
“The plain language indicates that the product, as expected to be covered by the PCOH, is a tangible/physical product.
text:
In 2014, the National Football League and NFL Properties, LLC (together, NFL) entered into a class action settlement in federal multidistrict litigation (MDL) resolving litigation brought by former players alleging the NFL failed to inform them of and protect them from concussion risks in football. Coverage litigation began long before the settlement was inked. On October 1, 2026, the coverage dispute inched closer to final resolution with the decision of the New York Appellate Division in Discover Prop. & Cas. Co., et al. v. Nat’l Football League, et al. —N.Y.S.3d —, No. 2025-03200, 2026 WL 2948933 (N.Y. App. Div. Oct. 1, 2026). The Appellate Division reversed key rulings entered by the New York Supreme Court, New York County, on cross-motions for summary judgment, finding each claim by or on behalf of a former player constitutes at least one “occurrence” under a primary policy issued by TIG Insurance Company (TIG) and that NFL football is not a “product” as that term is defined in the Products Completed Operations Hazard (PCOH). As a result, the court found that fifth-layer excess insurer American Guarantee and Liability Insurance Companies (AIGLIC) owes no indemnity coverage to NFL, because the first layer insurer, TIG, did not have an aggregate limit and the settlement capped the possible award for any one player below TIG’s per occurrence limit.

The underlying MDL, Matter of National Football League Players’ Concussion Injury Litig., 307 FRD 351, 361 (E.D Pa 2015), aff’d 821 F3d 410 (3d Cir 2016), cert denied 580 US 1030 (2016) consolidated the claims of approximately 5,000 players and over 300 “substantially similar lawsuits.” Discover Prop & Cas., 2026 WL 2948933 at *2. The MDL settlement provides three benefits to players suffering from “qualifying diagnoses” like chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE), including an uncapped monetary settlement with caps on individual awards that limited each player with a qualifying diagnosis to a maximum award between $1.5- $5 million, depending on certain variables. Id. at *3.

TIG had two policies that covered the NFL. The first was a primary general liability policy with a $1 million per occurrence limit, and the second was a follow form excess policy covering the next $15 million per occurrence. AIGLIC issued the fifth layer excess liability policy to the NFL that followed form to the TIG primary Policy. TIG, which defended pursuant to a reservation or rights, did not dispute the TIG Policy had no aggregate limit for most claims, but maintained that the losses fell under the Products Completed Operations Hazard (“PCOH”), which had a $1 million aggregate limit. Id. at *4. Thus, there were only two ways the NFL claims could trigger the AIGLIC policy: first, if all of the player’s concussions were considered to be a single occurrence, they could exceed the underlying policy limits. Second, if the claims fell within the PCOH coverage, which had a $1 million aggregate, they could exceed the underlying limits. TIG maintained that the claims constituted a single occurrence and also maintained that they fell within the PCOH coverage so the aggregate limit would be exhausted. AIGLIC argued its policy could not be triggered because each player’s alleged injury constitutes a separate occurrence and because NFL football is not a “product” so the PCOH aggregate limit was not triggered. Id. at 3-4. The court agreed with AIGLIC on all points.

Relevant Policy Language: The TIG Policy’s $1 million PCOH aggregate coverage limit was the “‘most’ TIG would ‘pay’ under Coverage A for damages because of ‘bodily injury’ and ‘property damage’ included in the ‘products-completed operations hazard,” including a “limited category” of bodily injury claims occurring “away from the premises the insured owned or rented which arose from ‘your product’ or ‘your work’ excepts products that are still in the insured’s physical possession or work that has not yet been completed or abandoned.” Id. at *6 (emphasis in original) (cleaned up). Used therein, “your product” meant “‘goods or products, other than real property, manufactured, sold, handled, distributed or disposed of’ by the insured, others trading under the insured’s name, and ‘containers (other than vehicles), materials, parts or equipment furnished in connection with such goods or products.” Id. (cleaned up).

The TIG Policy was also endorsed with “Liability to Participants” coverage – Coverage D – pursuant to which TIG agreed to “pay those sums that the Insured becomes legally obligated to pay as damages because of ‘bodily injury to any ‘participant’ subject to the limits of insurance.” Id. “Participants” included players. Id. The AIGLIC Policy provided the same coverage for damages covered by the TIG Policy.

The Appellate Division deemed the question of the number of occurrences to be the threshold inquiry. TIG argued that all of the players’ injuries were due to the singular event of NFL football, regardless of the time, place, manner or number of hits sustained in their career. Thus, according to TIG, the injuries arose from on common event that was “part of the same causal continuum, without intervening agents or factors.” Id., at *8. The court rejected this argument. Applying New York’s “unfortunate events test”, the court found that each player’s individual injuries constituted a single occurrence. Id. The court first looked at the TIG Policy’s “occurrence” definition “for the suggestion of an intent to group claims” then consider “whether there is a close temporal and spatial relationship between the incidents giving rise to injury or loss, and whether the incidents can be viewed as part of the same causal continuum without intervening agents or factors.” Id. TIG conceded there was no grouping language in its policy but posited that that an “ongoing single-occurrence finding is warranted under the ‘unfortunate event test’” because all players with Qualifying Diagnoses sustained those diagnoses the same way – “playing the singular event of NFL football.” Id. The court disagreed because the incident giving rise to the players’ injuries was not playing NFL football, but rather the head impacts, which took place at different times, on different fields, over at least two decades. Id. Those impacts, which affected thousands of former players who played thousands of games over decades in 90 different stadiums lacked the “temporal and spatial characteristics” required to unify them as a single occurrence, which the court concluded could not be said to have been “precipitated by a single causal continuum.” Id.

The court also rejected the position that the TIG Policy’s “occurrence” definition – “all bodily injury and property damage arising out of continuous or repeated exposure to substantially the same general conditions shall be considered as arising out of one occurrence” – meant all players injuries should be considered a single occurrence. Without aggregation-of-claims language identifying “repeated head impacts” as the operative incident that would give rise to liability, and nothing suggesting the head impacts constituted exposure to the same generally harmful conditions, the court was constrained to find grouping was not appropriate under the policy language and applied the results of the “unfortunate events test” to find at least one occurrence per player. Id. at **9-10.

The court also overturned the Supreme Court’s finding that NFL football was a “product” under the PCOH coverage. The lower court had concluded the term “product” could, as a matter of “common speech” include intangible items like NFL football. The Appellate Division found this reading failed to comport with the purpose of products-hazard coverage, which is meant to insure the party responsible for sending goods into the marketplace, protecting the insured from the risk of loss that occurs when the product leaves the seller’s normal business premises and causes damage elsewhere. In looking beyond, the policy language and finding a broader definition for the word “product” the Supreme Court ignored the reasonable expectations of the average insured purchasing PCOH coverage. The Court said it was improper to isolate the word ‘product’ from its context. “The plain language indicates that the product, as expected to be covered by the PCOH, is a tangible/physical product. Supreme Court should not have expanded the definition of ‘product’ to include intangible products simply because that interpretation is possible.” Id. at 12.

With multiple occurrences in play and no ‘product’ to bring the claims within the PCOH coverage, there was no possibility that the MDL settlement payments would ever reach AIGLIC’s $51 million threshold, so AIGLIC owed no coverage.

Discover highlights the uncertainty that can result when the meaning of undefined policy terms become the lynchpin between coverage and no coverage, and the importance of tying policy language to the nature of the risks meant to be insured against, particularly during the current explosion of artificial intelligence offerings, which can straddle the definition of product and service.

In the interest of brevity, we focused on two of the key rulings in this case. See the full opinion for why the court rejected TIG’s positions that: 1) football players neurodegenerative diseases do not constitute an “occurrence” because they are an inherent risk of the intentional violent impacts of NFL play; 2) the NFL could not meet its burden of showing that players recovering under the settlement did not sustain their injuries during the policy periods; 3) NFL’s notice of claim was untimely, and 4) NFL did not suffer a ‘loss’ because it was allegedly indemnified by the NFL Clubs. The court also discussed why the settlement was reasonable.

About Natalie C. Metropulos

text:
The Buffalo Bills got a week to heal.

The Baltimore Ravens gave Lamar Jackson another week to do the same.

Jackson missed his third straight game Sunday because of an ankle injury, and Baltimore lost 35-13 to the Cincinnati Bengals without him.

Now the Ravens have to decide whether the extra time was enough to get their quarterback back for Buffalo.

The Bills come out of their Week 7 bye hoping to get wide receiver D.J. Moore and defensive tackle Ed Oliver back after both missed the previous two games.

Baltimore also picked up another injury Sunday when rookie guard Vega Ioane left because of a knee injury.

Buffalo (5-1) hosts Baltimore (4-3) at 1 p.m. ET Sunday, Nov. 1, at Highmark Stadium.

NFL teams have to submit a report on practice participation on Wednesday, Thursday and Friday for a Sunday game. A game status report is due by 4 p.m. Friday for Sunday games.

Here is the Bills vs. Ravens injury update for Week 8:

Buffalo Bills injury update for Week 8

D.J. Moore, WR, shoulder

D.J. Moore has not played since Oct. 4.

Moore missed Buffalo's final two games before the bye after aggravating the injury against the New England Patriots in Week 4.

He did not practice Wednesday or Thursday before the Raiders game but returned on a limited basis Friday and was listed as questionable. Buffalo ultimately kept him inactive.

Moore originally suffered the shoulder injury against the Detroit Lions in Week 2. He returned the following week and played through it before aggravating the injury against New England.

Ed Oliver, DL, knee

Ed Oliver also missed Buffalo's final two games before the bye.

Oliver suffered his knee injury during the Bills' Week 4 loss to New England when former Buffalo fullback Reggie Gilliam hit his left leg near the sideline.

He missed five consecutive practices before returning on a limited basis the Friday before the Raiders game.

Oliver was listed as questionable but inactive in Las Vegas.

Dalton Kincaid, TE, ribs

Dalton Kincaid left Buffalo's victory over Las Vegas because of a rib injury but was able to return.

Kincaid went to the medical tent and then the locker room during the third quarter after appearing uncomfortable following a route.

The Bills listed him as questionable to return. Kincaid came back in the fourth quarter and caught a 14-yard pass three plays later.

Bradley Chubb, OLB, ribs

Bradley Chubb also left the Raiders game in Week 6 because of a rib injury and returned.

Chubb went out during the second quarter and was initially listed as questionable. He returned later in the first half and played 21 of Buffalo's 66 defensive snaps against Las Vegas.

T.J. Sanders, DL, shoulder

T.J. Sanders played against Las Vegas and recorded one tackle after being listed as questionable because of a shoulder injury.

Dee Alford, CB, ankle

Dee Alford returned against Las Vegas in Week 6 after missing Buffalo's win over the Los Angeles Rams in Week 5 because of an ankle injury. He had two tackles and one pass breakup in the victory over the Raiders.

Joshua Palmer, WR, shoulder

Joshua Palmer returned against Las Vegas after missing the Rams game because of a shoulder injury. He caught one pass for 37 yards against the Raiders.

C.J. Gardner-Johnson, S, suspended

C.J. Gardner-Johnson will not play against Baltimore. It's not because of injury.

The NFL suspended Gardner-Johnson without pay for one game after he spit at a Raiders player during the second quarter of Buffalo's Week 6 victory. Gardner-Johnson was ejected in the second quarter.

His suspension begins Oct. 26 and he can return to Buffalo's active roster Nov. 2, meaning he will miss Sunday's game against Baltimore.

Buffalo Bills injured reserve

Zane Durant, DL, neck

Zane Durant is eligible to return after beginning the season on injured reserve.

Buffalo can designate Durant to return and open his 21-day practice window when he is medically cleared.

Buffalo Bills physically unable to perform

Tyrell Shavers, WR, knee

Tyrell Shavers is eligible to return after beginning the season on the physically unable to perform list.

Shavers is recovering from the torn ACL he suffered during Buffalo's wild-card playoff victory last season.

The Bills can designate him to return and open his 21-day practice window when he is ready.

Buffalo Bills non-football injury

Dorian Strong, CB, neck

Baltimore Ravens injury update for Week 8

Lamar Jackson, QB, ankle

Lamar Jackson will be the biggest injury to monitor this week.

Jackson has missed Baltimore's last three games because of an ankle injury suffered Oct. 4.

He returned to practice last week and was limited Wednesday, Thursday and Friday. Jackson told reporters Friday that the ankle was improving but that running remained the issue.

"I'm just trying to move how I move," Jackson said. "If I can't do that, I can't help my team."

Baltimore listed Jackson as questionable against the Cincinnati Bengals before ruling him out Saturday. Tyler Huntley started for the third consecutive game and threw for 215 yards in the first half of Sunday's loss.

The Ravens are 1-2 without Jackson.

Vega Ioane, G, knee

Baltimore picked up another potentially significant injury Sunday.

Rookie first-round pick Vega Ioane left the Bengals game near the end of the first quarter because of a knee injury and did not return.

Emery Jones Jr. replaced him.

Jaylinn Hawkins, S, knee

Starting safety Jaylinn Hawkins missed Sunday's game because of a knee injury.

Broderick Washington Jr., DL, ankle

Broderick Washington Jr. has missed two consecutive games because of an ankle injury.

Andrew Vorhees, G, foot

Andrew Vorhees missed Sunday's loss to Cincinnati because of a foot injury.

Tavius Robinson, OLB, pectoral

Tavius Robinson will not play against Buffalo.

Robinson suffered a pectoral injury in Week 6 and Ravens coach Jesse Minter announced Friday that it will end his season.

Robinson is still leading the Ravens with 3.5 sacks this season.

text:
Monday morning brought injury updates on Green Bay Packers center Sean Rhyan, who left Sunday's loss to the Detroit Lions in the first quarter, and starting linebacker Zaire Franklin, who didn't play Sunday after injuring his shin in practice on Thursday.

According to Ian Rapoport of NFL Network, Rhyan is believed to have suffered a high-ankle sprain when Josh Jacobs fell into the back of his legs to finish off a run on the Packers' first drive. While more testing will be done on Monday, this type of ankle injury typically comes with a 4–6-week recovery timeline, so Rhyan will miss Thursday night against the Carolina Panthers and is a candidate for injured reserve.

Jacob Monk is the backup center, but he suffered a quad injury after replacing Rhyan in the first quarter and didn't return. Coach Matt LaFleur didn't think Rhyan or Monk would be available to go against the Panthers. John Williams played the final 58 snaps at center and could start on Thursday night. Rookie Jager Burton is another option, but he was inactive on Sunday.

The Packers won't have their starting center and probably won't have Franklin, one of their defensive captains, against the Panthers. Per Rapoport, Franklin has a hairline fracture in his leg after getting accidently kicked in the shin during Thursday's practice. Expecting him to be physically ready to play in a game just a week after this injury is probably unreasonable. The Packers have not placed Franklin on injured reserve, so it's possible he'll return within the four-week window. But Jonathan Gannon's defense will likely need Isaiah McDuffie and Ty'Ron Hopper to play all the snaps at linebacker against the Panthers.

More injury updates are likely to come later on Monday. LaFleur will answer questions from the media, and the Packers will release their first injury report of Week 8.

text:
NFL Week 7 injury roundup: Christian McCaffrey, Jaylen Waddle and more appeared first on ClutchPoints. Add ClutchPoints as a Preferred Source by clicking here.

The 2026 NFL season has already been filled with plenty of surprises. But as the midpoint of the season draws closer, some of the funkiness of the early season is beginning to even out. Only one NFL team remains undefeated and another winless following Week 7.

Sunday's games did not include headline-grabbing injuries like the past couple of weeks. However, NFL fans should keep an eye on all of these situations as the league's playoff picture will soon start coming into focus.

There are the most important injuries to watch following an exciting Week 7 of NFL action.

Watch sports LIVE with fuboTV (free trial)

Christian McCaffrey, San Francisco 49ers

The 49ers have dealt with so many injuries already this season. So when McCaffrey went down, 49ers fans probably started fearing the worst. Fortunately, McCaffrey's injury does not look too serious.

McCaffrey suffered a thigh injury during the first quarter against the Falcons. He left the game briefly, but was able to return in the second half.

CMC explained that his leg "just died on me" and it was difficult to get back on track throughout the rest of the game. Still, McCaffrey declared that he doesn't expect the injury to bother him moving forward.

San Francisco is now on its bye week, so McCaffrey will have extra time to get back to 100%.

Jaylen Waddle, Denver Broncos

The Broncos got cute and it ended up hurting them badly.

Denver dialed up a tricky reverse pitch play for Waddle with just under five minutes left in Sunday's win over Arizona. There was a fumble on the play and Waddle jumped on the ball to prevent a turnover.

Unfortunately, Waddle suffered a chest injury on the play and did not return to the game. Sean Payton took the blame for the awful play call immediately after the victory.

It remains to be seen how severe Waddle's injury really is. Broncos fans should keep their eyes peeled for an injury update on Waddle before Week 8.

Olaivavega Ioane, Baltimore Ravens

The Ravens lost Ioane to a knee injury during Sunday's loss to the Bengals. He did not return to finish the game.

The entire second half was a disaster for Baltimore, as they surrendered 35 unanswered points to Cincinnati in a tough divisional loss. Ioane's injury makes that result even worse.

Ravens fans should keep their eyes on the injury report ahead of Week 8 against the Bills. That could provide clues on the status of QB Lamar Jackson, too.

Taylor Moton, Carolina Panthers

Injuries just keep coming for the Panthers.

Not only did Carolina get absolutely destroyed by Tampa Bay, they also lost yet another offensive tackle. Moton fractured his fibula in Sunday's loss and will be out "a while" per head coach Dave Canales.

The Panthers are already without Ikem Ekwonu and Stone Forsythe at the position. That leaves Rasheed Walker and rookie Monroe Freeling as starters with practically no depth behind them.

Carolina's lack of health on the o-line could be a problem moving forward.

Sean Rhyan, Green Bay Packers

Green Bay suffered even more offensive line injuries in Week 7 against Detroit.

Packers center Sean Rhyan suffered an ankle injury early in Sunday's game and did not return. NFL insider Ian Rapoport reported on Monday that Rhyan's injury is believed to be a high ankle sprain.

"X-Rays were negative, and he has an MRI today. But high-ankle sprains are often 4-6 week injuries," Rapoport added.

Meanwhile, the Packers lost even more depth after Jacob Monk left the game with a quad injury.

Perhaps Green Bay will need to add even more veteran depth on the o-line after a truly disastrous first half of the season.

Cam Skattebo, New York Giants

Skattebo is officially out of the dog house.

The young running back ripped off 17 carries for 124 rushing yards and a touchdown against a tough Texans defense. But Skattebo appeared to injure himself on his biggest play of the game.

Skattebo reportedly felt something in his hamstring during his 42-yard overtime run that set up Devin Singletary for the walk-off touchdown.

Fortunately, NFL insider Mike Garafolo reported on Monday that "all indications this morning are he should be OK." The Giants are on their bye in Week 8, so Skattebo will have some extra rehab time as well.

In other Giants injury news, Tyrone Tracy Jr. left Sunday's game with a hamstring injury and did not return.

Rashid Shaheed, Seattle Seahawks

The Seahawks got a huge win against the Chiefs on Sunday Night Football. But it came at the cost of losing multiple players to injuries.

Shaheed collided with his teammate Jaxon Smith-Njigba in the end zone towards the end of the first half. He apparently suffered a knee injury and did not return for the second half. Shaheed plays a big role on offense and special teams for Seattle, so losing him for a long stretch would be a tough blow. Hopefully Seattle gives an update on his status on Monday.

In other Seahawks injury news, Charles Cross (ankle) and Velus Jones Jr. (hamstring) also left Sunday's game and did not return.

Aaron Jones, Minnesota Vikings

The Vikings just keep shuffling running backs this season.

Jordan Mason finally returned to action on Sunday following his thumb injury. He returned just in time to take over for Jones, who held down the fort while Mason was injured.

Jones left Sunday's game with a knee injury after ripping off a 17-yard run. He did not return.

ESPN's Kevin Seifert explained that Jones was already playing with a sprained left MCL before that injury. Hopefully Jones did not reaggravate that injury. It would be a shame if Minnesota lost their star running back after their undefeated start to the season.

Other notable injuries from Week 7 include Jets DT T'Vondre Sweat (knee), Saints safety Justin Reid (concussion), Texans WR Jaylin Noel (turf toe), and Lions CB Ennis Rakestraw Jr. (ankle).

Falcons rookie linebacker Kendal Daniels left the field on a stretcher last Sunday. A week later, he left the field a hero of the Falcons’ 29-20 upset of the previously undefeated 49ers.

“It’s been the craziest week of my life,” Daniels said, via Marc Raimondi of ESPN. “I’ve never not walked off the field after an injury. So, mentally, I had to be prepared and going back home and just making sure I was OK mentally more than anything and not playing timid, but I’ve never not gotten up from an injury. So, being stretched off the field -- I won’t let it happen again. It was a bad feeling, and I’m blessed to be able to play this week.”

Last week, Daniels dove to tackle Bears tight end Colston Loveland in the third quarter and Daniels’ head collided with Loveland’s left leg. Medical personnel attended to Daniels for almost 8 minutes before sending him to a local hospital for further evaluation of his neck.

On Sunday, Daniels iced the game with an interception of Brock Purdy. He also had nine solo tackles and a fumble recovery.

Coach Kevin Stefanski called it “remarkable.”

“I wasn’t thinking of [his neck injury],” Daniels said. “‘I think that was the last thing I was worried about was last week.”
