title: NFL Week 7 Lessons: Don't Be Fooled by the Steelers' Three-Game Winning Streak
description:
It’s still not time to believe in the Steelers I’ve been burned by the Steelers’ vortex of mediocrity a handful of times.
Don’t be fooled by Pittsburgh’s three-game winning streak, including Sunday’s victory over New Orleans.
That shouldn’t be enough to believe this will be the year the Steelers (5–2) end their seven-game playoff losing streak.
The Steelers won a 30–27 shootout against the Bengals in Week 3, then lost 27–24 to the Browns.
Perhaps Sheppard figured out what was wrong with his defense over the bye week because the unit looked different on Sunday.
text:
A few illusions might have developed from Sunday’s games.

The 49ers are no longer undefeated after losing 29–20 to the Falcons. Was this just a trap game, or is this the start of trouble for the injury-ravaged 49ers? It might be difficult to trust this team as a Super Bowl contender moving forward.

The Steelers are on a three-game winning streak after defeating the Saints, 16–10, in Paris, but it may be wise to hold off on saying this will be the year they’ll go far in the postseason. Should Pittsburgh get credit for beating up on three two-win teams?

Then there are the Rams, who got by the Raiders, 35–21. It was an impressive rushing performance, but was this a get-right game or just a one-week anomaly in Las Vegas?

Let’s break down a few of these potential illusions from the Week 7 schedule.

It’s still not time to believe in the Steelers

I’ve been burned by the Steelers’ vortex of mediocrity a handful of times. It’s a cycle that can look appealing at times, but it ended the same way for nearly a decade.

Don’t be fooled by Pittsburgh’s three-game winning streak, including Sunday’s victory over New Orleans. That shouldn’t be enough to believe this will be the year the Steelers (5–2) end their seven-game playoff losing streak.

Yes, there’s plenty to like about Pittsburgh’s positive stretch. The defense has been outstanding the past two weeks, and that unit was enough to overcome an up-and-down outing from Aaron Rodgers and his offense in the win over the Saints. (The Steelers only generated one touchdown and averaged 5.4 yards per gain.) Rodgers was better in the wins against the Colts and Buccaneers, but that’s three victories against a trio of teams that have two wins apiece.

It’s still tough to see the Steelers having enough firepower to hang with the AFC’s best in January. Pittsburgh prefers to slow down games because it has to with a 42-year-old Rodgers who occasionally has trouble getting the ball downfield to DK Metcalf (only two catches for 56 yards on Sunday). But they’re a well-balanced operation with underrated running back Jaylen Warren (18 carries, 101 yards). Additionally, the defense has turned a corner since the back-to-back rocky performances against divisional foes Cincinnati and Cleveland. The Steelers won a 30–27 shootout against the Bengals in Week 3, then lost 27–24 to the Browns.

If the game script goes their way, the Steelers are a tough out against most teams. However, the script hasn’t gone their way when it matters most, as evidenced by six one-and-done playoff appearances.

Pittsburgh has Cleveland and Cincinnati coming up again for its next two games. Perhaps I’ll start falling for the Steelers again if Rodgers outpaces Joe Burrow a second time and the defense shuts down the pesky Browns after the Week 4 loss during Thursday Night Football.

But for now, the Steelers’ three-game winning streak is misleading because they’ve faced three losing teams. Don’t trust them just yet.

49ers’ injury crisis continues to put damper on strong first half

It’s hard to get excited about what the 49ers have done during the first half of the season.

On one hand, they’re 6–1 with a sizable lead in the NFC West standings. On the other hand, the injuries haven’t stopped, and they finally lost a game, falling to the Falcons on Sunday.

It’s probably best to look at the full sample size here to not let one bad game in Atlanta diminish everything San Francisco has done for nearly two months. This is the best team in football, but this is also a team you can’t trust because of the injury waves.

Here’s a scenario we might be headed toward: the top-seeded 49ers being viewed as an underdog in a home playoff game because of several injuries to key players.

Heading into the Falcons game, concerns arose that the 49ers might not have enough healthy players to fill up the 48 game-day roster spots. They were without Mike Evans, Nick Bosa and Deebo Samuel Sr., and that doesn’t include the many players on injured reserve. On Sunday, San Francisco played for a stretch without Christian McCaffrey, who sustained a thigh injury.

I’ve already gone back and forth on my early assessment that the 49ers possibly not being true Super Bowl contenders because of all the injuries. Maybe this season has a ceiling, like last year, when this injury-ravaged team gassed out against the Seahawks in the divisional round.

For now, I’ll trust that the 49ers will get healthy at the right time, but that’s not a given with all the injury waves the past few seasons. San Francisco could afford to miss a few key players, but it needs Evans and McCaffrey to be true contenders in January.

Rams’ simplistic formula leads to bounce-back win in Las Vegas

Injuries forcing the Rams to simplify their operation could be a turning point in their season.

Coach Sean McVay called several running plays and ran the passing attack through Puka Nacua during a much-needed win over the Raiders. The Rams didn’t use flashy three-tight-end formations or forced plays to keep players involved.

The Rams (3–4) were physical and kept it simple, running the ball 38 times for a season-high 199 rushing yards against the Raiders. It was the first time since Week 1 that Matthew Stafford (23-of-29, 195 yards, 3 TDs, INT) didn’t record at least 30 passes, and the season opener doesn’t really count because Stafford didn’t finish the blowout loss against the 49ers. Stafford has already thrown over 50 passes in three games already this season.

The heavy passing attack is partly why Los Angeles only had two victories after six games. The Rams dug themselves a sizable hole in the standings without an identity on the field or a real voice to guide them through adversity, despite having a whopping 11 captains. It was as if McVay didn’t want to hurt anyone’s feelings and prioritized getting everyone involved.

But wide receiver Davante Adams, edge rusher Myles Garrett, tight end Terrance Ferguson and defensive tackles Poona Ford and Kobie Turner weren’t available for Sunday’s game in Las Vegas. The Rams also nearly didn’t have Nacua after he sustained a calf injury in practice earlier this week.

The Rams have plenty of talent, but they’re hard to beat with Nacua as the focal point of a well-balanced offense. McVay might also have finally found the formula for getting the most from his two running backs, Kyren Williams (16 carries, 99 yards, TD) and Blake Corum (17 carries, 93 yards, TD), the duo that combined for 192 rushing yards in Las Vegas.

If McVay continues to commit to the run, Williams and Corum will likely deliver more performances like that. This team might be close to finally forming an identity.

Lions’ defense finally shows improvements

It’s not surprising that the Lions defeated the Packers, 20–17. But few expected Detroit’s defense to stifle an offense that had been rolling for a few weeks and recently got back running back Josh Jacobs.

It was the kind of performance defensive coordinator Kelvin Sheppard had needed for a long time. It would have been difficult for coach Dan Campbell to continue defending him as his coordinator had Jordan Love lit up this suspect secondary. But Love (27-of-45, 274 yards, two TDs, INT) struggled to connect with emerging second-year wideout Matthew Golden (12 targets, six catches, 39 yards) and probably should have been picked off two or three times if Lions’ defenders hadn’t dropped balls.

Detroit (4–2) held Green Bay (4–3) to 324 yards and only 17 first downs. Perhaps Sheppard figured out what was wrong with his defense over the bye week because the unit looked different on Sunday. It also certainly helped that the team got back versatile safety Brian Branch, who registered an interception in his season debut.

Having a reliable defense would go a long way toward bolstering the Lions’ hopes of winning a competitive NFC North. Minnesota leads the division at 6–0, while Chicago sits in second at 5–2.

Broncos wide receiver Jaylen Waddle (chest) and defensive lineman Zach Allen (appeared to be hamstring) both went down with injuries in the fourth quarter. Waddle suffered his injury after falling on his own fumble on an end-around. After the game, coach Sean Payton called it a "dumb reverse call." Payton apologized for the "awful" call in his post-game press conference.

Waddle initially stayed down on the field before walking to the sideline and then into the locker room. He was previously limited in two days of practice last week with a chest injury. Denver announced Waddle as questionable to return, but he did not return to Sunday's game after totaling four catches for 48 yards prior to the injury.

Allen also went down in the fourth quarter and appeared to be favoring his right hamstring. After a visit to the team's blue medical tent, Allen was spotted standing on the sideline without his helmet for the end of the game. Allen went to the podium for a post-game press conference after the win and said, "Yeah, I'll be fine. Yeah, I'll be good," when asked about his injury.

Elsewhere on the injury front, cornerback Pat Surtain (ankle) missed his third straight game on Sunday and safety Talanoa Hufanga (ankle) sat out his second consecutive game. text:
Green Bay Packers linebacker Zaire Franklin is dealing with a hairline fracture in his leg, while center Sean Rhyan is believed to have suffered a high ankle sprain, sources told NFL Network's Ian Rapoport.

Rhyan left Sunday's loss to the Detroit Lions with an ankle injury. X-rays were negative, but he is expected to get an MRI on Monday. Rhyan would be expected to miss four to six weeks if imaging shows a high ankle sprain.

Not only did the Packers lose Rhyan after just four snaps against the Lions, but they also lost primary backup center Jacob Monk to a quad injury after five snaps. Second-year pro John Williams finished the game, playing the final 58 snaps of the game. Those were the first career regular-season snaps Williams has played on offense.

Coach Matt LaFleur said after the game he did not expect Rhyan or Monk to be available for Thursday's game against the Carolina Panthers.

Franklin suffered what LaFleur called a shin injury during a collision in practice last Thursday. On Friday, LaFleur said Franklin is not expected to go on injured reserve, meaning the team believes he will miss fewer than four games.

Although it's Franklin's first year with the Packers after coming to Green Bay in an offseason trade with the Indianapolis Colts, the ninth-year veteran quickly became a key part of the defense. He was elected defensive captain, rare for someone in the first year with a team, and has been the signal-caller for the defense.

Franklin ranks third on the team in tackles (41) and has two quarterback hits, a forced fumble and a pass breakup.

text:
The Detroit Lions secured a massive divisional win over the Green Bay Packers on Sunday.

Playing their first divisional opponent of the season, the Lions overcame some mistakes and were ultimately able to earn a hard-fought 20-17 victory over the Packers to advance to 4-2 on the season.

Running back Jahmyr Gibbs played a pivotal part in the victory, notchng 116 rushing yards on 29 carries. The dynamic running back played a key part on the final drive, as he converted the final third-down to cement the win.

On that game-sealing run, however, Gibbs landed awkwardly trying to slide onto the turf inbounds to keep the clock running and prevent the Packers from getting the ball back. Though the landing wasn't smooth, head coach Dan Campbell stated that he should be okay during his postgame press conference.

"We got him checked. He should be good. That's that whole, is it really worth going down?" Campbell said. "Or should he just go score? Sometimes I question that. Maybe he should've just (scored). But, all good. That's a good win."

Gibbs had slid to the turf two plays prior, on first-down, two yards short of the chains. This was done in an effort to maintain the running clock, but it nearly backfired after the Lions jumped resulting in a five-yard penalty.

However, on third-and-6, quarterback Jared Goff pitched the ball to Gibbs who burst around the left side before sliding after getting the first down. This allowed the Lions to run the clock all the way down to one second before taking a timeout to set up Jake Bates' game-winning field goal.

Campbell's update is a sigh of relief for Detroit, as Gibbs is one of the team's most dynamic talents and one of the league's best running backs. Signed to a three-year contract extension in the offseason, the Alabama product is off to another strong start through six games in 2026.

Detroit's offseason saw the team deal David Montgomery, who was Gibbs' counterpart in the backfield, to the Houston Texans and cement Gibbs as their top running back moving forward. This has come with an increased workload for him, as he has had at least 20 touches in five of the team's six games.

Up to this point, Gibbs has notched 620 rushing yards and nine total touchdowns, with seven on the ground and two as a receiver. Sunday's game against the Packers marked the first one this year where Gibbs was kept out of the end-zone.

title: NFL fans want injury answers fast. A Broncos doctor explains why it takes time
description:
Inside the injury process When a player gets injured during an NFL game, Mates described the initial evaluation area on the sideline as a triage tent, similar to an emergency room.
Medical personnel first assess the injury and determine whether the player can safely return or needs additional evaluation.
Depending on the injury, the process can continue after the game with further examinations and imaging to determine the appropriate treatment.
With professional athletes facing a limited competitive window, physicians sometimes must consider treatment options more quickly than they might in other circumstances.
The road back For athletes recovering from surgery or an injury, Mates described a three-phase process designed to gradually prepare them for competition.
text:
When an NFL player goes down with an injury, the questions come quickly.

What happened? How serious is it? And, perhaps most importantly, how long will he be out?

But according to Denver Broncos team physician and orthopedic surgeon Dr. Aaron Mates, the answers aren’t always as straightforward as fans and analysts might suggest.

Mates, who has worked with professional athletes across the NFL, MLB, NHL and other sports, said the evaluation process involves multiple medical professionals, diagnostic testing and a gradual determination of when an athlete can safely return to activity.

And one of the biggest misconceptions, he said, is that medical clearance automatically means a player is ready to go back out and compete.

“It’s when you say, ‘OK, from a medical standpoint, this player, this patient is fit to progress back toward activity,’” Mates said. “So it doesn’t mean you play tomorrow night.”

Instead, clearance marks the beginning of a progression that can take an athlete from rehabilitation to conditioning, practice and eventually a return to competition.

Inside the injury process

When a player gets injured during an NFL game, Mates described the initial evaluation area on the sideline as a triage tent, similar to an emergency room.

Medical personnel first assess the injury and determine whether the player can safely return or needs additional evaluation.

If further examination is necessary, the player may be taken to the training room for X-rays, additional testing and a more thorough assessment. Depending on the injury, the process can continue after the game with further examinations and imaging to determine the appropriate treatment.

The evaluation involves the head team physician, specialists such as Mates, athletic trainers and the player.

While the medical staff determines whether a return is safe, Mates emphasized that the athlete remains central to the decision-making process.

“Their voice is everything, because they’re the patient,” he said. “It’s no different than being in my clinic, it’s a doctor-patient relationship.”

Physicians must ensure players understand their injuries and treatment options, but they also have the responsibility to prevent an athlete from returning when doing so would be unsafe.

“We can say, ‘You can’t play,’” Mates said. “We can say, ‘This is not safe. We’re not clearing you.’”

That responsibility can become especially complicated when an injury occurs during the season, when teams are competing for a playoff spot or trying to make a postseason run.

Mates said the challenge of sports medicine isn’t necessarily the orthopedic treatment itself, but determining how the timing of an injury affects its management.

With professional athletes facing a limited competitive window, physicians sometimes must consider treatment options more quickly than they might in other circumstances.

“We can’t sit around and wait for something to heal for three months and it doesn’t heal, then do surgery,” he said.

The road back

For athletes recovering from surgery or an injury, Mates described a three-phase process designed to gradually prepare them for competition.

The first phase focuses on rehabilitation and recovery, including physical therapy and regaining strength and mobility.

The second phase shifts toward general conditioning, with activities such as running, jumping, balance work and changes in direction.

The third phase involves returning to the sport itself, including practice, sport-specific drills and simulated game situations.

For example, Mates mentioned he has treated hockey players who must complete land-based drills involving cutting, running and turning before he allows them to put on skates.

Football players follow a similar progression, working with trainers and conditioning staff before advancing toward full practice and game participation.

The goal is to ensure athletes can handle the demands of their sport rather than simply demonstrate that an injury has improved in a controlled medical setting.

The limits of injury reports

Another challenge for doctors comes from the speculation that often follows an injury.

Mates noted he has watched television coverage of athletes he has treated and heard injury assessments that were inaccurate, particularly when commentators attempt to identify an injury from video footage and predict a recovery timeline.

“I can’t tell you how many times I’ve been involved with an athlete who’s been injured, and then flip on whatever, ESPN or whatever, ‘SportsCenter,’ OutKick or whatever, and what they’re saying is completely wrong,” Mates said. “Or they’ll have a so-called specialist talking about what the guy saw on the video during the play, and what that injury is and what the recovery is and all these kind of things, and they’re completely wrong.”

He added that the public generally receives only the information a player and team choose to release because physicians must adhere to HIPAA rules.

That can leave fans with unanswered questions, especially when an injury report uses broad designations such as “day-to-day,” “week-to-week” or “questionable.”

Those labels don’t necessarily provide enough information to determine the severity of an injury or how close a player is to returning.

The uncertainty can become even more pronounced as sports betting increases interest in player availability and injury updates from the moment they happen.

For Mates, the distinction between public speculation and an actual medical evaluation is important: A diagnosis and recovery estimate require more information than what viewers can see during a play.

Advances in sports medicine

Despite concerns about injuries across professional sports, Mates said determining whether injuries are becoming more common requires looking beyond individual cases.

Researchers track injury data across leagues, helping inform safety protocols and rule changes. At the same time, modern athletes are faster and more athletic, potentially changing the physical demands placed on their bodies.

Mates noted advances in surgical techniques, rehabilitation, conditioning and nutrition have also helped change how athletes recover.

“The way we fix Achilles now is not how we did it 15 years ago,” he said. “There’s biological adjuvants, there’s rehab protocols, there’s constantly literature coming out. ... It’s the same across orthopedics. So if you got your knee replaced in 2026, it’s very different than 2010. Now we’re using robots for alignment and placement, back then it was just kind of manual guides.”

Mates also works with emerging treatments and biologic approaches, including platelet-rich plasma and cartilage repair techniques, as part of a broader effort to advance orthopedic care.

He mentioned experience treating elite athletes can help physicians develop approaches that eventually benefit patients outside professional sports.

Ultimately, Mates said, the priority remains the same regardless of the athlete or level of competition: making sure the patient is safe and healthy.

“We’re doctors, not fans,” he said. “So we need to keep that separation.”

text:
There wasn’t much to celebrate after the Kansas City Chiefs’ 20-3 loss to the Seattle Seahawks, but the injury situation might actually be one of those things.

The team was missing several pieces in Week 7, with Tyquan Thornton, Rashee Rice, Jaylon Moore, and Josh Simmons among the injured starters. Another starter on defense got banged up during the game, but his injury doesn’t appear to be anything serious.

“There’s not really any injuries to mention,” Reid said, before mentioning the lone injury. ” Nick (Bolton) had some spasms in his neck, and he’ll work through that and be OK.”

Bolton played some inspired run defense against the Seahawks on Sunday, leading the team with six solo stops, 11 combined tackles, and a tackle for loss. He was dinged in the third quarter, missing just a single snap. Bolton returned to the game and made a play that forced a Seattle field goal, extending the lead to 13. He was staggered a bit later in the second half, but didn’t leave the game.

The good news is that Bolton doesn’t appear to be at any risk of missing time. He’s been a force on defense this year and remains the team’s green dot and defensive play-caller.

The Chiefs should be healthier when they face the Broncos in Week 8

The Chiefs will look to bounce back against an AFC West rival in Week 8. It won’t be easy as they travel to Mile High Stadium to face the Denver Broncos, but the team should be healthier for this game.

Jaylon Moore will have a chance to clear the NFL’s concussion protocol during practice this week. They need him at right tackle for this one because Joshua Ezeudu struggled in his first start. It won’t be any easier facing Jonathon Cooper and Nik Bonitto next Sunday.

Similarly, the Chiefs’ receivers struggled to create separation in Week 7’s loss to Seattle. Rashee Rice isn’t exactly a burner at wide receiver. However, he’s another trusted target who can help open things up in the passing game for Kansas City. Rice is several weeks removed from the initial hamstring injury. He should realistically be able to return to the practice field in some capacity next Wednesday.

The injury bug is taking another chunk out of the San Francisco 49ers.

In what was the latest issue for the injury-riddled Niners, star running back Christian McCaffrey exited the team's Week 7 contest with a thigh ailment.

He was seen on the sideline and taken inside the medical tent. Broadcast cameras also showed the running back getting his left leg worked on.

McCaffrey missed an extended period of time in the first half, and his return was questionable.

It is just the latest injury issue for the Niners, who came into Week 7 without Mike Evans and plenty of other key pieces across the roster.

With a bye week looming in Week 8, San Francisco chose to be cautious with Evans. It remains to be seen how they will proceed with the star running back, who is the key to the Kyle Shanahan offense.

Here's the latest on McCaffrey.

Christian McCaffrey injury update

McCaffrey returned to the game to start the second half.

He warmed up during halftime and was spotted riding the stationary bike on the sideline prior to the start of the third quarter.

McCaffrey was seen jogging back to the locker room with 6:14 remaining in the first half. He didn't have a noticeable limp, but was listed as questionable to return with a thigh injury, the team announced.

The running back was seen getting his leg worked on by the training staff late in the first quarter against the Falcons in Week 7. In his absence, Kaelon Black handled the workload out of the San Francisco backfield. He burst through the defense for a 30-yard rushing touchdown to extend the Niners lead to begin the second quarter.

Jordan James is next in line behind Black on the depth chart.

"It sucks because I feel like I was going on a run there," McCaffrey said after the game. "My leg just died on me, just tried to get it going for the whole rest of the game. It just sucks having to play like that. I know I'll be alright, but it's just really frustrating."

text:
With six weeks still remaining between now and what could be the final weekend ever of NCAA conference championships, so many schools still have plenty to play for, but one player will be shifting their focus to the 2027 NFL Draft a little earlier than expected. According to ESPN’s Pete Thamel, top offensive tackle prospect Trevor Goosby suffered a knee injury this weekend and will miss the rest of his senior season, as a result.

Originally a three-star offensive tackle recruit out of Melissa HS (TX), Goosby’s first offers came from smaller schools like UT-San Antonio and nearby North Texas. He began getting interest and offers from some Power conference schools like Kansas and Oklahoma State, and near the end of his junior year, Goosby committed to a close-to-home Power 5 option in TCU. Early into the summer, though, the Longhorns came calling and floated him an offer. He scheduled an official visit for two weeks later, and at the end of the three-day courting ritual, he flipped his commitment to Texas.

Goosby had a lot of work to do once he arrived in Austin. He only made two game appearances as a true freshman and only saw garbage-time snaps and special teams work for most of his sophomore campaign, sitting behind future first-round pick Kelvin Banks Jr. Late in the season, though, Banks exited a rivalry game against Texas A&M early with an injury, and Goosby was tapped to fill in,. He would be asked to start at left tackle for the team’s conference championship against Georgia, as well.

In the College Football Playoff, Goosby filled in for another future NFL draft pick in right tackle Cameron Williams after Williams exited the school’s first-round game against Clemson with an injury. He started at right tackle for the Longhorns’ two last playoff games against Arizona State and Ohio State before getting eliminated.

Having proven he could handle work on the first-team offense under the brightest of lights, Goosby opened up his third year in Austin as the starting left tackle, and he’s held the role ever since. He earned first-team All-SEC honors in his first season as a full-time starter, and as the blindside blocker for the player many predicted might be the No. 1 overall pick of the 2027 NFL Draft, Goosby came into the 2026 campaign billed as a likely Day 1 pick himself.

ESPN’s Jordan Reid ranked Goosby as the fourth-best offensive tackle prospect and the 30th-best prospect overall just over a week ago. Pro Football Focus (subscription required) reset their big board three weeks ago, and Goosby checked in as the top overall offensive line prospect and the seventh-best prospect in the class. Listed by the school at 6-foot-7 and 325 pounds, the 21-year-old boasts elite size without sacrificing any athleticism or movement.

Goosby came into the season surrounded by expectations that he would become one of the first offensive lineman taken in the draft. He was sure to have challengers, though, as Texas stumbled recently, losing two games in a row, before returning to the win column this weekend.

Now, both Goosby and his team will have new challenges to confront. The Longhorns will look to stay alive in competition for a spot in the 12-team College Football Playoff, and Goosby will need to work his way back to full health. The injury will almost certainly impact his draft stock, and he could always choose to return to school if it damages his prospects too much. Until a clearer picture and timeline are produced, though, it’s difficult to determine how severe the impact will be.

12 hours ago

12:22 PM EDT

Bo Knows Sleepers?

AP Photo/Gregory Bull

OK, so starting Bo Nix in Week 7 straddles the line between brave and dumb--the Broncos quarterback has been dreadful in recent weeks.

But as Raza Umerani wrote at NFL.com, if ever there was a week for Nix to get going, this is it.

"Arizona is allowing 0.65 fantasy points per dropback this year, which is the highest mark since at least 2016," he said. "The Cardinals also have faced 9.2 air yards per attempt, the fifth-most in the league, and haven't been very good against downfield throws (10+ air yards), with the fifth-most yards per attempt allowed at 12.5 and nine touchdowns surrendered, only trailing the Commanders' 11. If there were ever a time to Bo-lieve, it's now."

Do you Bo-lieve?

12:08 PM EDT

Fantasy Football in a Nutshell

I love this hobby.

Whether it loves us back is another matter altogether.

13 hours ago

12:00 PM EDT

To Be Fair

Who hasn't outscored Omarion Hampton this year?

Sorry. That was mean.

True. But mean.

13 hours ago

11:51 AM EDT

Trust But Verify

It's understandable that fantasy managers want to believe that Philadelphia Eagles running back Saquon Barkley will return in Week 7.

But with Philly playing on Monday night, those without Dameon Pierce or another pivot are risking the dreaded donut.

One possibility? Flex Barkley and pick up Eagles wideout Darius Cooper, who could see a bump in targets with DeVonta Smith ruled out.

13 hours ago

11:45 AM EDT

Mr. Jones and Me

AP Photo/Bailey Hillesheim

Six weeks into the season, Minnesota Vikings running back Aaron Jones Sr. is RB18 in PPR points per game. The Vikings face an Indianapolis Colts defense Sunday allowing the seventh-most PPR points per game to running backs in 2026.

But with Jordan Mason active, workload concerns both sap some of Jones' upside and adds risk to starting him as a RB2.

What? You want things to be easy?

13 hours ago

11:34 AM EDT

Status Report

No big surprises here.

It will be interesting to see how Mason's return impacts the workload split in Minnesota.

13 hours ago

11:32 AM EDT

Bam Goes the Dynamite

After 17 touches for 98 total yards last week against the Rams, Arizona Cardinals running back Bam Knight is expected to once again see a heavy workload against the Denver Broncos with Jeremiyah Love (ankle) out.

The Broncos have been a plus matchup for opposing backs this year--fantasy managers in a pinch in the backfield could do worse in Week 7.

13 hours ago

11:22 AM EDT

Bust Alert

Sure, Quinshon Judkins is off the Week 7 injury report and will face the Tennessee Titans Sunday.

But with Dylan Sampson set to return from injured reserve Judkins is going to lose passing-down work, and he's been ineffective as a runner this season, averaging just 3.0 yards per carry.

Judkins is a low-ceiling RB2 in Week 7--at best.

13 hours ago

11:13 AM EDT

Free BTJ!

The notion of Jacksonville Jaguars wide receiver Brian Thomas Jr. being traded might not help fantasy managers now. But if there's a path to Thomas actually having some fantasy value over the second half, then it likely lies on another team.

13 hours ago

11:08 AM EDT

Gotta Love It

AP Photo/Melissa Tamez

The last time that Green Bay Packers quarterback Jordan Love played at Ford Field, he threw for 234 yards and four touchdowns.

In 2026, the Lions are dead last in pass defense at 297.4 yards per game, and no team has surrendered more fantasy points per game to quarterbacks.

Get where we're going with this?

14 hours ago

10:53 AM EDT

Sleeper Alert

AP Photo/Kin Cheung

Yes, Houston Texans wide receiver Jaylin Noel isn't a full-time player--he saw just a 49 percent snap share in Week 6.

But that lack of snaps didn't stop Noel from reeling in four passes for 107 yards and a touchdown in London last week, and Noel has posted at least 11.5 PPR points in each of the last three games.

14 hours ago

10:39 AM EDT

Mr. Rodgers' Neighborhood

This long bomb to DK Metcalf was followed by a touchdown pass to tight end Darnell Washington--the 540th of Aaron Rodgers' career.

Rodgers has 120 yards and a score in about a quarter and a half, continuing what has been arguably his best season since he last won MVP in 2021.

14 hours ago

10:33 AM EDT

A Muddied Mess

This isn't to say that fantasy managers can't trust any Giants running back in Week 7.

Actually, that's exactly what it means.

Just stay away from this mess altogether if possible.

14 hours ago

10:29 AM EDT

Hitting the Mark(s)

Last week against the Jacksonville Jaguars, Houston Texans running back Woody Marks had 17 touches for 81 total yards. It was the second straight week Marks had at least 15 touches and 80 scrimmage yards.

Look for another hefty workload Sunday against a New York Giants defense allowing just under 22 PPR points per game to the running back position this year.

14 hours ago

10:20 AM EDT

Bust Alert

AP Photo/Reed Hoffmann

Sitting Kansas City Chiefs tight end Travis Kelce isn't an option for most fantasy managers.

But after a hot start to the season, Kelce has cooled off of late, and Sunday in Seattle he faces a stingy Seahawks defense allowing the third-fewest PPR points per game to tight ends this year.

14 hours ago

10:06 AM EDT

Happy National Tight Ends Day

It's fitting given that this whole "holiday" was invented by George Kittle of the San Francisco 49ers that Kittle is in a potential smash spot in Week 7 against the Falcons.

Kittle should see a boatload of targets Sunday given that he's the only pass-catcher for the Niners who is still ambulatory.

15 hours ago

10:00 AM EDT

Raiders RB Mike Washington Jr. a Game-Time Decision

With rookie running back Mike Washington looking like a true game-time decision Sunday afternoon against the Los Angeles Raiders, Ashton Jeanty could be in for a heavy workload in Week 7.

The larger question is whether Jeanty can do anything with those touches after averaging a woeful 3.2 yards per carry so far this season.

15 hours ago

09:51 AM EDT

Sleeper Alert

AP Photo

The Tampa Bay Buccaneers will get quarterback Baker Mayfield back for Sunday's tilt with the Carolina Panthers. But the team will be without the services of top wide receiver Emeka Egbuka, who is in the concussion protocol.

That could mean an increase in target share for rookie wideout Ted Hurst, who showed some rapport with Mayfield before the latter injured his thumb.

15 hours ago

09:42 AM EDT

Full Workload for Josh Jacobs

Normally, one might expect the Green Bay Packers to ease Josh Jacobs in in his first game action of the season. After all, Jacobs has barely practiced and hasn't played a game this season.

But when you're averaging less than three yards a carry and under 60 yards a game on the ground as a team, "eased in" goes out the window.

Jacobs isn't without risk, but he's on the RB2 radar in Week 7.

15 hours ago

09:30 AM EDT

Puka Nacua Update

More than a few fantasy managers are antsy this week about the playing status of Los Angeles Rams wide receiver Puka Nacua, who is nursing a calf injury.

It sounds like Nacua is going to give it a go, but fantasy managers need a late-game pivot like Konata Mumpfield of the Rams, Tre Tucker of the Raiders or Cooper Kupp of the Seahawks (in a pinch) at the ready.

15 hours ago

09:22 AM EDT

Jonah Coleman's Return Muddies Broncos Backfield

AP Photo/David Zalubowski

After sitting out four games with an ankle injury, Denver Broncos running back Jonah Coleman has been activated off injured reserve and will play Sunday against the Arizona Cardinals.

JK Dobbins has been woeful as the team's lead back, averaging just 3.3 yards per carry. Coleman should eat into Dobbins' workload, with RJ Harvey maintaining his pass-catching role.

Because we didn't have enough murky backfields.

15 hours ago

09:15 AM EDT

49ers Activate WR Christian Kirk from IR

With both Mike Evans (Achilles) and Deebo Samuel Sr. (hamstring) ruled out for Week 7, the Niners need bodies at wide receiver.

The team is getting at least one player back--Christian Kirk is expected to play Sunday against the Atlanta Falcons.

The question is how much Kirk will play in his first game action of the season. But he's at least on the desperation "flex" radar.

15 hours ago

09:06 AM EDT

Giants RB Cam Skattebo to Resume Lead Back Duties

After a grand total of zero touches last week against the Saints, Cam Skattebo is expected to resume lead back duties Sunday against the Houston Texans.

With that said, Tyrone Tracy and Devin Singletary are going to mix in as well, and muddied backfields tend to make fantasy managers miserable.

Skattebo is a boom/bust RB2--at best.

text:
Denver Broncos wide receiver Jaylen Waddle slowly left the field and went into the team's blue medical tent after a botched end-around run in the fourth quarter of Sunday's game against the Arizona Cardinals.

After Waddle bubbled and fell on a toss from quarterback Bo Nix for a 12-yard loss, the receiver stayed down on the field and was tended to by the team's medical staff. He eventually was able to walk off the field and seemed to be favoring his left shoulder/chest area. Waddle was limited with a chest injury at two practices last week.

Susie Wargin reported that Waddle is questionable to return to the game with a chest injury.

Before leaving the game, Waddle totaled four catches for 48 yards on seven targets. After being evaluated in the medical tent, Waddle walked into the locker room with staff members.

The play that injured Jaylen Waddle

Elsewhere on the injury front, Broncos defensive lineman Malcolm Roach was evaluated for a possible concussion in the fourth quarter. Roach was cleared to return to the game.

Later in the fourth, defensive lineman Zach Allen went down favoring his right hamstring. Allen was eventually able to walk off the field and went into the team's blue medical tent. After a 30-16 win, Allen said "I'll be fine" in his post-game press conference.
